proof_steps.claim: The explicit incidence chart fixes vertical complex orientation followed by the positive base orientation to be the complex orientation of Z. The pullback of the positive point Thom class on S⁴ is the positive normal Thom class of its fiber CP¹; [F5] identifies its absolute class as the Poincaré dual of that fiber. A linear CP¹ has dual H²: H restricts with integral one to the line, and the integral projective cohomology ring gives H² as its positive degree-four generator. Hence π*u=H² for the positive generator u of H⁴(S⁴). Smooth evaluation gives E_twistor≅π*H, so c₂(E_twistor)=kH² is equivalent to c₂(H)[S⁴]=k. By [F4] this is q_N=-k; the same calculation verifies the forward map's charge clause. Framing is transported by evaluation at infinity. final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F4] $SU(N)$ is path connected, $\pi_1(SU(N))=\pi_2(SU(N))=0$, and $\pi_3(SU(N))\cong\mathbb Z$. [[lem-qftx-low-unitary-homotopy-inputs]]

proof_steps.claim:
Suppose $r=3$. By [F3, F4], $\pi_0(\mathcal G_m(P))\cong\pi_3(SU(N))\cong\mathbb Z$. The evaluation LES [F2, F6] has the component segment
$$\pi_1(SU(N))\longrightarrow\pi_0(\mathcal G_m(P))\longrightarrow\pi_0(\mathcal G(P))\longrightarrow\pi_0(SU(N)).$$
The outer terms are one-point sets by [F4]. The induced map on components is surjective by exactness, and its fibers are the orbits of $\pi_1(SU(N))$ on $\pi_0(\mathcal G_m(P))$ in the action clause of [F6]. That acting group is trivial, so each fiber is a singleton and the middle map is a bijection. Thus $\mathcal G(P)$ has infinitely many components. Since $\mathcal G(P)\to\overline{\mathcal G}(P)$ is a covering with $N$ sheets, components downstairs correspond to orbits of the finite deck group on components upstairs: a path downstairs lifts by [F7] to a path whose endpoint differs from its starting lift by one deck transformation, and each deck orbit is therefore one quotient component. Each orbit has at most $N$ elements, so infinitely many components remain.

Suppose $r=4$. By [F3] and [F5], $\pi_1(\mathcal G_m(P))\cong\pi_5(SU(N))\ne0$. In the evaluation LES, the map $\pi_1(\mathcal G_m(P))\to\pi_1(\mathcal G(P))$ has preceding term $\pi_2(SU(N))=0$ by [F4]; exactness makes it injective. The finite covering in [F2] induces an injection $\pi_1(\mathcal G(P))\hookrightarrow\pi_1(\overline{\mathcal G}(P))$ by [F6]. Hence $\pi_1(\overline{\mathcal G}(P))$ contains a nonzero subgroup. The two cases establish the statement for every $r,N,P$.

proof_steps.claim: Write $F_i=F_i^++F_i^-$ with $*_{g_X}F_i^+=F_i^+$ and $*_{g_X}F_i^-=-F_i^-$. Let $a=\int_X B(F_i^+\wedge *_{g_X}F_i^+)$ and $b=\int_X B(F_i^-\wedge *_{g_X}F_i^-)$. Orthogonality of the two Hodge eigenspaces [F3] makes the cross terms vanish; positivity of $B$ [F2] gives $a,b\geq0$. Consequently $\int_XB(F_i\wedge *_{g_X}F_i)=a+b$, while $\int_XB(F_i\wedge F_i)=a-b$. By [F1], $S_B=(a+b)/g^2$ and $q_B=(a-b)/(8\pi^2)$.

For nonnegative $a,b$, $a+b\geq|a-b|$, so the claimed bound follows after division by $g^2>0$. If $q_B>0$, then $a>b$ and equality is equivalent to $b=0$. Its integrand is the continuous nonnegative squared norm of $F_i^-$; if $F_i^-$ were nonzero at a point, it would be bounded away from zero on a neighborhood of positive Riemannian volume, contradicting $b=0$. Thus $F_i^-=0$. If $q_B<0$, equality in $a+b\geq b-a$ is equivalent to $a=0$; the same continuity and positivity argument gives $F_i^+=0$. If $q_B=0$, equality forces $a+b=0$, so nonnegativity gives $a=b=0$ and both components vanish, hence $F_i=0$. Conversely each of the three stated conditions makes its corresponding norm vanish and gives equality.

fact_uses.text: [F2] *Faithful closed embeddings.* Every complex affine algebraic group admits a finite-dimensional rational representation whose comorphism is surjective; the induced morphism $G\to GL(V)$ is a closed immersion, so $G$ is isomorphic to a closed subgroup scheme of $GL(V)$ ([[lem-affine-algebraic-group-faithful-rational-representation]]).

proof_steps.claim: Treat first connected $G$. By [F2] identify $G$ with a closed algebraic subgroup of $GL(W)$ in a faithful finite-dimensional rational representation. Smoothness [F3] and the Jacobian and holomorphic charts [F16] make $G(\mathbb C)$ a complex manifold. Regular multiplication, inversion and representation maps are holomorphic in these charts, so it is a complex Lie subgroup of $GL(W)$ with complex tangent algebra $\mathfrak g=T_eG\subseteq\operatorname{End}(W)$; differentiation preserves brackets by [F18]. Its underlying real Lie group is the closed embedded subgroup of [F5], by uniqueness there. Exponential naturality [F17] and [F4] imply $\exp(tX)\in G(\mathbb C)$ for $X\in\mathfrak g$ and $t\in\mathbb C$ (apply the real assertion to $tX$). These curves are analytic; no algebraicity of $t\mapsto\exp(tX)$ is asserted except when $X$ is nilpotent.

The converse recorded in the definition also holds, without using the omitted compact-existence direction. If every finite-dimensional rational $G$-module is completely reducible and $U\subseteq G$ is a closed normal unipotent subgroup, take a faithful finite-dimensional module $W$ from [F2] and a simple submodule $S\subseteq W$; by the fixed-vector definition of unipotence $S^U\neq0$, and $S^U$ is $G$-stable because $U$ is normal, so $S^U=S$ by simplicity and $U$ fixes every simple summand of $W$, hence all of $W$; faithfulness forces $U=1$. Thus linearly reductive implies reductive. Closed subgroups of a fixed-vector unipotent group $U$ are again unipotent, as follows. A faithful finite-dimensional module for $U$ from [F2] has a complete flag with trivial successive characters, by iterating the fixed-vector condition on its quotients, so $U$ is a closed subgroup of an upper unitriangular matrix group. For a closed subgroup $H\subseteq U$ and $h\in H$, the nilpotent matrix $\log h$ is a finite polynomial in $h-1$ and $t\mapsto\exp(t\log h)$ is polynomial. Every defining equation of $H$ vanishes on this curve at all nonnegative integers because these values are $h^n$, so it vanishes identically; the curve lies in $H$ and joins $1$ to $h$. Thus $H$ is connected. The Lie algebra of $H$ is strictly upper triangular, hence solvable. For any nonzero rational $H$-module, [F6] gives a Lie-invariant complete flag, which is $H$-invariant by step 2.1. Its diagonal characters are trivial on each curve $\exp(t\log h)$: an algebraic homomorphism $\mathbb G_a\to\mathbb G_m$ has polynomial coordinate and polynomial inverse, so is constant. Since every $h\in H$ lies on such a curve, the first flag line is fixed by $H$, proving the hereditary assertion. For the identity-component reductions: $G$ is reductive if and only if $G^\circ$ is by the conjugate-product argument of step 7.1 in one direction. For the other direction, if $G^\circ$ is reductive and $U$ is a normal unipotent subgroup of $G$, then $U\cap G^\circ=1$, so $U$ embeds in the finite group $G/G^\circ$. A nontrivial finite group over $\mathbb C$ is not unipotent: its regular representation has the nonzero augmentation submodule, on which the only possible invariant vectors are multiples of the sum of all basis vectors, and none has augmentation zero in characteristic zero. Hence $U=1$; $G$ is linearly reductive if and only if $G^\circ$ is, the forward direction by the implication linearly reductive $G\Rightarrow$ reductive $G\Rightarrow$ reductive $G^\circ$ proved above, followed by step 6.1 and the reverse by the finite averaging of step 7.1. Moreover smoothness makes the irreducible components of $G$ disjoint, so they are the connected components and the cosets of $G^\circ$; there are finitely many of them.

Assembling the clauses: (i) is step 6.1 for connected $G$ and step 7.1 for general reductive $G$, together with the converse implication proved in step 9.1; (ii) and (iii) are step 8.1; (iv) is step 9.2, whose hypothesis on $K$ is part of the clause and whose proof does not assert the existence of such a $K$; and the identity-component and converse statements recorded in the definition are step 9.1. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the named suppliers: the faithful embedding, smoothness and integrality inputs enter in steps 1.1 and 2.1, the Lie inputs and Weyl's theorem in steps 2.2-7.1, the sum-of-simples characterisation in step 8.1, the faithful module in step 9.1, and the Haar measure and compact complete reducibility in step 9.2. This proves all four clauses.

proof_steps.claim: The transformation $\phi\mapsto-\phi$ sends $\partial_\mu\phi\mapsto-\partial_\mu\phi$, so $S_0$, $S_6$, the current $\phi^3\partial^\mu\phi$, and the density $\phi^3(\Box-m^2)\phi$ are even. In Bilal's Hermitian convention [A1], $\mathscr A=-B$ and $\epsilon=-\alpha$. The linear evaluation $E^4_{0,\alpha}$ of [F3], with component rule $sB_\mu=\partial_\mu\eta$, gives the same infinitesimal four-form variation as [F1]; in Bilal's anti-Hermitian variables this is $-i\mathscr A=iB$ and $-i\epsilon=i\alpha$, matching the product-group charge-one connection. For the positive-chirality $SU(3)$ singlet of $U(1)_V$ charge one in [F3], $\operatorname{tr}_R(1)=1$ and $d(\mathscr A\wedge d\mathscr A)=d(B\wedge G)=G\wedge G$; the Abelian cubic term vanishes. Therefore $\delta_\alpha\Gamma_H=+\frac{1}{24\pi^2}\int_M\alpha G\wedge G=\mathcal A_H(\alpha,B)$. The neutral opposite-chirality partner contributes zero $U(1)_V$ cubic charge.

Vary the displayed local functional: $\delta_\alpha\Gamma_{\mathrm{WZ}}=-\frac{1}{24\pi^2}\int_M((\delta_\alpha\theta)G\wedge G+\theta\,\delta_\alpha(G\wedge G))=+\frac{1}{24\pi^2}\int_M\alpha G\wedge G=\mathcal A_H(\alpha,B)$ by step 1.1 and step 1.2.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F1] [[def-aqft-scheme-and-wilson-coefficients]]: each EFT coefficient vector lies in a finite complex coordinate space whose realification is isometric to a finite-dimensional real space; its logarithmic-scale trajectory solves the supplied realified beta-vector equation.

proof_steps.claim: Let $x_+(t)=\Phi_+(t,t_i)x_i$ and set $y(t)=\widehat M_t(x_+(t))$. The chain rule and [A2] give $y'(t)=\partial_t\widehat M_t(x_+(t))+D_x\widehat M_t(x_+(t))\,\beta_+(t,x_+(t))=\beta_-(t,y(t))$ for every $t\in K$. Thus $y$ is a low-energy RG trajectory on the whole common interval.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F4] [[def-aqft-chiral-power-counting]]: the HEFT chiral/loop grading is separate from canonical dimension, and its retained NLO classes may have arbitrary smooth functions of $h/v$; no identity with a finite SMEFT dimension truncation is part of that definition.

proof_steps.claim: The finite starting list is selected by canonical dimension in [F3], whereas [F4] defines a separate chiral/loop grading and allows arbitrary smooth radial functions. No step identifies those gradings or their operator lists. The construction used only the nonzero-doublet diffeomorphism and finite substitutions; it supplies neither a value at $H=0$ nor an inverse map from arbitrary HEFT data, a compact-to-algebraic invariant-space equality, or a UV-completion theorem.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F1] [[def-aqft-susy-wilsonian-action]]: the high- and low-energy actions use smooth classical N=1 chiral fields and a derivative-free holomorphic F-term, with real D-term data kept separate; all Wilsonian, renormalization, threshold, external-energy, regulator, and operator-suppression scales are supplied independently.

proof_steps.claim: Vary the terms depending on $X$ using the normalized physical action brackets in [F1]. At fixed chiral coordinates, $P_{\mathrm{raw}}=\partial^L_{\bar\theta^{\dot2}}\partial^L_{\bar\theta^{\dot1}}|_{\bar\theta=0}$ extracts the top barred coefficient, so $I_D(U)=I_F(P_{\mathrm{raw}}U)$ up to the spacetime total derivatives removed by [A3]. Since $[U]_D=-I_D(U)/4$ and $[Y]_F=I_F(Y)/2$, the physical transfer is $[U]_D=[P_{\mathrm{phys}}U]_F$ with $P_{\mathrm{phys}}=-P_{\mathrm{raw}}/2=+\bar D^{\dot\alpha}\bar D_{\dot\alpha}/4$. This is equivalently the minus-one-quarter formula with LOWER-FIRST contraction $\bar D_{\dot\alpha}\bar D^{\dot\alpha}$. Chirality annihilates the barred derivatives of the even variation $\delta X$, so the D variation is $[\delta X P_{\mathrm{phys}}(X^\dagger)]_F$. The superpotential variation is $[\delta X(MX+J)]_F$. Thus the physical chiral Euler equation is $P_{\mathrm{phys}}(X^\dagger)+MX+J=0$, and its projector has positive derivative degree one.

By definition, each $\bar D_{\dot\alpha}$ has positive derivative degree $1/2$, so $\Pi_0(P_{\mathrm{phys}}X^\dagger)=0$. Applying $\Pi_0$ to the equation in step 1.1 gives $MX+J(\Phi)=0$. Because $M>0$, this scalar linear equation has the unique solution $X_*=-J(\Phi)/M$.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F1] [[def-aqft-susy-wilsonian-action]]: the Wilsonian action has a derivative-free holomorphic chiral integrand $F_\lambda(\Phi,W)$ and a separate real D-term; its finite operator quotient, ordered basis, cutoff, and field coordinates are supplied data.

proof_steps.claim: The selected finite invariant-quotient/on-shell-equivalence interpretation carries the full-AC premise [A1]. Separately, by [F2] and [A3], the complete derivative-free holomorphic chiral integrand satisfies $F_\lambda(\Phi,W)=F_{\Lambda_0}(\Phi,W)$ coefficientwise for every formal perturbative order. Setting $W=0$ and restricting to the fixed light-field variables preserves this identity, so $W_\lambda(\Phi)=W_{\Lambda_0}(\Phi)$.

The map $P_{\mathrm{hol}}$ is the same linear coordinate projection at both scales by [A2]. Applying it to the equality in step 1.1 gives $P_{\mathrm{hol}}W_\lambda=P_{\mathrm{hol}}W_{\Lambda_0}$. Since the retained operators are a fixed ordered basis, equality of their coordinate vectors gives equality of each retained coefficient.

The gauge-coupling correction and the freedom of the real D-term are exactly the exceptions in [F2]. The conclusion concerns the fixed Wilsonian holomorphic coordinates, so it does not imply equality of one-particle-irreducible vertices or of coefficients after a scale-dependent field rescaling; the formal perturbative hypothesis in [A3] also excludes nonperturbative and continuum conclusions.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] [[lem-qftx-stable-adhm-partition-fixed-points-and-tangent-character]]: for the positive-FI stable quotient, the current Statement gives smooth complex dimension $2kN$, isolated fixed points bijective with $N$-tuples of partitions of total size $k$, and the tangent character displayed in the Statement. Its proof supplies the stable quotient, finite invariant affine atlas, and finite reduced proper fixed locus. It asserts no sheaf/ASD correspondence; the separate noncompact pushforward is supplied by [F4].

proof_steps.claim: By [A2] and [F2], the $T$-fixed points of $X_{k,N}^\zeta$ are isolated and correspond bijectively to the $N$-tuples $\vec Y$ with $|\vec Y|=k$. The tangent character at each point is the displayed character, so its additive weights, with multiplicity, have Euler product $E_{\vec Y}$.

Extend $T$ by the flavor circle acting trivially on the base. This does not change the fixed-point set, and at $\vec Y$ the top Chern insertion restricts to $N_{\vec Y}(\widetilde m)=\prod_\chi(w_\chi-\widetilde m)$ by the definition in [F1]. Since all tangent characters are nontrivial, their Chern classes are inverted in the localized coefficient field.

By the definition [F1], the pushforward in step 3.1 is $I_{k,N}^{\mathrm{adj}}(\widetilde m)$. For finite $N$ and fixed $k$ there are finitely many partition tuples, so each coefficient is a finite rational function in the stated field. The coefficient sequence therefore defines the displayed formal power series; at $k=0$, the unique empty tuple has empty numerator and denominator products equal to $1$.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F4] [[def-reductive-and-linearly-reductive-over-c]]: a complex algebraic group is reductive when it has no nontrivial closed normal unipotent subgroup, with unipotent understood by the fixed-vector condition on nonzero finite-dimensional rational modules.

proof_steps.claim: By F2 and A4, the admitted order-$k$ relation is implemented by an actual local invertible coordinate map $F_\epsilon$; the reductive-group condition F4 is the hypothesis carried by the quotient proposition. Any boundary relation has zero action by its boundary hypothesis, and any declared polynomial identity vanishes identically. All higher-order terms generated by the full pullback are retained.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F1] [[def-aqft-scheme-and-wilson-coefficients]]: the coefficient space is $\mathbb C^N$; $\rho_N$ is an isometry to $\mathbb R^{2N}$; the supplied RG domain is open in $I\times\mathbb R^{2N}$ and $\beta$ maps it continuously to $\mathbb R^{2N}$.

proof_steps.claim: Since $\Omega$ is open and $(t_0,x_0)\in\Omega$, choose $r,h_0>0$ so the compact cylinder $K=[t_0-h_0,t_0+h_0]\times\overline B(x_0,2r)$ lies in $\Omega$. Continuity of $\beta$ on $K$ gives a finite bound $M$, and [F3] gives a single state-Lipschitz constant $L$ there. Choose $0<h\le h_0$ with $h(M+1)\le r$ and $h(L+1)<1$; then $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] Stable word frames of length at most $k-1$ cover $X^s$; the complex gauge action is free and proper and its quotient has smooth holomorphic word-frame charts. [[lem-adhm-stable-quotient-and-torus-lift]]

proof_steps.claim: For $g\in GL(V)$ put $x'=g\cdot x$ and $M(g)^2=\sum_i\|B_i'\|^2+\|I'\|^2+\|J'\|^2$. A fixed word frame $C(x)$ exists by [F2]. Each column of $gC(x)=C(x')$ is a product of at most $k-1$ matrices $B_i'$ followed by $I'$ on a unit framing vector. Submultiplicativity and operator norm bounded by Frobenius norm give $\|g\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le A_x(1+M(g))^k$ for $A_x=\sqrt{k}\|C(x)^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. If $x$ is costable, the rows consisting of coordinate rows of $JB_{i_1}\cdots B_{i_m}$ span $V^*$: their common annihilator is the largest common $B_i$-invariant subspace in $\ker J$, hence zero. The same finite dimension-growth argument as for columns gives a row basis $D(x)$ using words of length at most $k-1$. Since $D(x')=D(x)g^{-1}$, the identical norm estimate gives $\|g^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le A_x'(1+M(g))^k$. This also proves costability is open, since it is covered by the nonvanishing determinants of finitely many such row frames.

Diagonalize $H$ by [F4], with real eigenvalues $\lambda_i$. Along the preceding path the squared $B_i'$ entries have factors $e^{2t(\lambda_a-\lambda_b)}$, the squared $I'$ entries have $e^{2t\lambda_a}$ and the squared $J'$ entries have $e^{-2t\lambda_a}$. The log determinant is affine in $t$. Hence $F_\zeta''$ is a sum of $4w^2|z|^2e^{2tw}$ over those entries and their listed weights $w$, and is nonnegative. It can vanish only when $[H,B_i']=0$, $HI'=0$ and $J'H=0$. Stability of $x'$ then forces $H=0$, by applying $H$ to all spanning word vectors. Thus the path is strictly convex for every nonzero $H$. Given two critical matrices $g_1,g_2$, diagonalize the positive matrix $(g_2g_1^{-1})^\dagger(g_2g_1^{-1})$ and take the positive logarithms of its eigenvalues to write $g_2g_1^{-1}=u e^H$ with $u$ unitary and $H$ Hermitian. The endpoints of $e^{tH}g_1$ are both critical, after removing $u$ by invariance. Strict convexity forces $H=0$, so $g_2=ug_1$. This proves uniqueness of the unitary orbit at either level.

At a balanced datum $x$, let $L_x:\operatorname{Herm}(V)\to\operatorname{Herm}(V)$ be $H\mapsto\frac{d}{dt}\mu_{\mathbb R}(e^{tH}\cdot x)|_{t=0}$. Step 4.1 gives $2\operatorname{tr}(H L_xH)=F_\zeta''(e^{tH})|_{t=0}>0$ for nonzero $H$, so $L_x$ is injective and hence invertible in finite equal dimensions. The map $(H,y)\mapsto\mu_{\mathbb R}(e^H\cdot y)-\zeta I$ is smooth. To see smoothness of the exponential in the matrix entries directly, differentiate its absolutely convergent power series: on a bounded matrix set, an order-$r$ derivative of its degree-$m$ term is bounded by a constant times $m^r R^{m-r}/m!$, a summable majorant; this applies through real block matrices as in [F4]. By [F5] the balancing $H=H(y)$ is locally $C^r$ for every finite $r$, and uniqueness glues these branches to the same smooth map. The same invertible derivative along the Hermitian gauge directions in $T_xX^s$ proves that the real-level locus is a smooth submanifold. The unitary group is compact (closed bounded matrices), its action there is free by [F2] and proper (inverse images are closed subsets of $U(V)$ times a compact coordinate projection); therefore its quotient is smooth by [F6]. The map to the complex quotient is smooth using local submersion sections in [F6]. On any word-frame chart [F2], the local balancing map just constructed, followed by the unitary quotient map, is its smooth inverse; step 4.1 proves independence of all choices. Thus the bijections are diffeomorphisms. The compact torus commutes with gauge actions and preserves both the complex equation and $\mu_{\mathbb R}$, so the bijections are equivariant. For $k=0$ all matrices and equations are empty and all quotients are points, proving every boundary case stated. No sheaf or ASD identification was used.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] The stable complex quotient has word-frame charts, is a geometric quotient, and has tangent space $\ker d_1/\operatorname{im}d_0$. [[lem-adhm-stable-quotient-and-torus-lift]]

proof_steps.claim: The Beilinson construction is natural under framed sheaf isomorphisms, so an isomorphism of framed sheaves induces maps on the cohomology vector spaces used in steps 1.2–6.2 and hence a single change of basis $g\in GL(V)$; the normalized Euler blocks force the recovered tuples to differ by $g\cdot(B_1,B_2,I,J)$. Conversely such a $g$ is an isomorphism of monads acting trivially on $W$, and therefore induces a framed sheaf isomorphism. This proves the pointwise inverse equivalence modulo $GL(V)$. For a finite-type data family, step 2.1 makes $\beta$ surjective on the total space, so $K=\ker\beta$ is locally free. The sequence $0\to V\mathcal O(-1)\to K\to\mathcal E\to0$ is exact and its terms before $\mathcal E$ are flat over the base. After tensoring with any residue field of the base, the first map remains sheaf-injective by step 1.1; hence $\operatorname{Tor}_1(k(s),\mathcal E)=0$. Since $\mathcal E$ is finite over each local ring of $\mathbb P^2\times S$ and its residue fiber is a vector space over the residue field, [F8] gives flatness over $S$. Under the stated relative cohomology and base-change hypotheses, the same constructions use vector bundles and are inverse for families.

Apply the family equivalence to $S=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$. A first-order deformation of the ADHM data is $(\dot B_1,\dot B_2,\dot I,\dot J)$ satisfying $d\mu_{\mathbb C}=0$; infinitesimal changes of basis are $d_0(\xi)=([\xi,B_1],[\xi,B_2],\xi I,-J\xi)$. Differentiating the monad gives the chain perturbation $(\dot\alpha,\dot\beta)$ with $\beta\dot\alpha+\dot\beta\alpha=0$, and a change by $d_0(\xi)$ is the corresponding chain homotopy. Since the family construction and its inverse commute with this dual-number base change, they induce inverse linear maps on first-order framed deformations and on the quotient tangent spaces $\ker d_1/\operatorname{im}d_0$.

[[thm-qftx-adhm-real-complex-quotient-correspondence]]

proof_steps.claim: The zero-level quotient result [F8] applies because step 6.1 established stability and both zero moments; it identifies each regular complex orbit with its unique unitary orbit. The explicit argument in step 5.2 is stronger for the framed real monads: it identifies their actual normalized isomorphisms with $U(V)$ and fixes the inverse extraction orbit. final_edge_fact_uses.text: [A1] The current real/complex quotient carrier proves that every regular complex orbit meets $\mu_{\mathbb R}=0$ in exactly one $U(k)$ orbit; it also proves the converse zero-level stability implies costability, smooth quotient charts and equivariance for the exact raw torus convention. Its full finite-dimensional proof is supplied there. [[thm-qftx-adhm-real-complex-quotient-correspondence]]

proof_steps.claim: By [A1], each regular zero-FI unitary orbit determines one regular complex $GL(k)$ orbit, and each regular complex orbit has exactly one balanced unitary representative. The two constructions are inverse because each orbit intersection is unique; the quotient map is a diffeomorphism in the word-frame charts. The exact torus action in [F1] commutes with both gauge actions, so this quotient identification is $T$-equivariant.

By [A2], every stable complex orbit gives one framed torsion-free $\mathbb P^2$ sheaf with the stated rank, framing and Hilbert polynomial, and the converse recovers the same orbit. Its locally-free locus is exactly the costable locus. Thus restricting [A1]'s complex quotient to regular orbits gives exactly that locally-free sheaf locus; the positive-FI stable quotient still contains the non-locally-free boundary. The family and first-order version is conditional on [A2]'s displayed base-change hypotheses and [A3], so no tangent claim is inferred outside that range.

The finite-dimensional quotient and $\mathbb P^2$ sheaf maps are $T$-equivariant by [A1]–[A2]. The Ward construction is natural under rotations and framing transformations by [A4]; the exact raw monad torus factors are directly calculated in the new block lemma cited by [A5], while the equivariance of inverse normalization remains part of [A5]. These exact interfaces make the composite $T$-equivariant. The same composition on first-order families is valid only under the base-change hypotheses of [A2]–[A4] and the deformation compatibility of [A5]. This proves the stated conditional torus and tangent clauses and leaves the positive-FI boundary separate.

fact_uses.text:
[F15] [[lem-ag-differentials-localization-base-change]]: an $A$-algebra
homomorphism $B\to C$ induces a canonical $C$-linear functoriality map
$C\otimes_B\Omega_{B/A}\to\Omega_{C/A}$, $c\otimes\mathrm db\mapsto
c\,\mathrm d(\text{image of }b)$.

proof_steps.claim: The pullback matrix. Let $\psi\colon C\to B$ be the $k$-algebra map induced by $f|_U\colon U\to V$, under the correspondence of [F8]. By [F15] there is a canonical $B$-linear functoriality map $\gamma\colon B\otimes_C\Omega_{C/k}\to\Omega_{B/k}$, $b\otimes\mathrm dc\mapsto b\,\mathrm d(\psi c)$; by [F13] the differentials $\mathrm dy_1,\dots,\mathrm dy_m$ generate the $C$-module $\Omega_{C/k}$, so their images generate $B\otimes_C\Omega_{C/k}$. Since $\mathrm du_{c+1},\dots,\mathrm du_n$ is a $B$-basis of $\Omega_{B/k}$ [F14], there are unique regular functions $a_{ij}\in B$ with $$\mathrm d(\psi y_j)=\sum_{i=c+1}^{n}a_{ij}\,\mathrm du_i\qquad(c<i\le n,\ 1\le j\le m);$$ denote by $A=(a_{ij})$ the resulting $(n-c)\times m$ matrix over $B$.

fact_uses.text: [F16] [[lem-ag-differentials-localization-base-change]]: for a ring map $A\to B$: base change gives $B'\otimes_B\Omega_{B/A}\cong\Omega_{B'/A'}$; localization gives $U^{-1}\Omega_{B/A}\cong\Omega_{U^{-1}B/V^{-1}A}$; and a ring map $B\to C$ carries a canonical $C$-linear functoriality map $C\otimes_B\Omega_{B/A}\to\Omega_{C/A}$, $c\otimes\mathrm{d}b\mapsto c\,\mathrm{d}(\text{image of }b)$.

proof_steps.claim: Apply the localization clause of [F16] to the injective ring map $\varphi\colon R\to S$ with $U=S\setminus\{0\}$ and $V=R\setminus\{0\}$: the image of $V$ in $S$ is contained in $U$ because $\varphi$ is injective, and $V^{-1}R=K$, $U^{-1}S=L$ are the fraction fields [F19]. This gives an isomorphism $U^{-1}\Omega_{S/R}\cong\Omega_{L/K}$, and [F17] identifies $U^{-1}\Omega_{S/R}$ with $L\otimes_S\Omega_{S/R}$. Hence $$\Omega_{S/R}\otimes_SL\cong\Omega_{L/K}$$ and, by step 3.1, the $L$-vector space $\Omega_{S/R}\otimes_SL$ has dimension $r$.

Fix a closed point $x\in U$ and put $y=f(x)\in V=Y_{\mathrm{reg}}$; both are $k$-rational points of the respective schemes [F2]. Let $\mathfrak m_x\subseteq S$ and $\mathfrak m_y\subseteq R$ be the corresponding maximal ideals. The local rings are $\mathcal O_{Y,y}=R_{\mathfrak m_y}$ and $\mathcal O_{X,x}=S_{\mathfrak m_x}$ [F31], and the induced map of local rings is the localization of $\varphi$ at these primes, which sends $a$ to $\varphi(a)$ [F29] and is local [F30]; hence the cotangent map $\bar f_x^\sharp\colon C_yY\to C_xX$ of [F27] sends the class of $a\in\mathfrak m_y$ to the class of $\varphi(a)$. The cotangent isomorphism [F26] at the $k$-rational points, applied on the charts $\operatorname{Spec}R$ and $\operatorname{Spec}S$ and combined with [F32], gives identifications $$\theta_y\colon C_yY\cong\Omega_{R/k}\otimes_R\kappa(y),\qquad \theta_x\colon C_xX\cong\Omega_{S/k}\otimes_S\kappa(x),$$ both sending $[a]\mapsto\mathrm{d}a\otimes1$. Let $\alpha\colon S\otimes_R\Omega_{R/k}\to\Omega_{S/k}$ be the functoriality map of [F16](3), $b\otimes\mathrm{d}a\mapsto b\,\mathrm{d}\varphi(a)$; it is the first map of the exact sequence $S\otimes_R\Omega_{R/k}\xrightarrow{\alpha}\Omega_{S/k}\to\Omega_{S/R}\to0$ of [F28]. Base changing this sequence along $S\to\kappa(x)$ and using the identification $(S\otimes_R\Omega_{R/k})\otimes_S\kappa(x) \cong\Omega_{R/k}\otimes_R\kappa(x)$ of [F25], together with the fact that $R\to\kappa(x)$ is evaluation at $y$, yields the exact sequence $$\Omega_{R/k}\otimes_R\kappa(y)\xrightarrow{\alpha_x} \Omega_{S/k}\otimes_S\kappa(x)\to\Omega_{S/R}\otimes_S\kappa(x)\to0$$ [F22]. For $a\in\mathfrak m_y$ one computes $\alpha_x(\theta_y([a]))=\alpha_x(\mathrm{d}a\otimes1) =\mathrm{d}\varphi(a)\otimes1=\theta_x([\varphi(a)]) =\theta_x(\bar f_x^\sharp([a]))$, so under the identifications $\theta_y$, $\theta_x$ the map $\alpha_x$ is precisely the cotangent map $\bar f_x^\sharp$; in particular $\operatorname{rank}\alpha_x=\operatorname{rank}\bar f_x^\sharp$.

fact_uses.text: [F6] [[lem-ag-differentials-localization-base-change]]: for a multiplicative set $U$ inside an $A$-algebra $B$ the canonical map $U^{-1}\Omega_{B/A}\to\Omega_{U^{-1}B/A}$ is an isomorphism, with inverse sending $\mathrm{d}(b/u)$ to $u^{-1}\mathrm{d}b-bu^{-2}\mathrm{d}u$; and for every $A$-algebra map $B\to C$ there is a natural $C$-linear map $C\otimes_B\Omega_{B/A}\to\Omega_{C/A}$.

proof_steps.claim: $\Omega_{K'/k}$ has $K'$-basis $\mathrm{d}t_1,\dots,\mathrm{d}t_r$. Indeed $k[T]\to K'$, $T_i\mapsto t_i$, identifies $k[T]$ with the polynomial ring on the algebraically independent elements $t_i$ by [F1], so by [F5] (with $A=k$ and $n=r$) the module $\Omega_{k[T]/k}$ is free on $\mathrm{d}T_1,\dots,\mathrm{d}T_r$; since a nonzero element of $k[T]$ maps to a nonzero element of $K'=k(T)$, the localisation isomorphism of [F6] applies with $U=k[T]\smallsetminus\{0\}$ and exhibits $\Omega_{K'/k}\cong K'\otimes_{k[T]}\Omega_{k[T]/k}$ with the images of $\mathrm{d}T_1,\dots,\mathrm{d}T_r$ as a $K'$-basis, and those images are exactly $\mathrm{d}t_1,\dots,\mathrm{d}t_r$.

Extension of derivations. Let $D\colon K\to L$ be a $k$-derivation. First extend $D$ to $K(B)$: each element of $K(B)$ lies in $K(B_0)$ for some finite $B_0\subseteq B$, and on the polynomial ring $K[B_0]$, for which $\Omega_{K[B_0]/K}$ is free on the $\mathrm{d}b$, $b\in B_0$, by [F5], the prescription $b\mapsto0$ for $b\in B_0$, together with $D$ on $K$, defines a unique $k$-derivation of $K[B_0]$ extending $D$; it extends uniquely to the fraction field $K(B_0)$ by the quotient rule $\mathrm{d}(c/d)=(d\,\mathrm{d}c-c\,\mathrm{d}d)/d^2$ of [F6], and for $B_0\subseteq B_1$ the extension on $K(B_1)$ restricts to the one on $K(B_0)$ by uniqueness, so a derivation $D_1\colon K(B)\to L$ extending $D$ is well defined on the union of the fields $K(B_0)$. Next let $x\in L$; then $K(B)(x)/K(B)$ is finite separable by step 4.1, hence simple, with minimal polynomial $Q$ of $x$ over $K(B)$ that is separable by [F10], so $Q'(x)\ne0$ by [F3] and [F4]. Substituting $K(B)$ for $K'$, $K(B)(x)$ for $K$ and $Q$ for $P$ in the construction of step 3.1 produces an extension of $D_1$ to $K(B)(x)$, and any two extensions of $D_1$ to $K(B)(x)$ agree, because their difference vanishes on $K(B)$ and takes at $x$ a value killed by $Q'(x)\ne0$. Declaring the value at $x$ to be that unique value defines $D_2(x)$ for every $x\in L$; it is a derivation because for $x,y\in L$ the field $K(B)(x,y)$ is finite separable over $K(B)$ by [F10] and [F12], carries an extension of $D_1$ by the same construction, and on it the derivation laws hold while its restrictions to $K(B)(x)$ and $K(B)(y)$ agree with the unique extensions, so the values $D_2$ assigns are additive and satisfy Leibniz.

Injectivity. Keep the notation of step 4.1, let $\rho\colon L\otimes_K\Omega_{K/k}\to\Omega_{L/k}$ be the natural map of [F6], and let $x=\sum_ic_i(1\otimes\mathrm{d}t_i)\in\ker\rho$, the elements $\mathrm{d}t_i$ being a $K$-basis of $\Omega_{K/k}$ by step 4.1. proof_steps.claim: Vary the terms depending on $X$ using the normalized physical action brackets in [F1]. At fixed chiral coordinates, $P_{\mathrm{raw}}=\partial^L_{\bar\theta^{\dot2}}\partial^L_{\bar\theta^{\dot1}}|_{\bar\theta=0}$ extracts the top barred coefficient, so $I_D(U)=I_F(P_{\mathrm{raw}}U)$ up to the spacetime total derivatives removed by [A3]. final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] Stable word frames of length at most $k-1$ cover $X^s$; the complex gauge action is free and proper and its quotient has smooth holomorphic word-frame charts. [[lem-adhm-stable-quotient-and-torus-lift]]

proof_steps.claim: For $g\in GL(V)$ put $x'=g\cdot x$ and $M(g)^2=\sum_i\|B_i'\|^2+\|I'\|^2+\|J'\|^2$. A fixed word frame $C(x)$ exists by [F2]. Each column of $gC(x)=C(x')$ is a product of at most $k-1$ matrices $B_i'$ followed by $I'$ on a unit framing vector. Submultiplicativity and operator norm bounded by Frobenius norm give $\|g\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le A_x(1+M(g))^k$ for $A_x=\sqrt{k}\|C(x)^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. If $x$ is costable, the rows consisting of coordinate rows of $JB_{i_1}\cdots B_{i_m}$ span $V^*$: their common annihilator is the largest common $B_i$-invariant subspace in $\ker J$, hence zero. The same finite dimension-growth argument as for columns gives a row basis $D(x)$ using words of length at most $k-1$. Since $D(x')=D(x)g^{-1}$, the identical norm estimate gives $\|g^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le A_x'(1+M(g))^k$. This also proves costability is open, since it is covered by the nonvanishing determinants of finitely many such row frames.

Diagonalize $H$ by [F4], with real eigenvalues $\lambda_i$. Along the preceding path the squared $B_i'$ entries have factors $e^{2t(\lambda_a-\lambda_b)}$, the squared $I'$ entries have $e^{2t\lambda_a}$ and the squared $J'$ entries have $e^{-2t\lambda_a}$. The log determinant is affine in $t$. Hence $F_\zeta''$ is a sum of $4w^2|z|^2e^{2tw}$ over those entries and their listed weights $w$, and is nonnegative. It can vanish only when $[H,B_i']=0$, $HI'=0$ and $J'H=0$. Stability of $x'$ then forces $H=0$, by applying $H$ to all spanning word vectors. Thus the path is strictly convex for every nonzero $H$. Given two critical matrices $g_1,g_2$, diagonalize the positive matrix $(g_2g_1^{-1})^\dagger(g_2g_1^{-1})$ and take the positive logarithms of its eigenvalues to write $g_2g_1^{-1}=u e^H$ with $u$ unitary and $H$ Hermitian. The endpoints of $e^{tH}g_1$ are both critical, after removing $u$ by invariance. Strict convexity forces $H=0$, so $g_2=ug_1$. This proves uniqueness of the unitary orbit at either level.

At a balanced datum $x$, let $L_x:\operatorname{Herm}(V)\to\operatorname{Herm}(V)$ be $H\mapsto\frac{d}{dt}\mu_{\mathbb R}(e^{tH}\cdot x)|_{t=0}$. Step 4.1 gives $2\operatorname{tr}(H L_xH)=F_\zeta''(e^{tH})|_{t=0}>0$ for nonzero $H$, so $L_x$ is injective and hence invertible in finite equal dimensions. The map $(H,y)\mapsto\mu_{\mathbb R}(e^H\cdot y)-\zeta I$ is smooth. To see smoothness of the exponential in the matrix entries directly, differentiate its absolutely convergent power series: on a bounded matrix set, an order-$r$ derivative of its degree-$m$ term is bounded by a constant times $m^r R^{m-r}/m!$, a summable majorant; this applies through real block matrices as in [F4]. By [F5] the balancing $H=H(y)$ is locally $C^r$ for every finite $r$, and uniqueness glues these branches to the same smooth map. The same invertible derivative along the Hermitian gauge directions in $T_xX^s$ proves that the real-level locus is a smooth submanifold. The unitary group is compact (closed bounded matrices), its action there is free by [F2] and proper (inverse images are closed subsets of $U(V)$ times a compact coordinate projection); therefore its quotient is smooth by [F6]. The map to the complex quotient is smooth using local submersion sections in [F6]. On any word-frame chart [F2], the local balancing map just constructed, followed by the unitary quotient map, is its smooth inverse; step 4.1 proves independence of all choices. Thus the bijections are diffeomorphisms. The compact torus commutes with gauge actions and preserves both the complex equation and $\mu_{\mathbb R}$, so the bijections are equivariant. For $k=0$ all matrices and equations are empty and all quotients are points, proving every boundary case stated. No sheaf or ASD identification was used.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] The stable complex quotient has word-frame charts, is a geometric quotient, and has tangent space $\ker d_1/\operatorname{im}d_0$. [[lem-adhm-stable-quotient-and-torus-lift]]

proof_steps.claim: The Beilinson construction is natural under framed sheaf isomorphisms, so an isomorphism of framed sheaves induces maps on the cohomology vector spaces used in steps 1.2–6.2 and hence a single change of basis $g\in GL(V)$; the normalized Euler blocks force the recovered tuples to differ by $g\cdot(B_1,B_2,I,J)$. Conversely such a $g$ is an isomorphism of monads acting trivially on $W$, and therefore induces a framed sheaf isomorphism. This proves the pointwise inverse equivalence modulo $GL(V)$. For a finite-type data family, step 2.1 makes $\beta$ surjective on the total space, so $K=\ker\beta$ is locally free. The sequence $0\to V\mathcal O(-1)\to K\to\mathcal E\to0$ is exact and its terms before $\mathcal E$ are flat over the base. After tensoring with any residue field of the base, the first map remains sheaf-injective by step 1.1; hence $\operatorname{Tor}_1(k(s),\mathcal E)=0$. Since $\mathcal E$ is finite over each local ring of $\mathbb P^2\times S$ and its residue fiber is a vector space over the residue field, [F8] gives flatness over $S$. Under the stated relative cohomology and base-change hypotheses, the same constructions use vector bundles and are inverse for families.

Apply the family equivalence to $S=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$. A first-order deformation of the ADHM data is $(\dot B_1,\dot B_2,\dot I,\dot J)$ satisfying $d\mu_{\mathbb C}=0$; infinitesimal changes of basis are $d_0(\xi)=([\xi,B_1],[\xi,B_2],\xi I,-J\xi)$. Since the family construction and its inverse commute with this dual-number base change, they induce inverse linear maps on first-order framed deformations and on the quotient tangent spaces $\ker d_1/\operatorname{im}d_0$.

u_a)$ invertible after localization by [F3], hence $ eta_a=(i_a^*\alpha/e_T(

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [A1] The current real/complex quotient carrier proves that every regular complex orbit meets $\mu_{\mathbb R}=0$ in exactly one $U(k)$ orbit; it also proves the converse zero-level stability implies costability, smooth quotient charts and equivariance for the exact raw torus convention. fact_uses.text:
[F7] [[lem-ag-separable-residue-cotangent-sequence]]: let $k$ be a field and $R$
a Noetherian local $k$-algebra with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ and residue field
$\kappa$, finitely generated and separably generated over $k$; then
$0\to\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2\to\Omega_{R/k}\otimes_R\kappa\to\Omega_{\kappa/k}\to0$
is exact. If in addition $\kappa/k$ is finite separable, then
$\Omega_{\kappa/k}=0$ and the first map is an isomorphism
$\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2\cong\Omega_{R/k}\otimes_R\kappa$.

proof_steps.claim: Choice. Assume the Axiom of Choice [F4]; it is consumed below only by the two Choice-dependent results [F6] and [F11], while the separable-residue supplier [F7] is choice-free.

The cotangent space of the fibre ring vanishes. The field $\kappa(x)$ is a finite separable extension of $\kappa(s)$ by step 3.1, hence separably generated over $\kappa(s)$ by [F8]; the ring $\bar R$ is a Noetherian local $\kappa(s)$-algebra with residue field $\kappa(x)$ by step 2.3, so the supplier [F7] applies and the injective cotangent map is an isomorphism $\bar{\mathfrak m}/\bar{\mathfrak m}^2\cong\Omega_{\bar R/\kappa(s)}\otimes_{\bar R}\kappa(x)=0$, the vanishing being step 3.2.

fact_uses.text: [F2] [[lem-ag-separable-residue-cotangent-sequence]]: for a Noetherian local $k$-algebra $R$ with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ and residue field $\kappa$ finitely generated and separably generated over $k$, the sequence $0\to\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2\to\Omega_{R/k}\otimes_R\kappa\to\Omega_{\kappa/k}\to0$ is exact; if $\kappa/k$ is finite separable, then $\Omega_{\kappa/k}=0$ and the first map is an isomorphism.

proof_steps.claim: The closed-point criterion. Let $\mathfrak m\subseteq A$ be maximal with $\kappa=A/\mathfrak m$ finite separable over $k$. The local ring $A_{\mathfrak m}$ is a Noetherian local $k$-algebra with residue field $\kappa$, which is finitely generated and separably generated over the perfect field $k$ by [F3]; since $\kappa/k$ is finite separable, [F2] gives $\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2\cong\Omega_{A_{\mathfrak m}/k}\otimes_{A_{\mathfrak m}}\kappa$, and $\Omega_{A_{\mathfrak m}/k}\otimes\kappa\cong\Omega_{A/k}\otimes_A\kappa$. By [F1] and [F4] the latter is the cokernel of the matrix $J(\mathfrak m)$ acting from $\kappa^r$ to $\kappa^n$, so its dimension is $n-\operatorname{rank}_\kappa J(\mathfrak m)$. Hence $\operatorname{edim}A_{\mathfrak m}=n-\operatorname{rank}_\kappa J(\mathfrak m)$ by [F8], and by [F8] again $A_{\mathfrak m}$ is regular if and only if $\operatorname{edim}A_{\mathfrak m}=\dim A_{\mathfrak m}$, that is, if and only if $\operatorname{rank}J(\mathfrak m)=n-\dim A_{\mathfrak m}$; both $\operatorname{edim}$ and $\dim$ are intrinsic, so the rank is independent of the generating set of $I$.

Local charts at regular points. Let $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}A$ with $A_{\mathfrak q}$ regular, let $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q\cap P$ correspond to $\mathfrak q$, and put $R:=P_{\mathfrak p}$, a regular local ring of dimension $d:=\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)$ by [F7], with ideal $I':=IR$ and quotient $R/I'=A_{\mathfrak q}$ of dimension $\dim A_{\mathfrak q}$. By [F6] there are $y_1,\dots,y_c\in I'$ forming an initial part of a regular system of parameters of $R$, with $c=d-\dim A_{\mathfrak q}$, and generating $I'$. Put $\mathfrak n:=\mathfrak pR$. The classes of the $y_j$ form a basis of $(I'+\mathfrak n^2)/\mathfrak n^2$: they span this subspace because they generate $I'$, and are linearly independent as part of a cotangent basis by [F5], with dimension $c$ by [F6]. Write $y_j=g_j/u_j$ with $g_j\in I$ and $u_j\in P\smallsetminus\mathfrak p$. Since each $u_j$ is a unit of $R$, the $g_j$ still generate $I'$ and their classes are nonzero scalar multiples of the corresponding $y_j$ classes, hence linearly independent. The map $\mathfrak n/\mathfrak n^2\to\Omega_{R/k}\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)\cong\kappa(\mathfrak p)^n$ is injective by [F2], the residue field $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ being finitely generated and separably generated over the perfect field $k$ by [F3], and the images of the classes of the $g_j$ are the vectors $(\partial g_j/\partial x_i\bmod\mathfrak p)_i$ by [F1]; these vectors are therefore linearly independent over $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$, so some $c\times c$ minor $h$ of the Jacobian matrix of $g_1,\dots,g_c$ satisfies $h\notin\mathfrak p$. Since $I$ is finitely generated and $I'=(g_1,\dots,g_c)R$, there is $s\notin\mathfrak p$ with $sI\subseteq(g_1,\dots,g_c)$; put $t:=sh\in A$. By [F10] the element $t$ is not in $\mathfrak q$ and becomes a unit in $A_t$, and in $A_t$ the ideal $I$ is generated by $g_1,\dots,g_c$ while $h$ is a unit, so $A_t\cong(P/(g_1,\dots,g_c))_t$ is a standard smooth $k$-algebra with $n$ variables and $c$ equations.
The three assertions are steps 1.1, 1.2 and 2.1 with the density statement of step 3.1; all of them use only the perfectness of $k$ through [F3] and [F2], and no later local-presentation theorem.

Then $0\to\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^{2}\to\Omega_{R/k}\otimes_R\kappa\to\Omega_{\kappa/k}\to0$ is short exact, the first map sending the class of $x$ to $\mathrm dx\otimes1$; if $\kappa/k$ is finite separable then $\Omega_{\kappa/k}=0$ and that map is an isomorphism $\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^{2}\cong\Omega_{R/k}\otimes_R\kappa$.

Since the residue fields of $A$ and $S$ are the field $k$, a finite separable extension of $k$, [F4] gives isomorphisms $\mathfrak m_y/\mathfrak m_y^{2}\cong\Omega_{A/k}\otimes_Ak$ and $\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^{2}\cong\Omega_{S/k}\otimes_Sk$ carrying the class of an element of the maximal ideal to $\mathrm d\square\otimes1$.

Forward direction: relative dimension $m-n$ and injectivity of the cotangent map. Composing the standard smooth presentation of $C$ over $D$ from step 2.3 with the standard smooth presentation of $D$ over $k$ from step 1.1 presents the finite-type $k$-algebra $C$ as standard smooth over $k$ with relative dimension $n+d$ [F13]; its localisation at the $k$-rational prime $\mathfrak q$ is $S$, so [F12] identifies that relative dimension with $\dim S=m$, whence $d=m-n$ and, by step 2.3, $\dim F=m-n$. The transitivity sequence $\Omega_{A/k}\otimes_AS\to\Omega_{S/k}\to\Omega_{S/A}\to0$ of [F5] is right exact, and tensoring it with $S\to k$ yields, using [F4] and [F18], the exact sequence $\mathfrak m_y/\mathfrak m_y^{2}\to\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^{2}\to\Omega_{S/A}\otimes_Sk\to0$, in which the first arrow is the map induced by $f^{*}$; since $\Omega_{S/A}\cong S^{d}$ the last term is a $k$-vector space of dimension $d$, so the image has dimension $m-d=n$, which equals $\dim_k(\mathfrak m_y/\mathfrak m_y^{2})=n$ by step 2.2 and forces the map to be injective.

Converse direction: the fibre is geometrically regular. Write $Q'\subseteq k[x_1,\dots,x_N]$ for the maximal ideal corresponding to $x$ in the presentation of step 1.1, and put $R':=k[x_1,\dots,x_N]_{Q'}$. The parameters $y_1,\dots,y_n\in A=D_{\mathfrak p}$ generate $\mathfrak pD_{\mathfrak p}$. Since $D$ is Noetherian, after shrinking $\operatorname{Spec}D$ around $y$ and its inverse-image chart around $x$, we may represent every $y_i$ by an element of $D$ and arrange that $\mathfrak pD=(y_1,\dots,y_n)D$ on these charts: first clear their denominators outside $\mathfrak p$, then invert an element outside $\mathfrak p$ annihilating the finite module $\mathfrak pD/(y_1,\dots,y_n)D$. Absorb the corresponding principal localisations into the polynomial chart of $C$. Write each image of $y_i$ in $C$ as $P_i/g^{e_i}$ with $P_i\in k[x_1,\dots,x_N]$ and $e_i\ge0$. Since $g$ is a unit of $C$, the images of the numerators $P_i$ generate the same ideal as those of the $y_i$, and each $P_i$ vanishes at $x$. The finite-type fibre algebra $B:=C\otimes_D k=C/\mathfrak pC$ is then presented on this chart by $B\cong(k[x_1,\dots,x_N]/(f_1,\dots,f_c,P_1,\dots,P_n))_g$, and its local ring at $x$ is $F\cong R'/I$ for $I:=(f_1,\dots,f_c,P_1,\dots,P_n)R'$ [F16]. The ring $R'$ is regular local of dimension $N$ by [F3] with $c=0$ and [F14], and $\dim F=m-n$ by step 3.1, so [F10] gives $\dim_k((I+Q'^{2})/Q'^{2})=N-\dim F=N-m+n=c+n$. The classes of the $c+n$ generators $f_1,\dots,f_c,P_1,\dots,P_n$ span that space, hence form a basis. By [F4] and [F7], their classes in $Q'/Q'^{2}$ are the $c+n$ rows of the Jacobian matrix evaluated at $Q'$, so some $(c+n)\times(c+n)$ minor $h$ does not lie in $Q'$. Localising the **finite-type algebra** $B$ at the image of $h$ gives a standard smooth $k$-presentation with the displayed $c+n$ equations [F1]; this open chart contains $x$. By [F3], after every field extension $K/k$ every local ring of $(B_h)\otimes_kK$ is regular. Every prime of the extended fibre lying over $x$ belongs to this chart because $h\notin Q'$, so the fibre $C\otimes_D k$ is geometrically regular at $x$ in the sense of [F15].

abla_{A_0}h)\xi$, $h
abla_{A_0}\xi$, and $h^2\xi$. These terms define a bounded map $H^{k+1}	o H^{k-1}$. They are compact: $(
abla_{A_0}h)\xi$ factors through the compact inclusion $H^{k+1}\hookrightarrow H^{k-1}$ followed by multiplication in the algebra $H^{k-1}$; $h

If no constant bounded $\|\xi\|_{H^{k+1}}$ by $\|\Delta_A\xi\|_{H^{k-1}}$, choose $\|\xi_j\|_{H^{k+1}}=1$ with $\Delta_A\xi_j\to0$. For a zero mode $\psi$, integration by parts gives $0=\|D_5\psi\|^2=\|D_4\psi\|^2+\|\partial_t\psi\|^2$. Thus $\psi$ is independent of $t$ and lies in $\ker D_4$; conversely every such spinor gives a periodic product zero mode. In general its complex dimension is $n_++n_-$, identifying the smooth negative-chirality kernel with the cokernel by the formal $L^2$ adjoint. final_edge_fact_uses.text: [A1] The exact rank-two theorem supplies the ordinary framed ASD connection of a regular rank-two datum by its raw forward monad/projection construction, extends it smoothly over infinity, and proves $q_2=-k$. proof_steps.claim: Stabilize a rank-one raw datum by $W'=\mathbb C\oplus\mathbb C$, $I'=(I,0)$ and $J'=(J,0)^t$, retaining $V,B_1,B_2$. Stabilization intertwines $T$ with the rank-two compact action having framing weights $(h,1)$. They hold for every first-order Hermitian family defined above, hence also for the subset satisfying the exact locally-free/cohomology-base-change hypotheses retained in [A1]; no extra family statement is obtained from an orbit-set bijection. proof_steps.claim: If $K=\varnothing$ or $f(K)\subseteq\mathcal A_\infty^*$, the constant homotopy suffices. Otherwise realize the given finite simplicial complex by its barycentric coordinates as a compact subset of $\mathbb R^q$, taking $q\ge1$. The compact family $f(\overline U_2)$ is uniformly stable under a sufficiently small $C^1$ perturbation: each member has the finite-loop positive margin in [F2], and a finite subcover gives one positive tolerance. Include this $C^1$ norm among the finitely many seminorms in which all forthcoming approximations are to be small.

Choose a smooth ambient cutoff $0\le\theta\le1$ which is zero on a neighborhood of $\overline U_0$ and one on a neighborhood of the disjoint compact set $K\setminus U_1$. Such a cutoff follows from finitely many ambient bumps separating the two compact sets. Define on $K$ the continuous family $h(s)=f(s)+\theta(s)(g(s)-f(s))$. The straight interpolation from $f$ to $h$ is fixed near $L$ and is $\delta$-small in every selected seminorm. By the uniform $C^1$ margin in step 1.1, choosing $\delta$ small ensures it is irreducible on $\overline U_2$. Its closed reducible-parameter set $R=\{s\in K:h(s)\notin\mathcal A_\infty^*\}$ is compact and contained in $K\setminus U_2$, hence in the ambient open region where $\theta=1$ and $h=g$ on $K$. If $R$ is empty the first interpolation already proves the result. Otherwise choose an ambient open $W$ with compact closure in $V\cap\{\theta=1\}$, containing $R$ and avoiding a neighborhood of $L$, and a smooth cutoff $0\le\chi\le1$ with compact support $T\subset W$, positive on $R$. All subsequent holonomy calculations use the ambient family $g$ on $W$; on the actual parameter subset $K\cap W$ this is exactly $h$.

Define on all of $K$ the final family $h_v(s)=h(s)+\chi(s)\sum_{j,a}v_{j,a}b_{j,a}(s)$, with the added term zero off $W$. The compact support $T$ and its spatial smoothness make this term continuous in every section seminorm, and its value uniformly small in any specified finite list by taking $v$ sufficiently small. If $\chi(s)>0$, then $s\in W$ and $h(s)=g(s)$, so $h_v(s)$ has the holonomy tuple $\Phi(s,v)$, which has no common invariant proper subspace by step 9.1. Therefore $h_v(s)$ is irreducible. If $\chi(s)=0$, then $s\notin R$ since $\chi$ is positive on $R$, so $h_v(s)=h(s)$ was already irreducible. The straight perturbation homotopy from $h$ to $h_v$ is fixed on an open neighborhood of $L$. Concatenate it with the interpolation in step 3.1. Choose $\delta$ and then $v$ within half of each requested seminorm tolerance; the triangle inequality gives the asserted bounds relative to the original $f$ for the entire concatenated homotopy. final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F3] [[thm-sobolev-compactness-and-elliptic-estimates-give-fredholm-hodge-decomposition]] supplies Green inverses and smooth kernels for compact scalar-symbol Laplace-type operators. proof_steps.claim: If $T(f,\omega)=0$ with $(f,\omega)\in H^1$, step 3.1 and weak regularity [F3] make both entries smooth and harmonic. By [F2], $f$ is constant and the harmonic two-form is zero, giving a one-dimensional complex kernel. The same vanishing has an elementary check: $d^*\omega=0$ and $*\omega=\omega$ imply $d\omega=0$; since $H^2=0$, write $\omega=d\beta$, and [F4] gives $\|\omega\|_2^2=\int\omega\wedge\overline\omega=\int d(\beta\wedge\overline\omega)=0$. For $T^*\alpha=0$, one has $d^*\alpha=0$ and $d\alpha$ anti-self-dual; hence $\|d\alpha\|_2^2=-\int d\alpha\wedge d\overline\alpha=0$ by [F4]. Thus $\alpha$ is harmonic and is zero by $H^1=0$. The Green inverse $G_1:L^2\to H^2$ of $\Delta_1$, which exists without a kernel by [F2]–[F3], gives the bounded right inverse $T^*G_1:L^2\to H^1$ of $T$. For the full Dirac operator use the block $\mathscr D=\begin{pmatrix}0&T^*\\T&0\end{pmatrix}$ under the unitary identifications. Its square is the direct sum of the Hodge Laplacians in step 3.1, with domain $H^2$ by [F3]. It is symmetric on $H^1$ by smooth density. If $v\in\operatorname{dom}\mathscr D^*$, choose $u\in H^1$ with $(\mathscr D+i)u=(\mathscr D^*+i)v$; then $v-u$ is in $\ker(\mathscr D^*+i)=\operatorname{ran}(\mathscr D-i)^\perp=0$. Thus the adjoint domain is $H^1$ and $\mathscr D$ is selfadjoint there. The same identities show its squared domain is $H^2$, using weak regularity when $u\in H^1$ and $\mathscr D u\in H^1$.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] [[thm-qftx-taubes-arbitrary-divisor-plane-vortex]]: for every effective finite divisor of degree $|n|$ there is a smooth finite-energy planar critical pair with flux $2\pi n$ (using conjugation for $n<0$); for the empty divisor it is the vacuum. The local unwound exterior gauge has $q=\sqrt\xi e^{h/2}$ and $A=-\tfrac12*dh$; that degree-changing exterior gauge is not asserted to extend globally. proof_steps.claim: For an end trace with exterior phase $n\theta+\phi$, choose a smooth radial cutoff $\eta$ which is zero on a disk containing the noncanonical region and one outside a larger disk. The real function $\chi=-\eta\phi$ extends smoothly by zero to the whole plane; the allowed gauge transformation $(q,A)\mapsto(e^{i\chi}q,A+d\chi)$ therefore makes the exterior phase exactly $n\theta$. This constructs the asserted degree-zero exterior phase cleanup without attempting to extend a degree-$n$ angular map across the disk. For the planar minimizer in [F2], write $P=|P|e^{i\vartheta}$ on the exterior; $\vartheta-n\theta$ is single-valued, smooth and tends to zero because $P(z)=z^n(1+O(|z|^{-1}))$ for $n\ge0$ (use the conjugate construction for $n<0$). Applying the same cutoff extension to $-(\vartheta-n\theta)$ changes its exterior fields to $q^*=\rho_*e^{in\theta}$ and $A^*=n\,d\theta-\tfrac12*dh$; hence $A^*-n\,d\theta$ decays exponentially.

In canonical exterior gauge write $q=\rho e^{in\theta}$ and $\alpha=A-n\,d\theta$. Directly, $D_Aq=e^{in\theta}(d\rho-i\rho\alpha)$, so the real and imaginary terms are orthogonal and $|D_Aq|^2=|d\rho|^2+\rho^2|\alpha|^2$. Apply step 3.1 first to $p_0$ and $p_*$, defining its finite energy to be $C_0$, and then to $p_*$ and $p_1$, defining its finite energy to be $C_1$. Combining steps 1.1 and 4.1 gives $0\le\inf\mathcal E_L-T_nL\le C_0+C_1-2\ell T_n$ for every $L\ge2\ell$; the right side is a finite constant independent of $L$, proving the bounded-remainder conclusion. final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] A square-zero smooth Dolbeault operator on a finite-rank bundle has local holomorphic frames, and intertwining maps are holomorphic. [[lem-qftx-local-integrable-dolbeault-frames]]

proof_steps.claim: In the chart w=λ₂/λ₁ on a real incidence fiber, the projected horizontal (0,1) directions are H₁=∂bar_z₁−w∂z₂ and H₂=∂bar_z₂+w∂z₁. Restrict H and ∇ to the totally real graph locus M=HP¹. Its smooth real incidence is diffeomorphic to Z by (P,[v])↦[v], with inverse [v]↦(span(v,jv),[v]); the explicit charts in [F3] verify smoothness. Under this identification dp(D) is exactly the span of H₁,H₂ in step 1.1: write X_z=((z₁,-bar_z₂),(z₂,bar_z₁)) and solve v(1,w)^T=0. Therefore the restricted smooth connection has F(H₁,H₂)=0 for every w, so all three self-dual coefficients in step 1.1 vanish. Hence it is ASD. Evaluation intertwines the original holomorphic operator on E with the reconstructed vertical/horizontal Dolbeault operator: it is holomorphic vertically, and on D its derivative is exactly the canonical relative derivative δ by step 3.1. These directions generate the (0,1) tangent in step 1.1, proving equality of the full operators, not just of underlying bundles.

Starting from A in step 1.1, its constant real-line sections identify the reconstructed smooth H with E. Along every alpha-plane the recovered connection has the same derivative as A; the cotangent uniqueness in step 3.1 makes the full connections equal. The unitary reality pairing and framing also agree. Starting from a Ward bundle, step 4.1 proves evaluation is a holomorphic isomorphism from the reconstructed pullback to the original bundle, and step 5.2 preserves its reality pairing and metric. These constructions and identities apply to morphisms as well, so descend to inverse maps on based unitary gauge and framed holomorphic isomorphism classes. No irreducibility or absence of parallel sections was used.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] For every continuous map from a finite polyhedron into $\mathcal A_\infty$, with irreducible values on a subpolyhedron, the relative avoidance lemma supplies a homotopy fixed on that subpolyhedron and an open neighborhood of it whose endpoint is entirely irreducible. Its complete argument and exact batch-56 inputs were inspected; the configuration and stabilizer suppliers now have current ready Step 1 records ([[lem-qftx-relative-finite-parameter-irreducible-avoidance]]).

proof_steps.claim: The affine space $\mathcal A_\infty$ contains $A_0$. Apply [F2] to the constant map from a one-point polyhedron with empty subpolyhedron and value $A_0$. Its endpoint is an element of $\mathcal A_\infty^*$, proving nonemptiness.

Let $A,B\in\mathcal A_\infty^*$. The affine path $\gamma(t)=(1-t)A+tB$ is continuous in the Fréchet topology and has irreducible endpoints. Apply [F2] with $K=I$ and $L=\{0,1\}$. The resulting endpoint path remains in $\mathcal A_\infty^*$ and fixes both endpoints, so the locus is path-connected.

Apply [F2] to $F$ with $K=D^{j+1}$ and $L=\partial D^{j+1}=S^j$. Its boundary is already irreducible, so the endpoint is a map $G:D^{j+1}\to\mathcal A_\infty^*$ agreeing with $u$ on the boundary. Choose the based point $x_0\in S^j$ with $u(x_0)=A$. Since the disk is convex, $C_t(x)=(1-t)x+tx_0$ remains in the disk and fixes $x_0$. Then $G(C_t(x))$ is a homotopy from $G$ to the constant map at $A$ that fixes $x_0$ and remains in $\mathcal A_\infty^*$. Restricting it to $S^j$ gives a based nullhomotopy of $u$; by [F3], its class in $\pi_j(\mathcal A_\infty^*,A)$ is zero. Since $j$ and $u$ were arbitrary, every stated homotopy group vanishes.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F3] For the stated Sobolev index, the smooth irreducible projection $\mathcal A_\infty^*\to\mathcal A_\infty^*/\overline{\mathcal G}_\infty$ is a locally trivial topological principal $\overline{\mathcal G}_\infty$-bundle with its actual $C^\infty$ quotient topology; the Sobolev irreducible locus $\mathcal A_k^*$ is open. [[thm-qftx-sobolev-smooth-irreducible-gauge-bundle]]

proof_steps.claim: Choose the fixed integer $k>r/2+1$. The smooth clause of [F3], applied with the configuration data [F2], makes $q_*$ a locally trivial principal $\overline{\mathcal G}^\infty(P)$-bundle. By [F4], its total space is nonempty, path connected, and has $\pi_j=0$ for every $j\ge1$, so it is weakly contractible in the sense used in [F6]. For a constant central gauge section $u=\zeta I_N$, the local action formula gives $A^u=A$ because $u^{-1}Au=A$ and $du=0$; hence reduced and full gauge groups have the same orbits on $\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P)$.

The locus $\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P)$ is gauge invariant: in the chosen frame, the based holonomy subgroup of $A^u$ is $u(p_m)^{-1}\operatorname{Hol}_{p_m}(A)u(p_m)$, so it has the same invariant subspaces up to conjugation. It is open: by [F2], the inclusion $\mathcal A^\infty(P)\hookrightarrow\mathcal A_k(P)$ is continuous, as each fixed $H^k$ norm is bounded by finitely many smooth derivative seminorms on the finite compact atlas. The smooth irreducible locus is the inverse image of the Sobolev irreducible locus, which is open by [F3]. The full orbit projection $q$ is open because, for any open $U\subseteq\mathcal A^\infty(P)$, its saturation $q^{-1}(q(U))=\bigcup_{u\in\mathcal G^\infty(P)}U\cdot u$ is open. For fixed smooth $u$, the map $A\mapsto u^{-1}Au+u^{-1}du$ is continuous in every finite-atlas derivative seminorm by the Leibniz rule; its inverse is the same formula for $u^{-1}$, so each gauge translate is a homeomorphism. Therefore $q(\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P))$ is open and $q|_{\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P)}$ is an open quotient map onto this subset. The reduced and full actions have the same orbits there, so their quotient topologies identify the reduced orbit space homeomorphically with $q(\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P))$; this proves the claim about $\iota$ in the Statement. If $q$ had a continuous section, its restriction to this open subset would take each irreducible orbit to a point in that same orbit, hence into $\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P)$. Via the stated homeomorphism, this would give a continuous section of $q_*$, contradicting step 3.1. Thus $q$ has no continuous section.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F6] For a smooth-coefficient elliptic operator on a compact manifold, distributional solutions gain two Sobolev derivatives when the right-hand side gains the corresponding Sobolev order, with the stated elliptic estimate. [[thm-elliptic-differential-operators-on-compact-vector-bundles-have-parametrices-and-regularity]]

proof_steps.claim: For the smooth-space clause, fix now a smooth irreducible center $A\in\mathcal A_\infty^*$ and use the Banach slice and trivialization established in step 4.1. Put $U_A=\Phi_A(S_{A,\varepsilon}\times\bar{\mathcal G}_{k+1})$ and $V_A=\pi_k(S_{A,\varepsilon})$. Since $U_A$ is open in $\mathcal A_k^*$, $U_A\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*$ is open in the stated $C^\infty$ topology; set $S_A^\infty=S_{A,\varepsilon}\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*$ and $V_A^\infty=\pi_\infty(S_A^\infty)$. For a smooth $B\in U_A$, its unique reduced gauge class from step 4.1 has a representative $u\in\mathcal G_{k+1}$. It satisfies $d_A^*(B^{u^{-1}}-A)=0$. Locally in a bundle frame, write $C_j=uB_j u^{-1}-(\partial_j u)u^{-1}-A_j$. Substitution in $d_A^*C=0$, use of $\partial_i(u^{-1})=-u^{-1}(\partial_i u)u^{-1}$, and multiplication on the right by $u$ isolate the equation $g^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j u=R(A,B,g;u,u^{-1},du)$ on each chart. Every term in $R$ is a finite product of smooth coefficients (including first derivatives of $A,B$) and factors among $u,u^{-1},du$; hence the principal operator is the scalar smooth Laplacian on each matrix entry. If $u\in H^{r+1}$ for $r\ge k$, then this right-hand side lies in $H^r$ by [F7] and the smooth coefficient bounds. Elliptic regularity [F6] gives $u\in H^{r+2}$. Iteration proves $u$ smooth; changing its representative by an element of the finite center preserves smoothness. Thus every smooth point of the Banach saturation has a smooth trivialization representative, and $U_A\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*=\pi_\infty^{-1}(V_A^\infty)$.

Suppose smooth $B_j\to B$ in $C^\infty$ within $U_A\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*$. The Banach trivialization from step 4.1 gives convergence of their slice representatives in $H^k$ and of their reduced gauge classes in $H^{k+1}$. In a quotient chart around the limiting class from step 1.1, choose lifts $u_j,u$ that converge in $H^{k+1}$; this is possible because the finite center acts by disjoint translates. The equation in step 5.2 and elliptic estimates [F6] bootstrap convergence: if $u_j\to u$ in $H^{r+1}$, then the assumed $C^\infty$ convergence gives $B_j\to B$ in $H^{r+1}$, and [F7] makes the right-hand sides converge in $H^r$. Apply the elliptic estimate to $u_j-u$, using also their already known $H^{k+1}$ convergence for the $L^2$ term, to get $u_j\to u$ in $H^{r+2}$. Induction gives convergence in every Sobolev order, which on compact $M$ is the $C^\infty$ section topology. The slice representatives converge in $C^\infty$ by their action formula. Conversely the forward action is continuous in the $C^\infty$ topology by multiplication and differentiation of smooth sections. The saturation $U_A\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*$ is open, and $V_A^\infty$ is open in the quotient because the quotient map is open: the saturation of any open set is a union of its open gauge translates. The restricted map $S_A^\infty\times\bar{\mathcal G}_\infty\to\pi_\infty^{-1}(V_A^\infty)$ is therefore a homeomorphism for the actual quotient topology, and it is equivariant. This proves the smooth-space topological principal bundle claim.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F3] [[thm-interior-w-two-p-estimate-for-uniformly-elliptic-equations]]: for $p>2$ on a two-dimensional ball, the interior $W^{2,p}$ norm is bounded by the local $L^p$ norms of the solution and its Laplacian.

proof_steps.claim: To obtain derivative decay, fix $\alpha<\alpha'<\sqrt\kappa$ and use step 3.3 at rate $\alpha'$. On each unit ball centered at large $z$, both $w$ and $\Delta w=\kappa(1-e^{-w})$ are $O(e^{-\alpha'|z|})$. By [F3] and [F5], $w$ has a $C^{1,\beta}$ norm of that order on the concentric half-ball for some $\beta>0$. Thus the right-hand side has a $C^{0,\beta}$ norm of the same order, and [F4] gives $C^{2,\beta}$ decay on a smaller ball. Inductively, for each multi-index $\gamma$, differentiating $\Delta w=\kappa(1-e^{-w})$ gives $\Delta D^\gamma w=\kappa e^{-w}D^\gamma w+G_\gamma$, where $G_\gamma$ is a finite sum of products of lower derivatives of $w$ and is exponentially small by the induction hypothesis. Applying [F3] and [F4] on nested unit balls gives the same $e^{-\alpha'|z|}$ bound for two more derivatives. Since $e^{-\alpha'|z|}\le e^{-\alpha|z|}$ outside a fixed disk, every finite derivative has the stated rate.

fact_uses.text: [F3] A $C^1$ diffeomorphism maps Lebesgue null sets to Lebesgue null sets, so composition of almost-everywhere classes with $\Phi$ or $\Psi$ is well defined independently of representatives ([[lem-c-one-diffeomorphisms-map-lebesgue-null-sets-to-null-sets]]).

proof_steps.claim: Since $\Psi$ has bounded first derivatives on $\overline{V_0}$, [F2] gives, for every nonnegative measurable $f$ on $V_0$ and $1\le p<\infty$, $$\int_{U_0}|f(\Phi(x))|^p\,dx=\int_{\Phi(U_0)}|f(y)|^p|\det D\Psi(y)|\,dy\le C\int_{V_0}|f(y)|^p\,dy.$$ For $p=\infty$, [F3] makes composition well defined on a.e. classes and gives $\|f\circ\Phi\|_{L^\infty(U_0)}\le\|f\|_{L^\infty(V_0)}$. Thus pullback by $\Phi$ is bounded on the stated $L^p$ spaces. The analogous estimate for $\Psi$ holds when $\Psi(V_0)\subseteq U_0$.

Exponent $p=\infty$. Let $u\in W^{k,\infty}(V_0;\mathbb K)$. Since $V_0$ has finite measure, [F8] gives $u\in W^{k,q}(V_0)$ for any finite $q\ge1$, so step 3.1 yields the same weak derivative formulas for $u\circ\Phi$ in one such $W^{k,q}(U_0)$. Each formula field $h_\alpha$ is in $L^\infty(U_0)$ because its factors $(D^\beta u)\circ\Phi$ are essentially bounded by [F3] and its coefficients are bounded; also $u\circ\Phi\in L^\infty(U_0)$ by [F3]. Hence these weak derivatives lie in $L^\infty$, giving $u\circ\Phi\in W^{k,\infty}(U_0)$ and the claimed norm bound.

Here $\mathbf V_{\vec Y}=e_1$ and $\mathbf W=e_1^{-1}$, whence $\mathbf V^\vee\mathbf V=1$, $\mathbf V^\vee\mathbf W^\vee=1$, and $t_1t_2\mathbf W\mathbf V=t_1t_2$. Substitution in the tangent character gives $t_1+t_2$; the two additive weights are $\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2$, so the Euler class is $\epsilon_1\epsilon_2$.

The degree-one coefficient is the sum over the single fixed point, so it equals $(\epsilon_1\epsilon_2)^{-1}$. This is a formal equivariant fixed-point contribution, not an asserted continuum path-integral value.

proof_steps.claim: A two-tuple of partitions with total size one places its single box in exactly one of the two colors, so the only possibilities are $(\{(0,0)\},\varnothing)$ and $(\varnothing,\{(0,0)\})$. Their quotient representatives have $V$-characters $e_1$ and $e_2$, respectively.

Interchanging the two colors gives the second displayed character and $E_2$.

Each fixed-point contribution is the reciprocal of its Euler product, so the degree-one coefficient is $E_1^{-1}+E_2^{-1}$. The TikZ drawing only records the two one-box colorings and is not used in this calculation.
