proof_steps.claim: Smoothness of the needed primitive does not require a theorem about varying complex structures. Choose smooth unit quaternionic frames of $Q_x$ on a base neighborhood and a smooth unitary frame of $E$. These identify the vertical problem exactly with the fixed $SU(2)$-invariant Hermitian $\mathcal O(-2)$ problem on $\mathbb CP^1$, componentwise in $E_x$. Set $B=\bar\partial^*G$ on vertical degree one. By [F3], $\bar\partial B=I-\Pi$, and by [F2] its degree-zero kernel is zero. The estimates [F4] and the first-order nature of $\bar\partial^*$ give $B:H^m\to H^{m+1}$ bounded for each $m$. For jointly smooth $f(x,t)$, base difference quotients converge in every fibre $H^m$ uniformly on compact base sets, by the Taylor formula and compactness of the fibre. Applying the fixed bounded $B$ shows $\partial_x^\beta(Bf)=B(\partial_x^\beta f)$ at every order in every $H^{m+1}$. Sobolev embedding on the fixed two-dimensional compact fibre, with arbitrarily large $m$, gives joint smoothness in $(x,t)$. For the horizontal coefficient problem, choose also a smooth unit quaternionic frame of $Q_x^\perp$. Together the two quaternionic frames give a smooth $Sp(2)$ transformation from a fixed pair of planes to $(Q_x,Q_x^\perp)$. Its complex-linear action on $\mathbb CP^3$ is holomorphic and preserves the Fubini–Study and tautological metrics. It therefore transports the horizontal quotient, its vertical Bott operator and its induced metric to the fixed $\mathcal O(-1)^{\oplus2}$ problem identified below. That inverse is likewise one fixed bounded operator componentwise, so the same derivative argument applies. Thus no moving-cokernel inverse or unproved parametric Green assertion is used.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F5] The fixed compact fibre Green inverse is bounded $H^m\to H^{m+2}$ for every integer $m\ge0$. [[thm-sobolev-compactness-and-elliptic-estimates-give-fredholm-hodge-decomposition]]

proof_steps.claim: For the global metric splitting, the mixed component of $\bar\partial(s\sigma)$ is a vertical degree-one form with coefficient $\mathcal O(-1)^{\oplus2}\otimes E_x$. On a fibre it has a unique vertical primitive by [F4]. The fixed-fibre $B=\bar\partial^*G$ construction and smooth-parameter difference-quotient argument in [F2], with the estimates [F5], make that primitive smooth over the base. The same fibrewise uniqueness makes it agree across frame and chart changes. Denote the horizontal correction by $\phi(s)$; then $\psi(s)=s\sigma+\phi(s)$ has zero mixed differential. If $s$ is the image of a closed representative $\alpha$, [F2]'s decomposition and closedness say that its horizontal remainder solves this same mixed equation. The difference is fibrewise holomorphic in $\mathcal O(-1)^{\oplus2}\otimes E_x$, hence zero by [F4]. Thus $\psi(s)=\alpha-\bar\partial_F\gamma$ is closed for a class image. The differential can still have a horizontal degree-two component for arbitrary $s$; the curvature component of the metric splitting is retained.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F3] For a smooth connection $A_0$, $\Delta_{A_0}$ is a smooth-coefficient, formally symmetric, nonnegative Laplace-type operator; the compact Hodge theorem gives a finite-dimensional smooth kernel, closed range, and the decomposition $H^r=\ker\Delta_{A_0}\oplus\Delta_{A_0}(H^{r+2})$ for every integer $r\ge0$. [[thm-sobolev-compactness-and-elliptic-estimates-give-fredholm-hodge-decomposition]], [[thm-elliptic-differential-operators-on-compact-vector-bundles-have-parametrices-and-regularity]]

proof_steps.claim: Apply [F3] with $r=k-1\ge0$ to $\Delta_{A_0}:H^{k+1}\to H^{k-1}$. Its kernel is finite dimensional, and the Hodge theorem gives the topological direct decomposition $H^{k-1}=\ker\Delta_{A_0}\oplus\Delta_{A_0}(H^{k+1})$. Thus its range is closed with codimension equal to the kernel dimension, so $\Delta_{A_0}$ is Fredholm of index zero. By [F6] and the compactness of $K_A$ from step 1.1, $\Delta_A=\Delta_{A_0}+K_A$ is Fredholm of index zero.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F4] The compact Sobolev inclusions $H^{s+1}\hookrightarrow H^s$ hold for all integer $s\ge0$, and the smooth reference operator has the elliptic estimate $\|\xi\|_{H^{k+1}}\le C(\|\Delta_{A_0}\xi\|_{H^{k-1}}+\|\xi\|_{L^2})$. [[thm-sobolev-compactness-and-elliptic-estimates-give-fredholm-hodge-decomposition]], [[thm-elliptic-differential-operators-on-compact-vector-bundles-have-parametrices-and-regularity]]

proof_steps.claim:
Fix the smooth reference connection $A_0$ from the configuration data and set $h=A-A_0\in H^k(T^*M\otimes\operatorname{ad}P)$. In a local orthonormal frame, $d_A=d_{A_0}+[h,\cdot]$ on zero-forms and $d_A^*=d_{A_0}^*-\iota_h$ on one-forms, where $\iota_h(a)=g^{ij}[h_i,a_j]$. Therefore $K_A:=\Delta_A-\Delta_{A_0}$ is a finite sum of terms of the forms $(
abla_{A_0}h)\xi$, $h
abla_{A_0}\xi$, and $h^2\xi$. These terms define a bounded map $H^{k+1}	o H^{k-1}$. They are compact: $(
abla_{A_0}h)\xi$ factors through the compact inclusion $H^{k+1}\hookrightarrow H^{k-1}$ followed by multiplication in the algebra $H^{k-1}$; $h
abla_{A_0}\xi$ and $h^2\xi$ first map boundedly into $H^k$ and then use the compact inclusion $H^k\hookrightarrow H^{k-1}$. Here $k-1>d/2$, so the needed multiplication bounds follow from [F8].

The smooth reference estimate [F4] and $\Delta_{A_0}=\Delta_A-K_A$ give $\|\xi\|_{H^{k+1}}\le C(\|\Delta_A\xi\|_{H^{k-1}}+\|K_A\xi\|_{H^{k-1}}+\|\xi\|_{L^2})$. The three terms in $K_A$ from step 1.1 satisfy $\|K_A\xi\|_{H^{k-1}}\le C_A\|\xi\|_{H^k}$. The Sobolev interpolation estimate $\|\xi\|_{H^k}\le\varepsilon\|\xi\|_{H^{k+1}}+C_\varepsilon\|\xi\|_{L^2}$ follows by finite-atlas localization and the estimate in [F5]. Choose $\varepsilon$ so that the resulting $H^{k+1}$ term is absorbed into the left side. This yields $\|\xi\|_{H^{k+1}}\le C_A'(\|\Delta_A\xi\|_{H^{k-1}}+\|\xi\|_{L^2})$.

If no constant bounded $\|\xi\|_{H^{k+1}}$ by $\|\Delta_A\xi\|_{H^{k-1}}$, choose $\|\xi_j\|_{H^{k+1}}=1$ with $\Delta_A\xi_j\to0$. By [F4], a subsequence converges in $L^2$; applying the estimate of step 2.2 to differences shows it is Cauchy in $H^{k+1}$. Its limit has $H^{k+1}$ norm one and lies in $\ker\Delta_A$, contradicting step 3.1. Thus $\|\xi\|_{H^{k+1}}\le C_A''\|\Delta_A\xi\|_{H^{k-1}}$. Together with bijectivity this proves the inverse $G_A$ is bounded.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] On a bounded extension domain, $W^{k,2}$ is a Banach algebra when $2k>d$, and the higher-order embedding gives $H^k\hookrightarrow C^1$ when $k>d/2+1$. The same estimates apply componentwise to finitely many localized bundle coefficients. [[cor-sobolev-algebra-above-the-critical-index]], [[thm-higher-order-sobolev-embedding]]

proof_steps.claim: Localize by the fixed finite partition and extend each compactly supported coefficient by zero into a bounded Euclidean ball. For $p=2$, $2k>d$; [F2] makes each localized $H^k$ coefficient a Banach algebra and gives its $C^1$ representative when $k>d/2+1$. The finite sum of these estimates proves the same algebra and embedding bounds for sections, matrix-valued functions, and forms in the chosen bundle atlas.

The finite-dimensional matrix exponential is smooth, has derivative the identity at zero on $\mathfrak{su}(N)$, and maps $\mathfrak{su}(N)$ into $SU(N)$. In the Banach algebra from step 2.1 its power series and every termwise derivative converge in $H^{k+1}$ on a sufficiently small ball, since the algebra norm is submultiplicative after an equivalent rescaling. The matrix logarithm series converges on a neighborhood of the identity; for a unitary matrix sufficiently close to identity its logarithm is anti-Hermitian, and its trace is zero because the determinant is one and the sum of the small eigenvalue angles lies in $2\pi\mathbb Z$. Hence pointwise $\exp$ and $\log$ give inverse smooth maps between neighborhoods of zero in $H^{k+1}(\operatorname{ad}P)$ and the identity in $\mathcal G_{k+1}$. The inverse-function theorem [F3] also supplies these local Banach charts. Their translated charts cover the group; changes of chart are smooth because the transition functions of $\operatorname{Ad}P$ act by smooth conjugation and the multiplication is a bounded bilinear Sobolev map. The pointwise product and inverse therefore close on $\mathcal G_{k+1}$ and are smooth, giving the asserted Hilbert Lie group.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F4] Every bounded sequence in $H^{k+1}$ of sections on the compact manifold has a subsequence converging in $H^k$. [[thm-elliptic-differential-operators-on-compact-vector-bundles-have-parametrices-and-regularity]], assertion 1.

proof_steps.claim: By [F4], a subsequence converges strongly in $H^k$ to a section $u$. The $H^k\hookrightarrow C^0$ embedding preserves the pointwise $SU(N)$ equations and the bundle transition law, so $u$ is a group-bundle section. In the gauge equation, $A_j\to A$, $B_j\to B$, and $u_j\to u$ in $H^k$; because $H^k$ is an algebra, $u_jB_j-A_ju_j\to uB-Au$ in $H^k$. Thus $du_j$ converges in $H^k$ and the local coefficients converge in $H^{k+1}$. The limit satisfies $du=uB-Au$, equivalently $B=A^u$, and $u\in\mathcal G_{k+1}$.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] The batch-56 stabilizer lemma states that evaluation identifies the Sobolev stabilizer with the centralizer of $\operatorname{Hol}_{p_m}(A)$ and proves that an irreducible standard representation has centralizer $Z_N$. Its full statement and proof were inspected and its current Step 1 record is ready. A smooth $A$ lies in each stated Sobolev connection space, so the $Z_N$ conclusion applies here ([[lem-qftx-gauge-stabilizer-and-properness]]).

proof_steps.claim: By [F1], $\mathcal A_\infty^*$ is exactly the set of connections whose holonomy action has no common proper nonzero invariant subspace. By [F2], for each such connection the stabilizer in the stated Sobolev gauge group is $Z_N$. The latter is the conditional stabilizer conclusion recorded separately from the holonomy criterion.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F1] The fixed-support Cauchy transform solves $\partial_{\bar w}Tq=q$ and maps compactly supported $C^{m,\alpha}$ data to $C^{m+1,\alpha}$ on every fixed disk with a finite bound. [[lem-local-holder-cauchy-transform-estimate]]

proof_steps.claim: First solve one equation with all other coordinates regarded as parameters $p$. Write $z_j=\rho w$ on a disk slightly larger than $|w|\le2$, choose a fixed smooth cutoff $\chi$ supported in $|w|<2$ and equal to one for $|w|\le1$, and put $a_\rho(w,p)=\rho A_j(\rho w,p)$. For fixed $0<\alpha<1$, its $C^\alpha_w$ norm is bounded uniformly on a compact parameter polydisc by $C\rho(M_0+\rho M_1)$, where $M_0,M_1$ bound $A_j$ and its first derivatives. Multiplication is bounded in the matrix Hölder norm by the product rule for increments, and [F1] bounds $K(p)u=T(\chi a_\rho u)$ on $C^\alpha(\overline D_2)$. Choose one positive $\rho$ making $\|K(p)\|<1/4$ for every parameter. By [F3], $g=1-K(p)g$ has a unique fixed point; $\|g-1\|\le\|K\|/(1-\|K\|)<1/3$, so $g$ is invertible everywhere. On $|w|<1$, [F1] gives $\partial_{\bar w}g=-a_\rho g$.

The coefficients depend smoothly on parameters as maps into $C^\alpha_w$, since all their parameter derivatives have uniform bounds on compact subsets. The inverse $(1+K(p))^{-1}$ is the uniformly convergent Neumann series; the identity $L(p+h)-L(p)=-L(p+h)(K(p+h)-K(p))L(p)$ for $L=(1+K)^{-1}$ gives its first derivative in operator norm, and induction gives derivatives of every order. Hence $g=L(p)1$ is smoothly parameter-dependent in $C^\alpha_w$. For each such derivative, the fixed-point equation and [F1] gain one $w$ derivative; induction gives all mixed $C^{m,\alpha}_w$ derivatives on the same radius, because only the inverse in the initial $C^\alpha$ space needs smallness. Thus $g$ is jointly smooth. If $A_j$ is holomorphic in an untouched coordinate, $K$ has zero antiholomorphic parameter derivative by [F2], and differentiating the inverse identity gives the same for $g$.

Gauge by this $g$ on the smaller disk. The transformed coefficient is $A_i'=g^{-1}(\partial_{\bar z_i}g+A_i g)$, and $A_j'=0$. The square-zero condition in a smooth frame is $\partial_{\bar z_i}A_j-\partial_{\bar z_j}A_i+[A_i,A_j]=0$, and it is preserved by the gauge transformation by direct conjugation of $(D'')^2$. Therefore every remaining $A_i'$ is holomorphic in $z_j$. Kill the next coordinate by steps 1.1–2.1 with a cutoff only in that coordinate. Their holomorphic-parameter assertion preserves $A_j'=0$. Continue through the finitely many coordinates, shrinking the respective coordinate disks as needed. The product of the resulting smooth invertible gauges has all transformed coefficients zero, proving the required local frame.

If $G$ and $H$ are two such frames, $D''G=D''H=0$ gives $\bar\partial(G^{-1}H)=0$. For smooth scalar functions this implies holomorphy: the one-variable Cauchy formula applies with the other variables fixed, and its iterated integral on a product of small circles gives a locally convergent joint power series. Thus the transition matrices are holomorphic, giving [F4]'s bundle structure; any other structure with the same $D''$ has the same class of holomorphic frames, hence agrees. In these frames an intertwining smooth bundle map has matrix $M$ with $\bar\partial M=0$, so is holomorphic by the same calculation, and the converse follows by the Leibniz rule. Rank zero is immediate and the finite gauge induction covers every positive finite rank.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] [[thm-sobolev-compactness-and-elliptic-estimates-give-fredholm-hodge-decomposition]] and [[thm-elliptic-differential-operators-on-compact-vector-bundles-have-parametrices-and-regularity]] give the weak regularity and shifted inverse for a formally symmetric scalar-symbol Laplace-type operator on the compact product.

proof_steps.claim: Chirality anticommutes with $D_4$ and is parallel, so $D_5^2=D_4^2-\partial_t^2$. It has scalar positive principal symbol and smooth coefficients. Formal symmetry follows from unitary connection compatibility and periodic integration by parts. The same shifted-resolvent argument applies to $D_4$ and $D_5$ on a general compact background: each square has scalar positive principal symbol, and [F2] gives the inverse of its positive shift from $L^2$ to $H^2$; multiplying by $D_j\mp i$ gives surjectivity of $D_j\pm i$ and the $H^1$ selfadjoint domain exactly as in [F1]. An $L^2$ weak chiral cokernel vector also has square zero distributionally; testing against smooth sections and using their $H^2$ density puts it in the adjoint domain of the selfadjoint square, hence in $H^2$, and [F2] then makes it smooth. This justifies identifying the cokernel with the negative-chirality kernel. Weak kernels are smooth by the same argument. For a zero mode $\psi$, integration by parts gives $0=\|D_5\psi\|^2=\|D_4\psi\|^2+\|\partial_t\psi\|^2$. Thus $\psi$ is independent of $t$ and lies in $\ker D_4$; conversely every such spinor gives a periodic product zero mode. In general its complex dimension is $n_++n_-$, identifying the smooth negative-chirality kernel with the cokernel by the formal $L^2$ adjoint. For the concrete round twist this dimension is $1$ by [F1]. This avoids any unproved general spectral-flow identity.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [A1] The exact rank-two theorem supplies the ordinary framed ASD connection of a regular rank-two datum by its raw forward monad/projection construction, extends it smoothly over infinity, and proves $q_2=-k$. Its exact GAGA, coupled-vanishing and intrinsic normal-form hypotheses are retained in the rank-one raw emptiness deduction. [[thm-qftx-zero-fi-regular-adhm-asd-correspondence]]

proof_steps.claim: Stabilize a rank-one raw datum by $W'=\mathbb C\oplus\mathbb C$, $I'=(I,0)$ and $J'=(J,0)^t$, retaining $V,B_1,B_2$. Then $I'J'=IJ$, $I'I'^\dagger=II^\dagger$ and $J'^\dagger J'=J^\dagger J$. The word span is unchanged and $\ker J'=\ker J$, so both moments and regularity are unchanged. On the finite stereographic chart the raw kernel matrix annihilates the added framing line, and its orthogonal projection is $P_1\oplus1$. Thus [A1] produces a smooth rank-two ASD connection whose restriction to that chart is a line connection plus the flat added line and whose charge is $q_2=-k$. By [F2] its determinant curvature vanishes. On that chart this curvature is exactly the first line's curvature, so the whole rank-two curvature is zero there. Smoothness makes it zero also at infinity, hence $q_2=0$ and $k=0$. Thus no regular rank-one zero-FI datum exists for $k>0$, conditional on the exact retained rank-two input. By [F6], a regular complex rank-one orbit would have such a zero-real-moment representative, so the same emptiness conclusion applies to the complex regular quotient.

A regular raw first-order family with $k>0$ would reduce to a prohibited datum from step 1.1, so none exists; the connection family for $k>0$ has no allowable special fiber by step 1.2. At $k=0$ the rank-zero internal $D$-module and all raw maps are uniquely zero, with trivial internal gauge group. Its forward monad is the constant framed line and its forward connection is $d$, also over $D$. Step 3.1 supplies a unique framed gauge from every first-order connection object to this one. Thus this explicit construction is an equivalence of the two first-order groupoids. Reduction and involution-preserving scalar maps commute with it, because the zero datum and the constant line pull back to themselves and the framed trivializing isomorphism is unique. The same argument after complexifying the real tangent spaces gives zero complexified tangent spaces; it does not assert a correspondence for arbitrary complex connections without the Hermitian real condition.

Stabilization intertwines $T$ with the rank-two compact action having framing weights $(h,1)$. In the zero-charge classification, inverse rotations and framing changes send a flat framed object to a flat framed object; the unique framed parallel trivialization identifies it with the same point. Its uniqueness also makes the first-order identifications equivariant. They hold for every first-order Hermitian family defined above, hence also for the subset satisfying the exact locally-free/cohomology-base-change hypotheses retained in [A1]; no extra family statement is obtained from an orbit-set bijection. Positive-FI rank-one stable data and their non-locally-free sheaves and formal fixed-point series were not used in any step.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] The finite-holonomy lemma states that $\mathcal A_\infty^*$ is open and supplies finite based loops witnessing each irreducible connection. Its complete authored proof and exact batch-56 inputs were inspected; the configuration and stabilizer suppliers now have current ready Step 1 records ([[lem-qftx-irreducible-finite-holonomy-witness]]).

proof_steps.claim: If $K=\varnothing$ or $f(K)\subseteq\mathcal A_\infty^*$, the constant homotopy suffices. Otherwise realize the given finite simplicial complex by its barycentric coordinates as a compact subset of $\mathbb R^q$, taking $q\ge1$. Let $U=f^{-1}(\mathcal A_\infty^*)$, an open neighborhood of $L$ by [F2]. Choose nested relatively open neighborhoods $U_0,U_1,U_2$ of $L$ in $K$ with $\overline U_0\subset U_1$, $\overline U_1\subset U_2$, and $\overline U_2\subset U$; if $L=\varnothing$ take them empty. The compact family $f(\overline U_2)$ is uniformly stable under a sufficiently small $C^1$ perturbation: each member has the finite-loop positive margin in [F2], and a finite subcover gives one positive tolerance. Include this $C^1$ norm among the finitely many seminorms in which all forthcoming approximations are to be small.

Choose a smooth ambient cutoff $0\le\theta\le1$ which is zero on a neighborhood of $\overline U_0$ and one on a neighborhood of the disjoint compact set $K\setminus U_1$. Such a cutoff follows from finitely many ambient bumps separating the two compact sets. Define on $K$ the continuous family $h(s)=f(s)+\theta(s)(g(s)-f(s))$. The straight interpolation from $f$ to $h$ is fixed near $L$ and is $\delta$-small in every selected seminorm. By the uniform $C^1$ margin in step 1.1, choosing $\delta$ small ensures it is irreducible on $\overline U_2$. Its closed reducible-parameter set $R=\{s\in K:h(s)\notin\mathcal A_\infty^*\}$ is compact and contained in $K\setminus U_2$, hence in the ambient open region where $\theta=1$ and $h=g$ on $K$. If $R$ is empty the first interpolation already proves the result. Otherwise choose an ambient open $W$ with compact closure in $V\cap\{\theta=1\}$, containing $R$ and avoiding a neighborhood of $L$, and a smooth cutoff $0\le\chi\le1$ with compact support $T\subset W$, positive on $R$. All subsequent holonomy calculations use the ambient family $g$ on $W$; on the actual parameter subset $K\cap W$ this is exactly $h$.

Define on all of $K$ the final family $h_v(s)=h(s)+\chi(s)\sum_{j,a}v_{j,a}b_{j,a}(s)$, with the added term zero off $W$. The compact support $T$ and its spatial smoothness make this term continuous in every section seminorm, and its value uniformly small in any specified finite list by taking $v$ sufficiently small. If $\chi(s)>0$, then $s\in W$ and $h(s)=g(s)$, so $h_v(s)$ has the holonomy tuple $\Phi(s,v)$, which has no common invariant proper subspace by step 9.1. Therefore $h_v(s)$ is irreducible. If $\chi(s)=0$, then $s\notin R$ since $\chi$ is positive on $R$, so $h_v(s)=h(s)$ was already irreducible. The straight perturbation homotopy from $h$ to $h_v$ is fixed on an open neighborhood of $L$. Concatenate it with the interpolation in step 3.1. Choose $\delta$ and then $v$ within half of each requested seminorm tolerance; the triangle inequality gives the asserted bounds relative to the original $f$ for the entire concatenated homotopy. All formulas are global on $K$, so faces and cofaces agree automatically.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F3] [[thm-sobolev-compactness-and-elliptic-estimates-give-fredholm-hodge-decomposition]] supplies Green inverses and smooth kernels for compact scalar-symbol Laplace-type operators. [[thm-elliptic-differential-operators-on-compact-vector-bundles-have-parametrices-and-regularity]] supplies Sobolev domains, weak regularity, smooth density and compact Sobolev inclusions.

proof_steps.claim: If $T(f,\omega)=0$ with $(f,\omega)\in H^1$, step 3.1 and weak regularity [F3] make both entries smooth and harmonic. By [F2], $f$ is constant and the harmonic two-form is zero, giving a one-dimensional complex kernel. The same vanishing has an elementary check: $d^*\omega=0$ and $*\omega=\omega$ imply $d\omega=0$; since $H^2=0$, write $\omega=d\beta$, and [F4] gives $\|\omega\|_2^2=\int\omega\wedge\overline\omega=\int d(\beta\wedge\overline\omega)=0$. For $T^*\alpha=0$, one has $d^*\alpha=0$ and $d\alpha$ anti-self-dual; hence $\|d\alpha\|_2^2=-\int d\alpha\wedge d\overline\alpha=0$ by [F4]. Thus $\alpha$ is harmonic and is zero by $H^1=0$. The Green inverse $G_1:L^2\to H^2$ of $\Delta_1$, which exists without a kernel by [F2]–[F3], gives the bounded right inverse $T^*G_1:L^2\to H^1$ of $T$. The range is therefore all $L^2$, the kernel is finite, and $T$ is Fredholm with index $1$. The unitary maps in step 2.1 transfer this conclusion to $D^+_{A_+}$.

For the full Dirac operator use the block $\mathscr D=\begin{pmatrix}0&T^*\\T&0\end{pmatrix}$ under the unitary identifications. Its square is the direct sum of the Hodge Laplacians in step 3.1, with domain $H^2$ by [F3]. It is symmetric on $H^1$ by smooth density. For $P=\mathscr D^2$, [F3] applied to the positive operator $P+1$ gives its inverse $B:L^2\to H^2$: its kernel is zero by the identity $((P+1)u,u)=\|\mathscr D u\|^2+\|u\|^2$. Then $(\mathscr D\mp i)B$ maps $L^2$ to $H^1$ and is a right inverse of $\mathscr D\pm i$. If $v\in\operatorname{dom}\mathscr D^*$, choose $u\in H^1$ with $(\mathscr D+i)u=(\mathscr D^*+i)v$; then $v-u$ is in $\ker(\mathscr D^*+i)=\operatorname{ran}(\mathscr D-i)^\perp=0$. Thus the adjoint domain is $H^1$ and $\mathscr D$ is selfadjoint there. The same identities show its squared domain is $H^2$, using weak regularity when $u\in H^1$ and $\mathscr D u\in H^1$.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F6] The disk is a bounded $W^{2,p}$-extension domain by [[thm-extension-theorem-for-bounded-smooth-domains]], and [[thm-higher-order-sobolev-embedding]] gives $C^{1,\beta}$ representatives for $p>2$ and $0<\beta<1-2/p$.

proof_steps.claim: Set $G_R(v)=\kappa+L_Rv-\kappa A_Re^v$ and choose $L_R\ge\kappa\max_{\overline D_R}(A_Re^{\psi_R})$. For $v\le\psi_R$, $G_R'(v)=L_R-\kappa A_Re^v\ge0$, so the iteration map $T_R=(-\Delta+L_R)^{-1}G_R$ is order preserving. The subsolution inequality from step 2.1 gives $v_0\le T_Rv_0$ and the supersolution inequality from step 1.2 gives $T_R\psi_R\le\psi_R$, by positivity of the resolver in step 1.3. Thus $v_0\le v_1\le\cdots\le\psi_R$; every iterate after $v_0$ has zero Dirichlet trace. Each has a smooth representative: starting from smooth $v_0$ and $A_R$, rewrite its shifted resolvent equation as a Laplace equation, use boundedness and [F5] for $W^{2,p}$, then [F6]–[F7] and local bootstrapping; this also identifies continuous representatives up to the boundary. These representatives realize the order pointwise.

Since $v_0\le v_R\le\psi_R$ and $A_R$ is bounded on $\overline D_R$, the right-hand side in step 4.1 lies in $L^p(D_R)$ for every finite $p$. For a prescribed $0<\alpha<1$, choose $p>2/(1-\alpha)$. The disk is bounded and smooth, so [F5] gives $v_R\in W^{2,p}$; [F6] gives a $C^{1,\beta}$ representative with $\beta>\alpha$ and zero boundary values. The nonlinear right-hand side is then $C^{0,\alpha}$, and [F7] upgrades the weak solution to $C^{2,\alpha}(\overline D_R)$. Repeated local Schauder bootstrapping, using [F9], makes $v_R$ smooth in $D_R$. Setting $u_R=u_{s,R}+v_R$ proves its distributional equation and logarithmic center behavior.

On any smaller compact disk $K\Subset U$, [F8] applied on finitely many nested balls and the uniform $L^\infty$ bound of step 7.1 yields uniform $W^{2,p}$ bounds for $w_R$ for every finite $p>2$, since its Laplacian is bounded. For a prescribed $0<\alpha<1$, choose $p>2/(1-\alpha)$ and then $\beta$ with $\alpha<\beta<1-2/p$; [F6] gives a uniform $C^{1,\beta}$ bound on a slightly larger compact disk. As $e^s$ is smooth and $\Delta w_R=\kappa(e^s e^{w_R}-1)$, the right-hand side has a uniform $C^{0,\alpha}$ bound there; [F9] then yields a uniform $C^{2,\alpha}$ bound on $K$. These bounds are independent of $R$ and are the local compactness estimates used for disk exhaustion.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F5] [[lem-qftx-round-s4-spin-twist-index-one]] proves the actual round $E=S^+$ bundle has charge $1$, Chern number $-1$, chiral kernel dimension $1$ and cokernel dimension $0$, by the exact Hodge intertwiner and Green inverse.

proof_steps.claim: For the concrete unit round sphere choose $E=S^+$ with the induced Levi-Civita connection. By [A4] and [F5], this is the actual self-dual charge-one bundle with chiral index $1$; by [F6] its periodic real product kernel has dimension one and its central inverse-determinant action is $-1$. Thus the index-one sector in [A1] is explicitly instantiated with a complete local mathematical proof. In that quaternionic spin model, right multiplication by a quaternionic unit $j$ is an antiunitary map $J_0$ on $S^+\oplus S^-$, with $J_0^2=-1$. It commutes with the four Clifford matrices and $\Gamma$ and is parallel: the transition and connection matrices act from the left and hence commute with right multiplication. The same operation $J_E$ on the $SU(2)$ twist is parallel, antiunitary and has square $-1$. Define $J_5=\Gamma J_0$ on the spin factor. Then $J_5^2=-1$, it anticommutes with each of the four tangent Clifford matrices, and it anticommutes with $c_5=i\Gamma$ because anti-linearity changes $i$ to $-i$. Thus it is the pseudoreal Spin(5) structure, since even products of Clifford matrices commute with it. On the complex tensor product set $J=J_5\otimes J_E$; it is well-defined and antiunitary, $J^2=1$, and $JD_5=-D_5J$. Hence $J$ preserves the kernel and $iD_5$ commutes with $J$.

Chirality anticommutes with $D_4$ and is parallel, so $D_5^2=D_4^2-\partial_t^2$. It has scalar positive principal symbol and smooth coefficients. Formal symmetry follows from unitary connection compatibility and periodic integration by parts. This justifies identifying the cokernel with the negative-chirality kernel. Weak kernels are smooth by the same argument. For a zero mode $\psi$, integration by parts gives $0=\|D_5\psi\|^2=\|D_4\psi\|^2+\|\partial_t\psi\|^2$. For the concrete round twist this dimension is $1$ by [F1]. This avoids any unproved general spectral-flow identity.

The constant central automorphism acts by $-1$ on both chiral spinor kernels and cokernels, and fixes the background connection. fact_uses.text: [L3] The localization sequence and affine homotopy invariance hold, and the Chow groups of projective space over a field are $\mathbb Z$ in each dimension $0,\dots,n$ generated by the linear classes ([[lem-chow-localization-and-vector-bundle-homotopy]], [[lem-chow-groups-of-projective-space]]).

proof_steps.claim: Pushforward identities. Let $V\subseteq X$ be an integral closed subscheme of dimension $m$, so that $\pi^*[V]=[\mathbb P(\mathcal E|_V)]$ is an $(m+r-1)$-cycle. First suppose $\mathcal E|_V$ is trivial. The zero schemes of $r-1$ coordinate sections of $\mathcal O(1)$ are relative hyperplanes meeting in a section $\sigma:V\to\mathbb P(\mathcal E|_V)$, so $\xi^{r-1}\cap\pi^*[V]=\sigma_*[V]$ and $\pi_*\sigma_*[V]=[V]$. For any $\mathcal E$ and $0\le s<r-1$, the cycle $\xi^s\cap\pi^*[V]$ has dimension $m+r-1-s>m$ and is supported on $\mathbb P(\mathcal E|_V)$, whose image has dimension $m$; hence its components push to zero by [L4]. For the top power with general $\mathcal E$, choose a dense open $U\subseteq V$ trivializing the bundle. The identity $\pi_*(\xi^{r-1}\cap\pi^*[V])=[V]$ holds over $U$, and its difference is in $A_m(V)$ supported on $V\setminus U$. This complement has dimension less than $m$, so localization [L3] makes the difference zero. Both identities extend by linearity to all $\alpha\in A_*(X)$.

Surjectivity over a trivializing open. Let $U\subseteq X$ be an open on which $\mathcal E$ is trivial, so that $\mathbb P(\mathcal E)|_U\cong U\times\mathbb P^{r-1}$. The Chow group of $U\times\mathbb P^{r-1}$ is generated by the classes $\xi^i\cap\pi^*\alpha$ with $0\le i\le r-1$ and $\alpha\in A_*(U)$: stratify $\mathbb P^{r-1}$ by the affine spaces $\mathbb A^j$, use the localization sequence and affine homotopy invariance [L3] to reduce every class to classes pulled back from the strata, and represent each stratum class as an $i$-fold cut with $\xi$ by repeated Cartier cutting of coordinate hyperplanes, which realizes it as $\xi^i\cap\pi^*$ of a class on $U$; the claim is compatible with the restriction to any smaller open by [L2].

Global surjectivity. It suffices to express an integral cycle $[V]$ on $\mathbb P(\mathcal E)$, and we induct on the dimension of the reduced image closure $W\subseteq X$. The cycle is supported on $\mathbb P(\mathcal E|_W)$. Choose a dense open $U\subseteq W$ trivializing the bundle. Step 1.2 expresses $[V]|_U$ in the required form; lift its coefficient classes from $A_*(U)$ to $A_*(W)$ using localization [L3]. The resulting difference is the pushforward of a cycle class on $\mathbb P(\mathcal E|_{W\setminus U})$. Each integral component of that cycle has image closure of dimension strictly less than $\dim W$, so induction expresses its class in the required form over its image. Push these expressions to $W$ and then $X$, using compatibility of flat pullback with a closed immersion and of caps with proper pushforward. The induction terminates because the integral image has finite dimension. For locally finite cycles the constructions remain locally finite: $\pi$ is proper, so the image closures of a locally finite family are locally finite; each residual family is supported within its respective image closure, and the dimension bound for a fixed-degree input cycle is uniform. Thus the same argument sums locally finitely without asserting that the whole base has finitely many components.

fact_uses.text: [L3] Projective pushforward of Chow classes is functorial and satisfies the projection formula ([[lem-proper-pushforward-of-cycles-well-defined]], [[lem-chow-ring-naturality-and-projection-formula]], [[thm-intersection-product-and-chow-ring-of-a-smooth-scheme]]); degrees on projective space are computed by the degree isomorphism of [[lem-chow-groups-of-projective-space]] and flat pullback is compatible with degree ([[lem-flat-pullback-chow-groups]]).

proof_steps.claim: The fibre computation. Let $\tau=\operatorname{ch}\cdot\operatorname{td}$; for the generator $\alpha=p_Y^*\beta\otimes p_{\mathbb P}^*[\mathcal O(m)]$ the left-hand side is $\tau(p_!\alpha)=\binom{m+n}{n}\operatorname{ch}(\beta)\operatorname{td}(T_Y)$ by step 1.1 and additivity/multiplicativity of $\tau$ on the base [L2]. The right-hand side is $p_*(\operatorname{ch}(\beta)\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal O(m))\operatorname{td}(T_{\mathbb P^n\times_kY}))$; the tangent bundle of the product is the direct sum of the pullbacks of the tangent bundles, so its Todd class is $\operatorname{td}(T_{\mathbb P^n})\operatorname{td}(T_Y)$ by [L2], and the projection formula for $p_*$ [L3] moves $\operatorname{ch}(\beta)\operatorname{td}(T_Y)$ out, leaving the fibre integral $p_*(\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal O(m))\operatorname{td}(T_{\mathbb P^n}))$. The Euler sequence $0\to\mathcal O\to\mathcal O(1)^{n+1}\to T_{\mathbb P^n}\to0$ follows on standard charts by differentiating the ratios $x_i/x_j$: its first map is the coordinate vector, and these derivatives identify the quotient with the tangent bundle. Consequently $\operatorname{td}(T_{\mathbb P^n})=(h/(1-e^{-h}))^{n+1}$ modulo $h^{n+1}$, so this fibre integral is the formal residue $\operatorname{Res}_{h=0}e^{mh}(1-e^{-h})^{-n-1}dh$, computed by substituting $z=1-e^{-h}$: then $dh=dz/(1-z)$ and $e^{mh}=(1-z)^{-m}$, and the residue equals the coefficient $[z^n](1-z)^{-m-1}=\binom{m+n}{n}$. Comparing with the left-hand side, the identity holds on every generator.

General projective bundles, and conclusion. A rank-zero bundle has empty projectivization and both Riemann-Roch sides are zero; assume positive rank for the following computation. The same computation applies to a general projective bundle projection $\pi:P=\mathbb P(\mathcal E)\to Y$ using the relative projective bundle generators of [L1] and the relative Euler sequence: after splitting $\mathcal E$ by a flag bundle the pushforward coefficient of a relative twist is the divided difference $\sum_iF(-x_i)/\prod_{j\ne i}(x_j-x_i)$ in the formal roots $x_i$. The relative Euler sequence in the lines convention is $0\to\mathcal O\to\pi^*\mathcal E\otimes\mathcal O(1)\to T_{P/Y}\to0$, from first-order deformations of a line. The pushforward formula follows algebraically from the projective relation $\prod_i(h+x_i)=0$ and $\pi_*h^{r-1}=1$: Lagrange interpolation on the nodes $-x_i$ reads its top remainder coefficient as that divided difference. The generator integrand is $e^{mh}\prod_j(h+x_j)/(1-e^{-x_j-h})$, whose divided-difference sum is the character of the relative symmetric power by the partial-fraction identity $\prod_j(1-ze^{-x_j})^{-1}=\sum_i\prod_{j\ne i}(1-e^{x_i-x_j})^{-1}(1-ze^{-x_i})^{-1}$; work initially with independent formal roots and invert their differences to justify interpolation and partial fractions. The resulting coefficients of the symmetric-power series are symmetric polynomials, so denominators cancel; truncation in the Chow grading then specializes correctly even when roots coincide. Thus with injective flag pullback and the base Todd projection formula the identity descends. Since the identity is additive in $\alpha$ and holds on the generators of $K_0$ for every $Y$ in the stated hypotheses, the diagram commutes; the case $Y=\operatorname{Spec}k$ is Hirzebruch-Riemann-Roch for $\mathbb P^n$.

Substitution in the tangent character gives $t_1+t_2$; the two additive weights are $\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2$, so the Euler class is $\epsilon_1\epsilon_2$.

The degree-one coefficient is the sum over the single fixed point, so it equals $(\epsilon_1\epsilon_2)^{-1}$. This is a formal equivariant fixed-point contribution, not an asserted continuum path-integral value.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] [[thm-adhm-fixed-point-instanton-count]]: fixed points are indexed by two-tuples of partitions of total size one, and the tangent character is $\mathbf V^\vee\mathbf V(t_1+t_2-1-t_1t_2)+\mathbf V^\vee\mathbf W^\vee+t_1t_2\mathbf W\mathbf V$.

proof_steps.claim: A two-tuple of partitions with total size one places its single box in exactly one of the two colors, so the only possibilities are $(\{(0,0)\},\varnothing)$ and $(\varnothing,\{(0,0)\})$. Their quotient representatives have $V$-characters $e_1$ and $e_2$, respectively.

For the first point, the ADHM convention [F1] gives $\mathbf W=e_1^{-1}+e_2^{-1}$ and $\mathbf W^\vee=e_1+e_2$, while $\mathbf V=e_1$. Substitution in [F2] gives $$t_1+t_2+\frac{e_2}{e_1}+t_1t_2\frac{e_1}{e_2}.$$ The corresponding additive weights are $\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2,a_2-a_1,\epsilon_1+\epsilon_2+a_1-a_2$, so their product is $E_1$.
