Let $ eta=(i_*)^{-1}(\alpha\cap[X]_T)$. On each component, the complex orientation and refined Gysin map give $i_a^!(\alpha\cap[X]_T)=i_a^*\alpha\cap[F_a]_T$. Since $\alpha\cap[X]_T=i_* eta$, the self-intersection formula [F3] gives $e_T(
u_a)\cap eta_a=i_a^*\alpha\cap[F_a]_T$. Properness of $F_a$ makes $e_T(
u_a)$ invertible after localization by [F3], hence $ eta_a=(i_a^*\alpha/e_T(
u_a))\cap[F_a]_T$. Applying $p_{a*}$ and summing the finitely many components yields the displayed formula. The degree is $2d-q$: division by the degree-$2c_a$ Euler class lowers the localized cohomological degree of the insertion from $q$ to $q-2c_a$, and capping with the degree-$2d_a$ fundamental class gives $2d_a-(q-2c_a)=2d-q$.

If $F=\varnothing$, [F2] makes the localized Borel–Moore groups of $X$ zero and the component sum is empty. If $F$ is finite, every $F_a$ is a point and $e_T(\nu_a)$ is the product of its nonzero tangent-character classes, so each summand is the stated reciprocal-Euler term. If $c_a=0$, the normal bundle is rank zero and its complex-oriented Euler class is $1$. These cases agree with the formula and the degree computation above.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] [[def-qftx-graded-trace-class-index-data]]: the heat operator is diagonal with eigenvalue $1$ on the zero-energy basis and $e^{-\beta\lambda}$ on each parity subspace at energy $\lambda>0$; it is trace class, so its diagonal family in the supplied Hilbert basis is absolutely summable.

proof_steps.claim: By [F1], $Q/\sqrt\lambda$ is a linear bijection between the finite-dimensional positive-energy parity eigenspaces, so $m_\lambda^+:=\dim\mathcal H_\lambda^+=\dim\mathcal H_\lambda^-=:m_\lambda^-$ for every $\lambda\in\Sigma$. On any supplied orthonormal basis of $\mathcal H_\lambda^\pm$, [F2] gives $\langle T_\beta e,e\rangle=e^{-\beta\lambda}$ for each basis vector. Therefore the positive-energy contribution to the signed basis sum at this fixed $\lambda$ is $e^{-\beta\lambda}(m_\lambda^+-m_\lambda^-)=0$.

By [F2], the full diagonal family is absolutely summable. For the partition into its energy blocks, the absolute value of each block sum is at most the sum of the absolute values in that block; hence the family of block sums is also absolutely summable. To see that its sum equals the original sum, fix $\varepsilon>0$ and choose a finite set of basis vectors whose omitted absolute tail is below $\varepsilon$. Only finitely many energy blocks meet that finite set, and the omitted absolute tail bounds the difference between the full sum and the sum of those complete block sums. Letting $\varepsilon$ decrease to zero proves that grouping by energy preserves the sum. Step 1.1 cancels every positive-energy block; each zero-energy even basis vector contributes $1$ and each zero-energy odd basis vector contributes $-1$. The remaining finite sum is $m_0^+-m_0^-$, independent of $\beta$. The proof uses no trace cyclicity and no positive-energy eigenvector outside the given discrete decomposition.

fact_uses.text: [L2] Bivariant operations and their axioms; flat pullback along a vector bundle is bijective with inverse $s_N^!$; the zero-section and excess identities hold after every base change ([[def-bivariant-chow-operations]], [[lem-vector-bundle-chow-homotopy-invariance]], [[lem-zero-section-gysin-and-excess-vector-subbundle]]).

proof_steps.claim: Bivariant axioms. For each base $T'$ the operation is $c(Z,T,N)_{T'}=s_{N'}^!\,a_*\sigma_{Z'/T'}$, a composite of the well-defined specialization $\sigma_{Z'/T'}:A_m(T')\to A_m(C_{Z'}T')$ of [L1], the proper pushforward $a_*$, and the bijection $s_{N'}^!=(p'^*)^{-1}$ of [L2]. Proper compatibility: push a lift of the pulled-back class forward along the given proper morphism and use that Cartier Gysin commutes with proper pushforward [L3]. Flat compatibility: pull the lift back and use flat/Cartier compatibility. Divisor compatibility: apply the Cartier Gysin to the lift and use that two Cartier Gysins commute [L3], noting that the ordinary restriction of the result is the lift of the desired input. Base restriction is simply the reindexing of the family. These verifications are exactly the three bivariant axioms of [L2].

Base change. Under a base change the blowup of $\mathcal I\mathcal O_{T'}$ admits a closed immersion into the base change of the original blowup, induced by the surjection of Rees algebras of step 1.1, and this immersion is an isomorphism over the ordinary part $\mathbb A^1_{T'}$; the induced proper morphism between the two deformation families is therefore an isomorphism over the ordinary fibres, and pushing a lift along it exhibits the two infinity operations as equal after pushforward. Consequently the cone portions of the two operations define the same class after pushforward to $N'$, and since proper pushforward, open restriction and $(p'^*)^{-1}$ are bivariant, the operation is compatible with arbitrary base change.

The excess factor. Suppose the cone embedding factors through a vector subbundle $N'_0\subseteq N'$ of rank $d_0$; write the cone specialization pushed into $N'_0$ as $p_0'^*\beta$ for a class $\beta$ on $Z'$, using the bundle-pullback bijection for $N'_0$ from [L2]. Applying the excess identity $s_{N'}^!a'_*p_0'^*\beta=c_{\operatorname{rank}(N'/N'_0)}(N'/N'_0)\cap\beta$ of [L2] to the vector subbundle inclusion $a':N'_0\hookrightarrow N'$ gives that the operation defined with $N'$ equals the operation defined with $N'_0$ multiplied by the top Chern operator of the quotient bundle $N'/N'_0$; this is the asserted excess factor.

fact_uses.text: [L2] Chern classes are operational and central among bivariant operations; the zero-section and excess identities hold ([[lem-operational-chern-classes-and-whitney-formula]], [[lem-zero-section-gysin-and-excess-vector-subbundle]]).

proof_steps.claim: Commutation with bivariant operations. Test equality of two bivariant operations on the fundamental class of an integral $T'\to T$, allowing a proper birational modification by [L3]. If the inverse image of $Z$ in $T'$ is all of $T'$, the cone is the zero section and $c(Z,T,N)$ is the top Chern operator of the virtual normal bundle by [L1] with $N'_0=0$, hence central by [L2]. Otherwise blow up the nonzero ideal defining the inverse image of $Z$: on the blowup the inverse image is an effective Cartier divisor $D$, the pulled-back conormal surjection maps onto $\mathcal I_D/\mathcal I_D^2$, an invertible sheaf. Locally this surjection onto a free rank-one module splits; dualizing gives a subbundle injection $N_{D/\widetilde T'}\hookrightarrow N|_D$ with locally free quotient $Q$, and the excess formula of [L1] gives $c=c_{\operatorname{top}}(Q)\cap D^!$. The factor $c_{\operatorname{top}}(Q)$ commutes with every bivariant operation by [L2] and the Cartier factor $D^!$ commutes by the Cartier axiom [L3]; pushing the resulting identity forward along the blowup proves commutation on the original integral base.

Sections of smooth morphisms. Let $s:Z\hookrightarrow P$ be a regular immersion followed by a smooth projection $p:P\to T$ with $ps$ flat of the expected relative dimension. Locally write $T=\operatorname{Spec}A$, $P=\operatorname{Spec}B$, $Z=\operatorname{Spec}C$; the Koszul resolution of $C$ over $B$ has $A$-flat terms because $B$ is smooth hence flat over $A$, and its quotient $C$ is $A$-flat by hypothesis, so the successive kernels are $A$-flat by the Tor vanishing criterion; tensoring with any $A'$ therefore stays exact, so the regular equations remain regular after every base change, and the normal cone of the base-changed embedding is the full base-changed normal bundle with fundamental cycle the bundle pullback. Inverting bundle pullback gives $s^!p^*=(ps)^*$; when $ps=\operatorname{id}$ this is $s^!p^*=1$.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] [[thm-adhm-fixed-point-instanton-count]]: the fixed points for $N=1,k=1$ are indexed by the one one-box partition, and their tangent character is computed from the ADHM deformation complex.

proof_steps.claim: There is exactly one partition of $k=1$ for $N=1$, namely $Y_1=\{(0,0)\}$, so [F2] gives the unique fixed point. Here $\mathbf V_{\vec Y}=e_1$ and $\mathbf W=e_1^{-1}$, whence $\mathbf V^\vee\mathbf V=1$, $\mathbf V^\vee\mathbf W^\vee=1$, and $t_1t_2\mathbf W\mathbf V=t_1t_2$. Substitution in the tangent character gives $t_1+t_2$; the two additive weights are $\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2$, so the Euler class is $\epsilon_1\epsilon_2$.

The degree-one coefficient is the sum over the single fixed point, so it equals $(\epsilon_1\epsilon_2)^{-1}$. This is a formal equivariant fixed-point contribution, not an asserted continuum path-integral value.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] [[thm-adhm-fixed-point-instanton-count]]: fixed points are indexed by two-tuples of partitions of total size one, and the tangent character is $\mathbf V^\vee\mathbf V(t_1+t_2-1-t_1t_2)+\mathbf V^\vee\mathbf W^\vee+t_1t_2\mathbf W\mathbf V$.

proof_steps.claim: A two-tuple of partitions with total size one places its single box in exactly one of the two colors, so the only possibilities are $(\{(0,0)\},\varnothing)$ and $(\varnothing,\{(0,0)\})$. Their quotient representatives have $V$-characters $e_1$ and $e_2$, respectively.

For the first point, the ADHM convention [F1] gives $\mathbf W=e_1^{-1}+e_2^{-1}$ and $\mathbf W^\vee=e_1+e_2$, while $\mathbf V=e_1$. Substitution in [F2] gives $$t_1+t_2+\frac{e_2}{e_1}+t_1t_2\frac{e_1}{e_2}.$$ The corresponding additive weights are $\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2,a_2-a_1,\epsilon_1+\epsilon_2+a_1-a_2$, so their product is $E_1$. Interchanging the two colors gives the second displayed character and $E_2$.

Each fixed-point contribution is the reciprocal of its Euler product, so the degree-one coefficient is $E_1^{-1}+E_2^{-1}$. The TikZ drawing only records the two one-box colorings and is not used in this calculation.

proof_steps.claim:
The residual $U(1)$ action sends
$I\mapsto gI$ and $J\mapsto Jg^{-1}$; it preserves the raw representative's
orbit, and its stabilizer is trivial because $gI=I$ with $I\ne0$ forces
$g=1$. The framed $W$ coordinates at infinity are fixed, so they introduce

On any chart away from $p$ where $z_1$ or $z_2$ is a unit, the same equations show that $\gamma$ is onto and its kernel is generated by $\alpha$. Hence $K/\operatorname{im}\alpha\cong I_p$ globally, where $I_p$ is the ideal sheaf of $p$.

At $p$, the local ideal $(x,y)$ is not principal: if it were generated by one element in the regular local ring $\mathbb C[x,y]_{(x,y)}$, its quotient by the maximal ideal would have dimension at most one, whereas $(x,y)/(x,y)^2$ has dimension two. This exhibits a positive-FI stable point outside the costable, locally-free zero-FI locus; the correspondence with ordinary ASD moduli is restricted to that zero-FI locus and does not absorb this boundary point.

proof_steps.claim: In the Grothendieck group, exactness of the monad gives $[\mathcal E]=(2k+N)[\mathcal O]-k[\mathcal O(-1)]-k[\mathcal O(1)]$. By [F1], its Chern character is $(2k+N)-ke^{-H}-ke^H=N-kH^2$, because the constant terms cancel to $N$, the linear terms cancel, the quadratic contribution is $-kH^2$, and terms of degree at least four vanish on $Z$. Therefore $c_1(\mathcal E)=0$ and $c_2(\mathcal E)=-\operatorname{ch}_2(\mathcal E)=kH^2$.

proof_steps.claim: For a finite-type algebraic base $S$, tensor the relative diagonal Koszul resolution by the flat family and use the assumed base-change isomorphisms [A1]. The direct-image terms are vector bundles of ranks $k,2k+N,k$, and the finite filtered complex commutes with residue-field restriction. On every fiber, step 6.1 gives the monad. The right end map is surjective on every fiber, hence surjective by Nakayama [F8], and its kernel $K$ is locally free. Locally on $S$, write the remaining exact sequence as $0\to P^{-1}\to K\to\mathcal E\to0$, with $P^{-1}$ and $K$ flat over the base. Tensoring by any residue field $k(s)$ stays injective at the left because the fiber complex is a monad on the whole projective plane. Thus $\operatorname{Tor}_1^{\mathcal O_{S,s}}(k(s),\mathcal E)=0$, equivalently the maximal-ideal multiplication map is injective. Since $\mathcal E$ is finite over the local ring of $\mathbb P^2\times S$, [F6] proves flatness over $S$. The same base-change maps identify the relative middle cohomology with the given family. This is precisely the family range stated and does not assert base change outside it.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [A1] Under full AC, the batch-67 scalar cohomology theorem states that for every $0\le r\le3$, $H^0(\mathbb P^r,\mathcal O)=\mathbb C$ and $H^q(\mathbb P^r,\mathcal O)=0$ for $q>0$. [[thm-qftx-gaga-analytic-projective-dolbeault-scalar-cohomology]]

proof_steps.claim: Fix $r\in\{1,2,3\}$. In the first sequence of [F1], the map $H^0(\mathbb P^r,\mathcal O)\to H^0(\mathbb P^{r-1},\mathcal O)$ is restriction of constants and hence is the identity $\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$. Exactness therefore gives $H^0(\mathbb P^r,\mathcal O(-1))=0$. The adjacent higher groups of $\mathcal O$ and $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{r-1}}$ vanish by [A1]; the long exact sequence then gives $H^q(\mathbb P^r,\mathcal O(-1))=0$ for every $q>0$.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] The conditional analytic twist result gives $H^0(\mathbb P^3,\mathcal O)=\mathbb C$, $H^q(\mathbb P^3,\mathcal O(-1))=0$ for all $q\ge0$, and $H^q(\mathbb P^3,\mathcal O(-2))=0$ for $q=0,1,2$. [[lem-qftx-positive-real-monad-analytic-twist-cohomology]]

proof_steps.claim:
Pull back $0\to U_1\otimes\mathcal O(-1)\to K'\to F'\to0$ along $K\to F\xrightarrow f F'$. Its extension obstruction and ambiguity are respectively
$H^1(K^*\otimes U_1\otimes\mathcal O(-1))$ and $H^0(K^*\otimes U_1\otimes\mathcal O(-1))$. Dualizing the first sequence of step 1.1 and tensoring by $U_1\otimes\mathcal O(-1)$ gives
$$
0\to (U')^*\otimes U_1\otimes\mathcal O(-2)\to S^*\otimes U_1\otimes\mathcal O(-1)\to K^*\otimes U_1\otimes\mathcal O(-1)\to0.
$$
The long exact sequence and [F2] make both groups zero, so the lift $\phi:K\to K'$ exists and is unique.

Extend $\phi$ across $K\hookrightarrow S\otimes\mathcal O$ using $0\to K'\to S_1\otimes\mathcal O\to U_1'\otimes\mathcal O(1)\to0$. The obstruction and ambiguity are $H^1((U')^*\otimes S_1\otimes\mathcal O(-1))$ and $H^0((U')^*\otimes S_1\otimes\mathcal O(-1))$, both zero by [F2]. Hence there is a unique middle map $g:S\otimes\mathcal O\to S_1\otimes\mathcal O$ extending $\phi$.

The restriction $g\alpha$ lands in $\operatorname{im}\alpha'$ because its class in $F'$ is $f$ applied to the zero class of $\alpha$. Since $\alpha'$ is injective, this defines a unique map $p:U\otimes\mathcal O(-1)\to U_1\otimes\mathcal O(-1)$. Since $\beta'g$ vanishes on $K$, it factors uniquely through $(S\otimes\mathcal O)/K\cong U'\otimes\mathcal O(1)$, defining the third chain map. The chain equations hold by construction. Every matrix entry of these maps is a global holomorphic section of $\mathcal O$, hence is constant by [F2]. Any other lift agrees on $K$ by step 1.2 and on $S$ by step 1.3; injectivity of $\alpha'$ and surjectivity of $\beta$ then force equality of both end maps.

By step 1.4, $h_F$ has a unique chain lift $h=(p,H,r):M\to D(M)$. The displayed diagram records its two chain equations; it is notation only, and the equations and uniqueness are established in the text.
$$
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
U\otimes\mathcal O(-1) \arrow[r,"\alpha"] \arrow[d,"p"'] &
S\otimes\mathcal O \arrow[r,"\beta"] \arrow[d,"H"] &
U'\otimes\mathcal O(1) \arrow[d,"r"]\\
(U')^*\otimes\mathcal O(-1) \arrow[r,"-\beta^\#"'] &
S^*\otimes\mathcal O \arrow[r,"\alpha^\#"'] &
U^*\otimes\mathcal O(1)
\end{tikzcd}
$$
Thus the squares assert $H\alpha=-\beta^\#p$ and $r\beta=\alpha^\#H$. Its dual $D(h)$ lifts the same self-pairing, so uniqueness gives $h=D(h)$; in particular $H=H^\dagger$ and the end maps are adjoints under the pairing's identifications. The lift is an isomorphism: lift $h_F^{-1}$ by step 1.4 and use uniqueness to identify both composites with the identity lift. The middle map $H$ is therefore nondegenerate. In bases identifying the end spaces by this lift, the chain equation is $H\alpha(z)=-\beta(jz)^\dagger$. Replacing $z$ by $jz$ and using linearity in homogeneous coordinates yields both displayed identities in the Statement.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F1] The Chern character is additive on exact complexes, $\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal L)=e^{c_1(\mathcal L)}$ for a line bundle, and $\operatorname{ch}_2=\tfrac12(c_1^2-2c_2)$. [[def-chern-character-and-todd-class]]

proof_steps.claim:
In the algebraic Chow ring, [F1] and $H=c_1(\mathcal O(1))$ give
$$
\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal F)=(2k+N)-ke^{-H}-ke^H=N-kH^2,
$$
because $H^4=0$ on the complex threefold and the odd powers cancel. Thus $c_1^{\rm alg}(\mathcal F)=0$ and $c_2^{\rm alg}(\mathcal F)=kH^2$. In the underlying topological category the same exact sequences are exact sequences of complex vector bundles, so [F5] and the line-class identity $c_1(\mathcal O(1))=H$ give
$$
c(\mathcal F)=\frac{1}{(1-H)^k(1+H)^k}=(1-H^2)^{-k}=1+kH^2
$$
through degree six, since $H^4=0$. Hence the topological classes are $c_1(\mathcal F)=0$, $c_2(\mathcal F)=kH^2$, and $c_3(\mathcal F)=0$. The universal formulas $\operatorname{ch}_1=c_1$, $\operatorname{ch}_2=\tfrac12(c_1^2-2c_2)$, and $\operatorname{ch}_3=\tfrac16(c_1^3-3c_1c_2+3c_3)$ then give the topological $\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal F)=N-kH^2$. This compares only the identical finite line-bundle resolution and its line class, not arbitrary analytic and algebraic cohomology.

proof_steps.claim: A fiber $L_x=\pi^{-1}(x)$ is a complex linear $\mathbb P^1\subset\mathbb P^3$. The restriction of $\mathcal O(1)$ to this linear $\mathbb P^1$ has first Chern number $1$; [F2] then identifies its Poincaré dual as $H_{\rm top}^2$. Thus $\pi^*u=H_{\rm top}^2$.

proof_steps.claim: Let $K=\ker\beta$. The locally split sequence $0\to U\otimes\mathcal O(-1)\to K\to F\to0$ and [F1] give an isomorphism $H^0(K)\to H^0(F)$. Since $K\subseteq S\otimes\mathcal O$ and $H^0(\mathcal O)=\mathbb C$, every global section of $K$ is a constant vector $s\in S$. Its image in $F$ is a global section exactly when $\beta(z)s=0$ for every $z$, equivalently $\beta_i s=0$ for every coefficient. Hence $H^0(F)=L$.

For a real line $\ell$, a constant vector $l\in L$ defines a section of $F|_\ell$. final_edge_fact_uses.text: [A1] The exact rank-two theorem supplies the ordinary framed ASD connection of a regular rank-two datum by its raw forward monad/projection construction, extends it smoothly over infinity, and proves $q_2=-k$. Its exact GAGA, coupled-vanishing and intrinsic normal-form hypotheses are retained in the rank-one raw emptiness deduction. [[thm-qftx-zero-fi-regular-adhm-asd-correspondence]]

proof_steps.claim: Stabilize a rank-one raw datum by $W'=\mathbb C\oplus\mathbb C$, $I'=(I,0)$ and $J'=(J,0)^t$, retaining $V,B_1,B_2$. Then $I'J'=IJ$, $I'I'^\dagger=II^\dagger$ and $J'^\dagger J'=J^\dagger J$. The word span is unchanged and $\ker J'=\ker J$, so both moments and regularity are unchanged. On the finite stereographic chart the raw kernel matrix annihilates the added framing line, and its orthogonal projection is $P_1\oplus1$. Thus [A1] produces a smooth rank-two ASD connection whose restriction to that chart is a line connection plus the flat added line and whose charge is $q_2=-k$. By [F2] its determinant curvature vanishes. On that chart this curvature is exactly the first line's curvature, so the whole rank-two curvature is zero there. Smoothness makes it zero also at infinity, hence $q_2=0$ and $k=0$. Thus no regular rank-one zero-FI datum exists for $k>0$, conditional on the exact retained rank-two input. By [F6], a regular complex rank-one orbit would have such a zero-real-moment representative, so the same emptiness conclusion applies to the complex regular quotient.

A regular raw first-order family with $k>0$ would reduce to a prohibited datum from step 1.1, so none exists; the connection family for $k>0$ has no allowable special fiber by step 1.2. At $k=0$ the rank-zero internal $D$-module and all raw maps are uniquely zero, with trivial internal gauge group. Its forward monad is the constant framed line and its forward connection is $d$, also over $D$. Step 3.1 supplies a unique framed gauge from every first-order connection object to this one. Thus this explicit construction is an equivalence of the two first-order groupoids. Reduction and involution-preserving scalar maps commute with it, because the zero datum and the constant line pull back to themselves and the framed trivializing isomorphism is unique. The same argument after complexifying the real tangent spaces gives zero complexified tangent spaces; it does not assert a correspondence for arbitrary complex connections without the Hermitian real condition.

Stabilization intertwines $T$ with the rank-two compact action having framing weights $(h,1)$. In the zero-charge classification, inverse rotations and framing changes send a flat framed object to a flat framed object; the unique framed parallel trivialization identifies it with the same point. Its uniqueness also makes the first-order identifications equivariant. They hold for every first-order Hermitian family defined above, hence also for the subset satisfying the exact locally-free/cohomology-base-change hypotheses retained in [A1]; no extra family statement is obtained from an orbit-set bijection. Positive-FI rank-one stable data and their non-locally-free sheaves and formal fixed-point series were not used in any step.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F3] The stable complex ADHM equation locus has a free proper gauge action and a Hausdorff second-countable complex quotient of dimension $2kN$, with tangent $\ker d_1/\operatorname{im}d_0$. Word-frame slices give holomorphic quotient charts and explicit character gauge lifts at fixed points. [[lem-adhm-stable-quotient-and-torus-lift]]

proof_steps.claim: Apply [F3] to the displayed equation and stability condition. Its proof uses the declared holomorphic implicit-function supplier, proves properness by word-frame bounds on both the gauge transformation and its inverse, and constructs holomorphic quotient charts. Thus the quotient here is a Hausdorff second-countable complex manifold, with tangent $\ker d_1/\operatorname{im}d_0$ and complex dimension $2kN$. For $k=0$ the quotient is a point. This is the stable complex quotient; no real moment-map or sheaf/ASD identification is inferred.

At a $T$-fixed quotient point represented by $x$, [F3] gives the unique gauge lift $g(t)=C(x)\operatorname{diag}(e_{\alpha_\ell}t_1^{a_\ell}t_2^{b_\ell})C(x)^{-1}$ from a standard-framing word basis. This is a smooth representation of the compact torus itself. The fixed-orbit equations give $g(t)I(w_\alpha)=e_\alpha I(w_\alpha)$ and $g(t)B_i=t_iB_i g(t)$, so all weights generated by stability have the form $e_\alpha t_1^it_2^j$ with $i,j\ge0$. Under $t_1t_2hJ=Jg(t)^{-1}$, a nonzero component from a $V$-weight $\chi$ to the $\beta$th framing line requires $\chi=e_\beta t_1^{-1}t_2^{-1}$. Distinct integer characters on the compact torus cannot satisfy this equality with any generated weight, so $J=0$. The moment equation then gives $[B_1,B_2]=0$. No Zariski-density or algebraic lifting assertion is used.

The label set in step 6.1 is finite: for $k>0$ every box of a size-at-most-$k$ downward-closed diagram has both coordinates less than $k$, so the possible tuples lie in a finite collection of subsets; $k=0$ has only the empty tuple. Hence the fixed locus is a finite set in the Hausdorff quotient from [F3], and each point is isolated. By [F3] the quotient has a finite invariant affine atlas with algebraic action of $T_{\mathbb C}=(\mathbb C^*)^{N+2}$. In each slice its coordinate functions are eigenfunctions. A point fixed by the compact torus has every nonzero-weight coordinate equal to zero, since each nontrivial integer character is nontrivial on that compact torus; conversely these equations make the point fixed by $T_{\mathbb C}$. Thus the two fixed loci have the same point set. The fixed subscheme is smooth by [F4], because $T_{\mathbb C}$ is diagonalizable and hence linearly reductive. Its fixed ideal in these affine coordinates is generated by the nonzero-weight coordinates. Linearizing that ideal, using the tangent-kernel description in [F4], identifies its tangent with the invariant tangent subspace. A smooth fixed scheme with a finite point set has dimension zero at every point, so that subspace is zero. Therefore every complex tangent weight is a nonzero character. Its associated $u_\chi$ is a nonzero integer linear polynomial in the algebraically independent variables and is invertible in $K$. The tangent has complex dimension $2kN$, so the Euler product has exactly $2kN$ factors counted with multiplicity.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [A1] Absolute projective GAGA on P³ supplies an exact tensor equivalence and cohomology comparison. [[thm-qftx-projective-gaga-for-monad-data]]

proof_steps.claim: Algebraize the holomorphic bundle using [A1]. Its algebraic sheaf is locally free: the holomorphic bundle is dualizable, the exact tensor equivalence transports its evaluation and coevaluation and reflects their triangle identities, and those identities give a finite dual basis on each local algebraic chart, hence a finite projective module. In a splitting C⁴=A⊕B into two-planes, a graph chart of G consists of X:A→B and the incidence is (X,[λ])↦[λ,Xλ], with p a product with P(A). In the library quotient convention it is the projective bundle of the dual of the tautological subbundle. Thus [F1] gives properness, finite presentation and flatness, and e*E is a coherent locally free sheaf flat over G.

At a real line L, absolute P³ GAGA applied to the coherent algebraic sheaf i*(E|L), for the closed immersion i:L→P³, identifies its cohomology with that of the trivial analytic restriction. This uses no GAGA on the Grassmannian: closed-immersion direct image is exact, and its analytification is the same local quotient-module tensor construction. Hence the algebraic fiber cohomology is C^N in degree zero and zero above by [F3]. Its degree-one base-change map has zero target, so is surjective. By [F2] that map is an isomorphism; the finite stalk of R¹p*e*E has zero residue fiber, and Nakayama kills it on a neighborhood. The degree-one local-freeness criterion of cohomology/base change now gives surjectivity in degree zero. Its degree-zero case makes H=p*e*E a finite locally free rank-N bundle with all degree-zero base-change maps isomorphisms near L.

Analytify this actual evaluation isomorphism. On every local product V×P¹, a holomorphic function is constant on each P¹ fiber by the maximum principle, and its remaining function on V is holomorphic by evaluation at a fixed point. Thus p_an*O=O. Trivializing H locally gives p_an*p_an*H_an=H_an, where the inner star denotes pullback and the outer star denotes direct image. Consequently the analytic direct image of e_an*E is H_an, its evaluation is the analytified evaluation, and all degree-zero analytic fiber maps are isomorphisms. The same product calculation after any base change identifies the base-change maps. No circular assumption of analytic base-change surjectivity or broad Grauert theorem is used.

The quaternionic involution on G sends a graph X to j_B X j_A^{-1}; its fixed graph matrices form the real four-dimensional quaternionic subspace, whose complexification is the entire graph space. These charts embed HP¹ smoothly and totally really into G. On its incidence family evaluation is a diffeomorphism onto Z: the inverse sends [v] to (span_C(v,jv),[v]), smoothly in projective charts, and j²=-1 excludes dependence of v,jv. Restrict H_an to this real locus to obtain the smooth rank-N bundle with the claimed fibers and evaluation. The positive pairing induces its Hermitian matrix by evaluating local section frames at a smoothly chosen point on each line; this proves smoothness and positivity, independently of parallelness. At infinity the given unitary frame induces the section-bundle frame. All arguments use only the stated local absolute comparison.

proof_steps.claim: Vary the terms depending on $X$ using the normalized physical action brackets in [F1]. At fixed chiral coordinates, $P_{\mathrm{raw}}=\partial^L_{\bar\theta^{\dot2}}\partial^L_{\bar\theta^{\dot1}}|_{\bar\theta=0}$ extracts the top barred coefficient, so $I_D(U)=I_F(P_{\mathrm{raw}}U)$ up to the spacetime total derivatives removed by [A3]. Since $[U]_D=-I_D(U)/4$ and $[Y]_F=I_F(Y)/2$, the physical transfer is $[U]_D=[P_{\mathrm{phys}}U]_F$ with $P_{\mathrm{phys}}=-P_{\mathrm{raw}}/2=+\bar D^{\dot\alpha}\bar D_{\dot\alpha}/4$. This is equivalently the minus-one-quarter formula with LOWER-FIRST contraction $\bar D_{\dot\alpha}\bar D^{\dot\alpha}$. Chirality annihilates the barred derivatives of the even variation $\delta X$, so the D variation is $[\delta X P_{\mathrm{phys}}(X^\dagger)]_F$. The superpotential variation is $[\delta X(MX+J)]_F$. Thus the physical chiral Euler equation is $P_{\mathrm{phys}}(X^\dagger)+MX+J=0$, and its projector has positive derivative degree one.

By definition, each $\bar D_{\dot\alpha}$ has positive derivative degree $1/2$, so $\Pi_0(P_{\mathrm{phys}}X^\dagger)=0$. Applying $\Pi_0$ to the equation in step 1.1 gives $MX+J(\Phi)=0$. Because $M>0$, this scalar linear equation has the unique solution $X_*=-J(\Phi)/M$.

proof_steps.claim: For $g\in GL(V)$ put $x'=g\cdot x$ and $M(g)^2=\sum_i\|B_i'\|^2+\|I'\|^2+\|J'\|^2$. A fixed word frame $C(x)$ exists by [F2]. Each column of $gC(x)=C(x')$ is a product of at most $k-1$ matrices $B_i'$ followed by $I'$ on a unit framing vector. Submultiplicativity and operator norm bounded by Frobenius norm give $\|g\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le A_x(1+M(g))^k$ for $A_x=\sqrt{k}\|C(x)^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. If $x$ is costable, the rows consisting of coordinate rows of $JB_{i_1}\cdots B_{i_m}$ span $V^*$: their common annihilator is the largest common $B_i$-invariant subspace in $\ker J$, hence zero. The same finite dimension-growth argument as for columns gives a row basis $D(x)$ using words of length at most $k-1$. Since $D(x')=D(x)g^{-1}$, the identical norm estimate gives $\|g^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le A_x'(1+M(g))^k$. This also proves costability is open, since it is covered by the nonvanishing determinants of finitely many such row frames.

Diagonalize $H$ by [F4], with real eigenvalues $\lambda_i$. Along the preceding path the squared $B_i'$ entries have factors $e^{2t(\lambda_a-\lambda_b)}$, the squared $I'$ entries have $e^{2t\lambda_a}$ and the squared $J'$ entries have $e^{-2t\lambda_a}$. The log determinant is affine in $t$. Hence $F_\zeta''$ is a sum of $4w^2|z|^2e^{2tw}$ over those entries and their listed weights $w$, and is nonnegative. It can vanish only when $[H,B_i']=0$, $HI'=0$ and $J'H=0$. Stability of $x'$ then forces $H=0$, by applying $H$ to all spanning word vectors. Thus the path is strictly convex for every nonzero $H$. Given two critical matrices $g_1,g_2$, diagonalize the positive matrix $(g_2g_1^{-1})^\dagger(g_2g_1^{-1})$ and take the positive logarithms of its eigenvalues to write $g_2g_1^{-1}=u e^H$ with $u$ unitary and $H$ Hermitian. The endpoints of $e^{tH}g_1$ are both critical, after removing $u$ by invariance. Strict convexity forces $H=0$, so $g_2=ug_1$. This proves uniqueness of the unitary orbit at either level.

At a balanced datum $x$, let $L_x:\operatorname{Herm}(V)\to\operatorname{Herm}(V)$ be $H\mapsto\frac{d}{dt}\mu_{\mathbb R}(e^{tH}\cdot x)|_{t=0}$. Step 4.1 gives $2\operatorname{tr}(H L_xH)=F_\zeta''(e^{tH})|_{t=0}>0$ for nonzero $H$, so $L_x$ is injective and hence invertible in finite equal dimensions. The map $(H,y)\mapsto\mu_{\mathbb R}(e^H\cdot y)-\zeta I$ is smooth. To see smoothness of the exponential in the matrix entries directly, differentiate its absolutely convergent power series: on a bounded matrix set, an order-$r$ derivative of its degree-$m$ term is bounded by a constant times $m^r R^{m-r}/m!$, a summable majorant; this applies through real block matrices as in [F4]. By [F5] the balancing $H=H(y)$ is locally $C^r$ for every finite $r$, and uniqueness glues these branches to the same smooth map. The same invertible derivative along the Hermitian gauge directions in $T_xX^s$ proves that the real-level locus is a smooth submanifold. The unitary group is compact (closed bounded matrices), its action there is free by [F2] and proper (inverse images are closed subsets of $U(V)$ times a compact coordinate projection); therefore its quotient is smooth by [F6]. The map to the complex quotient is smooth using local submersion sections in [F6]. On any word-frame chart [F2], the local balancing map just constructed, followed by the unitary quotient map, is its smooth inverse; step 4.1 proves independence of all choices. Thus the bijections are diffeomorphisms. The compact torus commutes with gauge actions and preserves both the complex equation and $\mu_{\mathbb R}$, so the bijections are equivariant. For $k=0$ all matrices and equations are empty and all quotients are points, proving every boundary case stated. No sheaf or ASD identification was used.

proof_steps.claim: Conversely, let $\mathcal E$ be a framed torsion-free sheaf with the stated Hilbert polynomial. The preceding Beilinson lemma constructs its monad, with terms $V_1\mathcal O(-1)$, $M\mathcal O$, and $V_2\mathcal O(1)$ of ranks $k,2k+N,k$. Its restriction to $L_\infty$ remains exact at the ends because $\mathcal E$ is locally free there. Put $K=\ker\beta|_{L_\infty}$. The sequence $0\to V_1\mathcal O(-1)\to K\to W\mathcal O\to0$ splits since $\operatorname{Ext}^1(W\mathcal O,V_1\mathcal O(-1))=V_1\otimes W^*\otimes H^1(\mathcal O(-1))=0$.

The remaining line extension $0\to V_1\mathcal O(-1)\oplus W\mathcal O\to M\mathcal O\to V_2\mathcal O(1)\to0$ has class in $\operatorname{Hom}(V_2,V_1)\otimes H^1(\mathcal O(-2))$, since $H^1(\mathcal O(-1))=0$. Twist by $\mathcal O(-1)$ and take cohomology. The connecting map $V_2\to V_1\otimes H^1(\mathcal O(-2))$ is an isomorphism: the adjacent groups $H^0(\mathcal O(-1))$ and $H^1(\mathcal O(-1))$ vanish, while $H^1(\mathcal O(-2))\cong\mathbb C$. Thus $V_2$ is identified with $V_1$ by this canonical extension class. Choosing a basis of $V_1$ and using the fixed framed basis of $W$ identifies $M=V\oplus V\oplus W$ and the line maps with the two Euler blocks in the Statement. Any other such choice differs by one simultaneous element of $GL(V)$.

On $L_\infty$, the complex is $0\to V\mathcal O_{L_\infty}(-1)\xrightarrow{(-z_1,-z_2,0)^T}(V\oplus V\oplus W)\mathcal O_{L_\infty}\xrightarrow{(z_2,-z_1,0)}V\mathcal O_{L_\infty}(1)\to0$. The first two $V$ summands form the Euler resolution of the zero sheaf on the line, while the $W$ summand passes unchanged to middle cohomology. The framing is therefore the canonical identification $\mathcal E|_{L_\infty}=W\otimes\mathcal O_{L_\infty}$. In the Grothendieck group, the monad gives $[\mathcal E]=[(V\oplus V\oplus W)\mathcal O]-[V\mathcal O(-1)]-[V\mathcal O(1)]$. Taking Euler characteristics after twisting by $\mathcal O(m)$ and using $\chi(\mathcal O(d))=\binom{d+2}{2}$ yields $\chi(\mathcal E(m))=N\binom{m+2}{2}-k$.

If $k=0$, $V=0$, all four maps and both equations are the unique zero-dimensional maps, stability and costability are vacuous, and the monad is $0\to W\mathcal O\to0$. Its middle cohomology is the framed bundle $W\mathcal O$ with Hilbert polynomial $N\binom{m+2}{2}$. Conversely, [F3] constructs this same zero-term monad from every framed sheaf with that polynomial, so the framing identifies each such sheaf with $W\mathcal O$. Thus both moduli spaces are points, and all empty-matrix and Euler-block conventions are satisfied.

proof_steps.claim: For any Ward bundle use [F3] to form the analytic vector bundle H over a complex-open neighborhood U of every real line in G=Gr(2,4), with holomorphic evaluation p*H≅e*E on the universal family. On a graph chart X:A→B, incidence is (X,[λ])↦[λ,Xλ]. The distribution D=ker(de) consists of matrix variations v with vλ=0 and no λ variation. It is a holomorphic involutive rank-two subbundle, since it is tangent to the fibers of the submersion e. The restriction of p*Ω¹_U to D has kernel B*⊗O(-1) on each projective-line fiber and target D*≅O(1)². The O(-1) vanishings in [F3] give Ω¹_U≅p_*D*. Equivalently, on the graph chart a linear covector on Hom(A,B) restricts to a section on all kernels vλ=0; the map is injective because those kernels span Hom(A,B), and both coefficient spaces have dimension four. This gives the holomorphic sheaf isomorphism without any extra analytic base-change assumption.

The explicit incidence chart fixes vertical complex orientation followed by the positive base orientation to be the complex orientation of Z. The pullback of the positive point Thom class on S⁴ is the positive normal Thom class of its fiber CP¹; [F5] identifies its absolute class as the Poincaré dual of that fiber. A linear CP¹ has dual H²: H restricts with integral one to the line, and the integral projective cohomology ring gives H² as its positive degree-four generator. Hence π*u=H² for the positive generator u of H⁴(S⁴). Smooth evaluation gives E_twistor≅π*H, so c₂(E_twistor)=kH² is equivalent to c₂(H)[S⁴]=k. By [F4] this is q_N=-k; the same calculation verifies the forward map's charge clause. Framing is transported by evaluation at infinity. All constructions use incidence, evaluation and unique relative connections, so commute with the specified projective rotations and framing transformations. They therefore give the claimed T-equivariant bijection and all stated invariants, conditional on the exact absolute GAGA comparison [A1].

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [A2] Local coherent polydisc acyclicity: “Assume AC. Let $F$ be coherent analytic on a neighborhood of a point $x$ in $\mathbb C^N$. There is a coordinate polydisc $W$ about $x$ such that for every nonempty coordinate polydisc $D\subset W$ and every $q>0$, $H^q(D,F|_D)=0$. Scalar sheaf cohomology on such $D$ is computed by its smooth Dolbeault resolution. One can choose $W$ subordinate to a partial finite-rank free resolution of $F$ of length exceeding $2N$. The assertion is local in the supplied resolution neighborhood; no untwisted projective Cartan A/B or global Stein generation theorem is asserted.” ([[thm-qftx-gaga-analytic-local-coherent-polydisc-acyclicity]]). Only its positive-degree polydisc vanishing clause is used below.

proof_steps.claim: Suppose $1\le r\le3$ and fix $x\in P^r$. Apply [A1] to $\mathcal F$ at $x$ with length $2r$ to obtain a chart neighborhood $W_0$ with a partial free resolution. Its first relation kernel $K_0$ is coherent by [A1]. Apply [A1] again to $K_0$ at $x$ with length $2r$, and choose a neighborhood $W_1\subseteq W_0$ on which that kernel resolution is defined. Apply [A2] to $\mathcal F$ at $x$ to obtain a polydisc neighborhood $W_2$. Choose concentric coordinate polydiscs $D'_x\Subset D_x$ with $\overline{D_x}\subseteq W_1\cap W_2$. Then $D'_x$ is a neighborhood of $x$.

The sets $D'_x$ cover $P^r$. Compactness [F1] gives finitely many centers $x_1,\ldots,x_s$ whose smaller polydiscs still cover; set $U_i=D_{x_i}$ and $U'_i=D'_{x_i}$. Each singleton $U_i$ and $U'_i$ is $\mathcal F$-acyclic by [A2]. For every nonempty finite intersection of at least two of the $U_i$, the intersection lemma [F4] applies using the length-$2r$ resolution of $\mathcal F$ on the closure of any participating $U_i$. It also applies to the corresponding intersections of the $U'_i$, since their closures lie inside those same resolution neighborhoods. Thus both finite covers are acyclic for $\mathcal F$.

To compare two finite admissible covers, retain the given presentation $\pi_I$ on every nonempty intersection $U_I$ of either parent cover, and write $K_I=\ker\pi_I$; there are only finitely many such coherent kernels by [A1]. First shrink each parent cover to open sets $B_i$ with $\overline{B_i}\subset U_i$, still covering $P^r$: at every point choose a coordinate polydisc with compact closure in some parent member, take a finite subcover by compactness [F1], and for each parent member take the union of its finitely many assigned polydiscs. Do this for both parent covers. At a point $x$, repeat step 1.2 for $\mathcal F$ and its new presentation kernel. In addition, for every parent intersection $U_I$ containing $x$, use [A1] to choose a length-$2r$ resolution neighborhood of its particular kernel $K_I$. Intersect these finitely many neighborhoods. Choose nested polydiscs $D'_x\Subset D_x$ whose closures lie in this intersection and in one selected $B_i$ from each parent cover. Also choose $\overline{D_x}$ disjoint from every $\overline{B_j}$ whose parent $U_j$ does not contain $x$; those are finitely many closed sets missing $x$. Compactness gives a finite cover $\mathcal W$ by some of the $D'_x$, with the selected parent assignments. As in steps 1.2, 2.1 and 3.1, its intersections are $\mathcal F$-acyclic and have surjective finite-presentation section maps. Now take a nonempty refined intersection $T=D'_{x_0}\cap\cdots\cap D'_{x_k}$ and one parent cover. Let $I$ be its distinct assigned parent indices. Since $D'_{x_0}$ meets each selected $B_i$, the avoidance condition implies $x_0\in U_i$ for every $i\in I$. Hence the closure of $D'_{x_0}$ lies inside a resolution neighborhood for this very $K_I$. Applying [F4] to $K_I$ on $T$ gives $H^1(T,K_I)=0$, so [F9] proves surjectivity of the section map of the SAME parent presentation $\pi_I|_T$. Its section map on $U_I$ is surjective by parent admissibility. Moreover $\overline T$ is compact in $U_I$, since each refined polydisc has compact closure in its assigned parent. Thus [F5] applies to $\Gamma(U_I,\mathcal F)\to\Gamma(T,\mathcal F)$ using that common presentation. By [F3], the resulting target quotient topology agrees with the chosen one on $T$. This works for both parent covers and all tuples; no newly chosen presentation is substituted for a parent presentation without proving its section surjectivity.

Indeed, in the $m=1$ sequence of [F10], $H^1(\mathbb P^r,\mathcal O)=0$ by [A1], so restriction $H^0(\mathbb P^r,\mathcal O(1))\to H^0(\mathbb P^{r-1},\mathcal O(1))$ is surjective and its kernel is the defining hyperplane coordinate times $H^0(\mathcal O)=\mathbb C$. If the topological bundle is $\pi^*E$, naturality gives $\pi^*c_2(E)=kH_{\rm top}^2=k\pi^*u$; since $\pi^*u$ is a generator, $c_2(E)=ku$. This is conditional on the pullback hypothesis and asserts no Ward correspondence.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F4] Proper pushforward is functorial, closed inclusions are proper, and cap product with an equivariant cohomology class sends $[X]_T$ to Borel–Moore degree $2d-q$. [[def-qftx-localized-equivariant-borel-moore-data]]

proof_steps.claim: Let $f:X\to Y$ be a proper $T$-equivariant map between smooth separated finite-type varieties with finite invariant affine covers and proper fixed loci $F_X,F_Y$. Its restriction $f^T:F_X\to F_Y$ is proper, and the square formed by $i_X,i_Y,f^T,f$ commutes because $f$ sends fixed points to fixed points. Functoriality of proper Borel–Moore pushforward gives $f_*i_{X*}=i_{Y*}f^T_*$. After localization both $i_{X*}$ and $i_{Y*}$ are isomorphisms by [F2], so applying their inverses and then the proper traces proves $p_{Y*}^{\mathrm{loc}}f_*=p_{X*}^{\mathrm{loc}}$. If $X\to\mathrm{pt}$ itself is proper, then $p_{F*}=p_{X*}i_*$; composing with $i_*^{-1}$ proves $p_*^{\mathrm{loc}}=p_{X*}$.

Let $ eta=(i_*)^{-1}(\alpha\cap[X]_T)$. On each component, the complex orientation and refined Gysin map give $i_a^!(\alpha\cap[X]_T)=i_a^*\alpha\cap[F_a]_T$. Since $\alpha\cap[X]_T=i_* eta$, the self-intersection formula [F3] gives $e_T(
u_a)\cap eta_a=i_a^*\alpha\cap[F_a]_T$. Properness of $F_a$ makes $e_T(
u_a)$ invertible after localization by [F3], hence $ eta_a=(i_a^*\alpha/e_T(
u_a))\cap[F_a]_T$. Applying $p_{a*}$ and summing the finitely many components yields the displayed formula. The degree is $2d-q$: division by the degree-$2c_a$ Euler class lowers the localized cohomological degree of the insertion from $q$ to $q-2c_a$, and capping with the degree-$2d_a$ fundamental class gives $2d_a-(q-2c_a)=2d-q$.

fact_uses.text: [L2] For positive Euclidean dimensions, the Borel product is the Euclidean Borel sigma-algebra; in particular this applies to $\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n$ and $\mathbb C\times\mathbb C\cong\mathbb R^4$ ([[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]]).

proof_steps.claim: The pair $(h_1,h_2):\mathbb R^{2n}\to\mathbb C^2$ is Borel measurable: the preimage of every open rectangle $U\times V$ is $h_1^{-1}(U)\cap h_2^{-1}(V)$, and such rectangles generate the product Borel sigma-algebra by [L2]. Complex multiplication $\mathbb C^2\to\mathbb C$ is continuous, so [L3] makes $H=h_1h_2$ Borel measurable. For fixed $x$, the map $y\mapsto(x,y)$ is continuous, and its composite with $H$ is the stated measurable section.

fact_uses.text: [L1] The Borel sigma-algebra on $\mathbb R^{m+n}$ is $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n)$. ([[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]])

proof_steps.claim: Each $Q_N$ from [A1] has finite $\lambda_{m+n}$-measure by [L3], and finite product measure by [L2] and [L3]; step 1.1 shows these values agree. The same step gives agreement on the whole generating pi-system, while [L1] identifies its generated sigma-algebra with $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^{m+n})$. Therefore [L5] implies $\lambda_m \times \lambda_n=\lambda_{m+n}$ on every Borel set.

fact_uses.text:
[F3] For Borel functions $a,b$, $(x,y)\mapsto a(x-y)b(y)$ is Borel on
$\mathbb R^{2n}$; $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^{2n})=\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n)\otimes
\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n)$. ([[lem-borel-representatives-make-the-convolution-integrand-borel-measurable]], [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]], [[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]])

proof_steps.claim: Choose a finite-valued representative $f_0$ vanishing outside $K$. By [F2] and [A1], apply the completed-measurable representative theorem separately to the real and imaginary parts of $f_0$, reset any nonfinite exceptional values to zero, and combine them using [F16] to obtain a finite Borel representative equal to $f_0$ almost everywhere. Reset it to zero off $K$ and call it $\widetilde f$. Set $\Phi(0)=0$; its displayed radial formula is continuous away from the singleton pole, so it is Borel. By [F3], $H(x,y)=\Phi(x-y)\widetilde f(y)$ is Borel, hence product-measurable for $\beta_n\otimes\beta_n$. The open balls $B(0,m)$ are Borel and exhaust $\mathbb R^n$; they have finite $\beta_n$-measure by [F4], so $\beta_n$ is sigma-finite.

Let $\varphi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^n)$ and choose $m$ with $\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subset B(0,m)$. The function $H(x,y)=\Phi(x-y)\widetilde f(y)$ is Borel by [F3]. The pullback of the Borel function $-\Delta\varphi$ by the first-coordinate projection is Borel: the preimage of a Borel set $E$ is $E\times\mathbb R^n$, which belongs to the product sigma-algebra and hence to the Euclidean Borel sigma-algebra by [F3]. The test function is smooth, so $\Delta\varphi$ is continuous; [F16] gives its Borel measurability. Thus $G(x,y)=H(x,y)(-\Delta\varphi(x))$ is Borel by [F16]. Since $\Delta\varphi$ is bounded and compactly supported, step 4.1 shows $G$ is integrable on the product. Fubini therefore gives $\int_{\mathbb R^n}Nf(x)(-\Delta\varphi(x))\,dx=\int_K\widetilde f(y)\left(\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Phi(x-y)(-\Delta\varphi(x))\,dx\right)dy.$ The inner integral is $\varphi(y)$ by the translated point-source identity [F12]. Hence the right side is $\int_K\widetilde f(y)\varphi(y)\,dy$.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F1] For \(k=\mathbb R\), the selected Borel definition uses the same product Milnor model and gives \(A_T(\mathbb R)=\mathbb R[u_1,\ldots,u_r]\) with \(u_i\) the coordinate character class. [[def-torus-equivariant-cohomology-cartan-model]] [[lem-torus-classifying-space-cohomology]]

proof_steps.claim: The rational character formula is [F2]. For the real formula, restrict a smooth character to the coordinate circles; the rational supplier [F2] gives its integer vector \(\mathbf n\). The associated one-dimensional representation \(\mathbb C_{\chi_{\mathbf n}}\) is the tensor product of the coordinate representations \(\mathbb C_{\chi_i}^{\otimes n_i}\), interpreting negative powers as duals; taking associated bundles preserves this tensor-product isomorphism. Additivity and duality in [F3] give \(c_1(L_{\chi_{\mathbf n}})=\sum_i n_i u_i\) over \(\mathbb R\) as well, since the real generators in [F1] are the coefficient images of the same tautological Euler classes. The formula is unique because restriction to each coordinate circle recovers \(n_i\).

The empty product is \(1\), concatenation of two finite character lists multiplies their products, so \(1\in\mathscr S_T(k)\) and \(\mathscr S_T(k)\) is multiplicatively closed. For each nontrivial character \(\mathbf n\ne0\), step 1.1 gives the nonzero linear polynomial \(\sum_i n_i u_i\); a polynomial ring over a field is an integral domain, so every finite product of these classes remains nonzero. If \(r=0\), the generating list is empty and the set is \(\{1\}\). Hence \(0\notin\mathscr S_T(k)\) in all cases.

For a continuous left \(T\)-action on \(X\), the projection \(ET\times_T X\to BT\) makes singular cohomology a module over \(A_T(k)\) by pullback and cup product; pulling back first Chern classes defines the character actions used in the localization. The Borel space and module are defined for empty \(X\) as zero, and for \(r=0\) the localization changes no module because \(\mathscr S_T(k)=\{1\}\). This verifies the constructions in the Definition.

proof_steps.claim: By [F3], each nontrivial character has $u_\chi=\sum_i n_i u_i\neq0$ in the polynomial domain $R_T$. proof_steps.claim: By [F2], $i_*$ is an isomorphism in each degree after localization, so its inverse is a unique $S_T^{-1}R_T$-linear map. The proper inclusion $i$ and the proper map $p_F$ give the stated Borel–Moore pushforwards by [F1].

Composition of the inverse with $p_{F*}$ is therefore a well-defined degree-preserving map on the localized Borel–Moore groups. final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ is the quotient topological group, each class has a representative in $[0,1)$, it is compact Hausdorff and second-countable, and its quotient map is open. proof_steps.claim:
By [A1], for any sequence $(A_n)$ of nonempty sets the family
$\mathcal F=\{A_n:n\in\mathbb N\}$ has a choice function $g$. The composite
$n\mapsto g(A_n)$ is an indexed selector, even if some sets $A_n$ repeat.
Thus [F1] holds and supplies the countable-choice premise in the quotient
circle definition [F2].

For one factor, [F2] makes each quotient interval $q(I)$ open because
$q$ is open, and $q|_I$ is injective because $I$ has length less than $1$.
Its inverse chart is continuous: $q|_I$ is a continuous open bijection onto
$q(I)$. These charts cover the circle. If two charts overlap, local lifts
differ by an integer; this integer is locally constant, so each transition
map is locally a translation and hence smooth. The charts therefore define a
smooth one-manifold without boundary compatible with the quotient topology.

Addition and inversion on one factor are smooth in these charts. Near any
pair of points, choose local real lifts $x,y$ and an output chart around their
sum; after shrinking the input intervals, the coordinate expression for
addition is $x+y$ plus one fixed integer. Near any point, choose local lifts
for it and its inverse; the coordinate expression for inversion is $-x$ plus
one fixed integer. Both expressions are smooth. With the group law already
given by [F2], this is a Lie group by [F6]. Its underlying circle is compact,
Hausdorff and connected by [F2] and [F3], and it is abelian by the quotient
addition law.

The circle has a finite CW structure with one vertex $[0]$ and one open
$1$-cell, the image of $(0,1)$; its characteristic interval has both
endpoints attached to that vertex. For $T$, index product cells by subsets
$J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,r\}$: coordinates in $J$ lie in the open $1$-cell and
all other coordinates equal $[0]$. Each cell is an open cube of dimension
$|J|$, its closure meets only cells indexed by subsets of $J$, and its
characteristic cube is the product of the factor characteristic intervals;
identify each closed cube with a closed disk of the same dimension. The map
$q^r:[0,1]^r\to T$ is a continuous surjection because every coordinate class
has a representative in $[0,1]$ by [F2]. If $K$ is closed in the cube,
then $K$ is compact, $q^r(K)$ is compact, and $q^r(K)$ is closed because $T$
is Hausdorff by [F2] and [F3]. Thus $q^r$ is a quotient map. It is the
characteristic map for the top cell. Every lower-cell characteristic cube is
obtained by precomposing $q^r$ with the continuous coordinate insertion that
fixes omitted coordinates at $0$, so the quotient topology of $q^r$ already
makes every characteristic map continuous; conversely $q^r$ is itself one of
those maps. Hence this quotient topology is exactly the weak topology
determined by the finitely many characteristic cubes. This gives a finite CW
structure with the identity as a $0$-cell. The singleton
identity is a subcomplex, so [F7] gives the homotopy extension property for
its inclusion.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F18] The fixed product torus is a compact connected abelian Lie group, and each period-one basis vector exponentiates to its coordinate circle subgroup as specified in the local torus definition. [[def-standard-product-torus-as-a-compact-lie-group]]

proof_steps.claim: Pullback naturality [F13] shows that $d$ preserves the $T$-fixed forms. For $t\in T$, the left action law and commutativity give $a_t\circ a_{\exp(-s e_i)}=a_{\exp(-s e_i)}\circ a_t$; differentiating at $s=0$ shows $(a_t)_*X_{e_i}=X_{e_i}$. By the pointwise definition [F9], contraction by each $X_{e_i}$ preserves invariant forms, while $u_i$ is fixed by the stipulated trivial action on the polynomial factor. Both terms therefore preserve the diagonal $T$-fixed subspace, so $d_T:C_T(M)\to C_T(M)$ is well-defined.

Put $\phi_s=a_{\exp(-s e_i)}$. The local torus definition [F18] identifies $\exp(-s e_i)$ with the coordinate one-parameter subgroup, so the group law gives $\phi_{s+h}=\phi_s\circ\phi_h$. Differentiating at $h=0$ gives $\frac{d}{ds}\phi_s(p)=(d\phi_s)_pX_{e_i}(p)=X_{e_i}(\phi_s(p))$ by step 1.4. Thus $\phi_s$ is the flow of $X_{e_i}$. For an invariant form $\alpha$, $\phi_s^*\alpha=\alpha$ for every $s$; differentiating at zero and using [F10] gives $\mathcal L_{X_{e_i}}\alpha=0$. Substitution in step 1.5 proves $d_T^2\alpha=0$ on $C_T(M)$.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F1] [[def-abbv-equivariant-integration-conventions]]: equivariant integration is real Borel fiber integration, a character of weight $m$ has Euler class $m u$, and the product orientation fixes the component-integration signs.

proof_steps.claim: The first-factor action fixes exactly $p_0=[1:0]$ and $p_\infty=[0:1]$, while it fixes every point of the second factor. Thus $M^T=F_0\sqcup F_\infty$, with each component a copy of $\mathbb{CP}^1$. The normal bundle is the tangent line of the first factor at its fixed point; in the coordinates $z_1/z_0$ and $z_0/z_1$ its weights are $+1$ on $F_0$ and $-1$ on $F_\infty$.

The normal complex line is the first factor and the fixed-component tangent space is the second. Moving the real two-dimensional first-factor orientation past the real two-dimensional second-factor orientation has sign $(-1)^{2\cdot2}=+1$, so the induced component orientations agree with the product orientations.

The dual tautological fiber at $p_0$ has weight $0$ and at $p_\infty$ has weight $-1$, so the first-factor class restricts to $0$ and $-u$. Thus the contribution from $F_0$ is $0/u=0$; on $F_\infty$, the restricted class is $(-u)\eta$ and the normal Euler class is $-u$, leaving $\eta$, whose integral is $1$. The fixed-component sum is therefore $1$.

Product fiber integration factors over the two compact oriented factors. On the first $\mathbb{CP}^1$, the section of $\mathcal O(1)$ induced by $\ell(z_0,z_1)=z_0$ has one positive transverse zero at $p_\infty$, so its Euler integral is $1$ by the normalized Thom-class zero count; the second-factor integral of $\eta$ is $1$ by definition. Hence $\int_M\alpha=1\cdot1=1$, agreeing with step 3.1.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F1] [[def-abbv-equivariant-integration-conventions]]: a character of weight $m$ has equivariant Euler class $m u$ in real Borel cohomology; equivariant integration uses the complex orientation.

proof_steps.claim: A point $[z_0:z_1]$ is fixed by every $\lambda$ precisely when it lies on one coordinate axis, so the fixed set is $\{p_0,p_\infty\}$. In the coordinate $w=z_1/z_0$ near $p_0$, the action is $w\mapsto\lambda w$, giving tangent weight $+1$; in $v=z_0/z_1$ near $p_\infty$, it is $v\mapsto\lambda^{-1}v$, giving weight $-1$. The complex orientations agree with $M$, so the Euler denominators are $u$ and $-u$.

The tautological fiber at $p_0$ is the trivial coordinate line, and at $p_\infty$ it is the weight-$+1$ coordinate line. Dualizing gives the fixed-fiber weights $0$ and $-1$ for $\mathcal O(1)$, hence $x|_{p_0}=0$ and $x|_{p_\infty}=-u$.

The linear functional $\ell(z_0,z_1)=z_0$ defines a section of $\mathcal O(1)$ that vanishes only at $p_\infty$. In the local coordinate $v=z_0/z_1$ and the dual tautological frame there, its coefficient is $v$, so its unique zero is transverse with positive local degree $+1$. Pulling the normalized Thom class back by a transverse section counts its isolated zeros with these local degrees: excision reduces the pairing to the degree of the section on the boundary of a small disk around each zero. Hence the ordinary Euler number is $1$. Restricting the Borel pushforward to the basepoint of connected $BT$ gives this ordinary Euler number, and $H^0(BT;\mathbb R)=\mathbb R$; therefore $\int_{\mathbb{CP}^1}x=1$, independently confirming the localized sum.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] [[thm-adhm-fixed-point-instanton-count]]: the fixed points for $N=1,k=1$ are indexed by the one one-box partition, and their tangent character is computed from the ADHM deformation complex.

proof_steps.claim: There is exactly one partition of $k=1$ for $N=1$, namely $Y_1=\{(0,0)\}$, so [F2] gives the unique fixed point. Here $\mathbf V_{\vec Y}=e_1$ and $\mathbf W=e_1^{-1}$, whence $\mathbf V^\vee\mathbf V=1$, $\mathbf V^\vee\mathbf W^\vee=1$, and $t_1t_2\mathbf W\mathbf V=t_1t_2$. Substitution in the tangent character gives $t_1+t_2$; the two additive weights are $\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2$, so the Euler class is $\epsilon_1\epsilon_2$.

The degree-one coefficient is the sum over the single fixed point, so it equals $(\epsilon_1\epsilon_2)^{-1}$. This is a formal equivariant fixed-point contribution, not an asserted continuum path-integral value.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] [[thm-adhm-fixed-point-instanton-count]]: fixed points are indexed by two-tuples of partitions of total size one, and the tangent character is $\mathbf V^\vee\mathbf V(t_1+t_2-1-t_1t_2)+\mathbf V^\vee\mathbf W^\vee+t_1t_2\mathbf W\mathbf V$.

proof_steps.claim: A two-tuple of partitions with total size one places its single box in exactly one of the two colors, so the only possibilities are $(\{(0,0)\},\varnothing)$ and $(\varnothing,\{(0,0)\})$. Their quotient representatives have $V$-characters $e_1$ and $e_2$, respectively.

For the first point, the ADHM convention [F1] gives $\mathbf W=e_1^{-1}+e_2^{-1}$ and $\mathbf W^\vee=e_1+e_2$, while $\mathbf V=e_1$. Substitution in [F2] gives $$t_1+t_2+\frac{e_2}{e_1}+t_1t_2\frac{e_1}{e_2}.$$ The corresponding additive weights are $\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2,a_2-a_1,\epsilon_1+\epsilon_2+a_1-a_2$, so their product is $E_1$. Interchanging the two colors gives the second displayed character and $E_2$.

Each fixed-point contribution is the reciprocal of its Euler product, so the degree-one coefficient is $E_1^{-1}+E_2^{-1}$. The TikZ drawing only records the two one-box colorings and is not used in this calculation.

proof_steps.claim: By [A2], [F5] and [F6], the concrete background has index one, real product-kernel parity one and central line action $-1$, so the specified physical test [F1] applies. Compactness of the unit cotangent sphere bundle gives $p_j(x,\xi)\ge c|\xi|^2I$ uniformly. Thus [L1] applies to $\Delta$, using exactly the given spectral heat data. Its principal symbol may be matrix-valued.

Write $n=\dim M$ and $J_x$ for the normal-coordinate volume density. For $y=\exp_x(\sqrt t\,v)$ in the chosen neighborhood, [L1] and step 1.1 imply that $t^{n/2}J_x(\sqrt t\,v)\sum_j(-1)^j\operatorname{tr}(\rho_g^j K_t^j(g^{-1}y,y))$ tends pointwise to $\sum_j(-1)^j\operatorname{tr}(\rho_g^j|_{E_x^j}\,k_{x,1}^j(dg_x^{-1}v,v))$. Simplicity makes $dg_x^{-1}-I$ invertible. Local distance comparison in the normal chart therefore gives $d(g^{-1}y,y)\ge c_x\sqrt t\,|v|$. Choose $L>n$; bounded density, unitary $\rho_g$ and [L1] bound the extended-by-zero rescaled density by $C(1+c_x|v|)^{-L}$, integrable on $T_xM$. Outside these neighborhoods compactness gives $d(g^{-1}y,y)\ge\delta>0$, so [L1] bounds the full complementary trace integral by $C t^{(L-n)/2}\to0$. By [F2], the heat-supertrace limit is consequently the sum of these tangent integrals. No uniform-integral-bound-to-convergence implication is used.

Since $dg_x$ is orthogonal, $|\det(dg_x^{-1}-I)|=|\det(I-dg_x)|$. The change of variables $w=(dg_x^{-1}-I)v$ therefore contributes $|\det_{\mathbb R}(I-dg_x)|^{-1}$. By [L1], the constant-coefficient tangent heat kernel has integral $I_{E_x^\bullet}$. Its graded fiber trace after composition with $\rho_g$ is $\sum_j(-1)^j\operatorname{tr}(\rho_g|_{E_x^j})$. For $n=0$, the tangent integral and determinant are both the empty-dimensional values $1$, so the same expression holds. Summing the finitely many contributions proves the stated limit.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F1] Fourier transformation preserves Schwartz space continuously, with its differentiation and polynomial-multiplication identities; Fourier inversion holds there. proof_steps.claim: Work in one precompact bundle chart and write $p(y,\xi)=\sum A^{ij}(y)\xi_i\xi_j$. The matrices need not commute. For a parameter derivative, the matrix exponential satisfies $\partial e^{-p}=-\int_0^1e^{-(1-s)p}(\partial p)e^{-sp}\,ds$, obtained by differentiating the matrix ODE defining the exponential. Iterating this identity and differentiating in $\xi$ expresses every derivative in $y,\xi$ as finitely many simplex integrals of products of polynomial derivatives of $p$ and exponential factors whose time lengths sum to one. Since $p\ge c'|\xi|^2I$ uniformly on the chart closure, the product norm is at most a polynomial in $|\xi|$ times $e^{-c'|\xi|^2}$. Thus $e^{-p(y,\cdot)}$ is a uniformly bounded smooth Schwartz family. By [F1] its inverse transform $k_y(w)$ has all uniformly bounded Schwartz seminorms, and $\int k_y(w)\,dw=e^{-p(y,0)}=I$. This uses Fourier inversion on Schwartz functions, not an exchange of an undamped double Fourier integral.

Let $\kappa_i$ be finitely many charts with smooth unitary frames, and let $\phi_i$ be a partition subordinate to compact subsets of those charts. Choose smooth cutoffs $\chi_i(y,z)$ supported where both points lie in chart $i$, equal to one near $y=z$ whenever $z\in\operatorname{supp}\phi_i$. Write volume as $w_i(z)\,d\kappa_i(z)$. Define $Z_t(y,z)$ in these frames by the finite sum of $\phi_i(z)\chi_i(y,z)w_i(z)^{-1}t^{-n/2}k_{i,z}((\kappa_i(y)-\kappa_i(z))/\sqrt t)$, interpreting each summand as a bundle map. In each summand the principal coefficients are frozen at the source $z$. Step 1.1, local equivalence of chart distance and $d$, and cutoff support give $\|Z_t(y,z)\|\le C_LH_{t,L}(y,z)$, where $H_{t,L}=t^{-n/2}(1+d(y,z)/\sqrt t)^{-L}$. Moreover $Z_tf\to f$ in $L^2$ for smooth $f$: put $\kappa_i(y)-\kappa_i(z)=\sqrt t\,v$, use the uniform integrable Schwartz bound, and use $\sum_i\phi_i=1$ and $\int k_{i,y}=I$. For $R_t=(\partial_t+P_y)Z_t$, the frozen principal part cancels $\partial_t$. The remaining principal term contains $A(y)-A(z)=O(d(y,z))$ and two derivatives of the frozen kernel; lower terms contain at most one derivative. The bound $d(y,z)t^{-1}H_{t,L+1}\le t^{-1/2}H_{t,L}$ therefore gives $\|R_t(y,z)\|\le C_Lt^{-1/2}H_{t,L}(y,z)$. Derivatives of cutoffs are supported away from the diagonal and obey the same bound by choosing additional Schwartz decay.

Fix $x$ and put $y=\exp_x(\sqrt t\,a)$, $z=\exp_x(\sqrt t\,b)$. In a chart, Taylor expansion gives $(\kappa_i(y)-\kappa_i(z))/\sqrt t\to d\kappa_i|_x(a-b)$, the frozen symbol tends to $p_i(x,\xi)$, and all frame maps, partition weights and density factors tend to their values at $x$. Linear change of cotangent variables in the absolutely convergent Fourier integral transforms each limiting chart expression into $\phi_i(x)k_x(a-b)$: the coordinate Jacobian cancels $w_i(x)$ because normal-coordinate volume density at $x$ is one. Summing gives $k_x(a-b)$. All convergences are uniform on bounded $a,b$ by step 1.1. By step 4.1, $t^{n/2}\|K_t-Z_t\|\le C\sqrt t$, so it has zero limit. This proves the rescaled limit and all assertions for $n>0$. If $M$ is empty the claims are vacuous; for $n=0$, compact $M$ is finite and differential operators act separately on its fibers, so ordinary matrix exponentiation gives exactly the asserted finite-dimensional limit.

proof_steps.claim: A global section of $\mathcal O(-k)$, $k=1,2$, would have an entire coefficient $f_0(t)$ with $f_0(t)=t^{-k}f_\infty(1/t)$. By the normally convergent expansions in [F2], the left side has only powers $t^n$ with $n\ge0$, whereas the right side has only powers $t^n$ with $n\le-k$. Uniqueness of Laurent coefficients forces every coefficient to vanish. Thus both degree-zero groups vanish.

A one-cochain on the two-chart overlap has a normally convergent Laurent expansion $g(t)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}a_nt^n$. Coboundaries subtract the entire $t$-series with $n\ge0$ and the series $t^{-k}f_\infty(1/t)$ with $n\le-k$. These two tails converge on their respective entire charts by [F2]; the cover is acyclic for both twists because $r=1$ and $k=1,2$. For $k=1$ they exhaust every integer exponent, so the analytic first cohomology is zero. For $k=2$ the sole remaining exponent is $n=-1$; its coefficient cannot be a coboundary, and it identifies the analytic first cohomology with $\mathbb C$.

proof_steps.claim: Smoothness of the needed primitive does not require a theorem about varying complex structures. Choose smooth unit quaternionic frames of $Q_x$ on a base neighborhood and a smooth unitary frame of $E$. These identify the vertical problem exactly with the fixed $SU(2)$-invariant Hermitian $\mathcal O(-2)$ problem on $\mathbb CP^1$, componentwise in $E_x$. Set $B=\bar\partial^*G$ on vertical degree one. By [F3], $\bar\partial B=I-\Pi$, and by [F2] its degree-zero kernel is zero. The estimates [F4] and the first-order nature of $\bar\partial^*$ give $B:H^m\to H^{m+1}$ bounded for each $m$. For jointly smooth $f(x,t)$, base difference quotients converge in every fibre $H^m$ uniformly on compact base sets, by the Taylor formula and compactness of the fibre. Applying the fixed bounded $B$ shows $\partial_x^\beta(Bf)=B(\partial_x^\beta f)$ at every order in every $H^{m+1}$. Sobolev embedding on the fixed two-dimensional compact fibre, with arbitrarily large $m$, gives joint smoothness in $(x,t)$. For the horizontal coefficient problem, choose also a smooth unit quaternionic frame of $Q_x^\perp$. Together the two quaternionic frames give a smooth $Sp(2)$ transformation from a fixed pair of planes to $(Q_x,Q_x^\perp)$. Its complex-linear action on $\mathbb CP^3$ is holomorphic and preserves the Fubini–Study and tautological metrics. It therefore transports the horizontal quotient, its vertical Bott operator and its induced metric to the fixed $\mathcal O(-1)^{\oplus2}$ problem identified below. That inverse is likewise one fixed bounded operator componentwise, so the same derivative argument applies. Thus no moving-cokernel inverse or unproved parametric Green assertion is used.

proof_steps.claim: For the global metric splitting, the mixed component of $\bar\partial(s\sigma)$ is a vertical degree-one form with coefficient $\mathcal O(-1)^{\oplus2}\otimes E_x$. There are finitely many components by [F1], so \(H_T^*(F;k)\) and its localization split into the finite product of the component rings treated in step 3.1. The finite-dimensional matrix exponential is smooth, has derivative the identity at zero on $\mathfrak{su}(N)$, and maps $\mathfrak{su}(N)$ into $SU(N)$. In the Banach algebra from step 2.1 its power series and every termwise derivative converge in $H^{k+1}$ on a sufficiently small ball, since the algebra norm is submultiplicative after an equivalent rescaling. Hence pointwise $\exp$ and $\log$ give inverse smooth maps between neighborhoods of zero in $H^{k+1}(\operatorname{ad}P)$ and the identity in $\mathcal G_{k+1}$. final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] [[thm-qftx-taubes-arbitrary-divisor-plane-vortex]]: for every effective finite divisor of degree $|n|$ there is a smooth finite-energy planar critical pair with flux $2\pi n$ (using conjugation for $n<0$); for the empty divisor it is the vacuum. The local unwound exterior gauge has $q=\sqrt\xi e^{h/2}$ and $A=-\tfrac12*dh$; that degree-changing exterior gauge is not asserted to extend globally. Separately, removing only the smooth degree-zero polynomial phase correction relative to $n\theta$ by a global cutoff gauge yields the canonical winding representative $q=\sqrt\xi e^{h/2}e^{in\theta}$, $A=n\,d\theta-\tfrac12*dh$.

proof_steps.claim: For an end trace with exterior phase $n\theta+\phi$, choose a smooth radial cutoff $\eta$ which is zero on a disk containing the noncanonical region and one outside a larger disk. The real function $\chi=-\eta\phi$ extends smoothly by zero to the whole plane; the allowed gauge transformation $(q,A)\mapsto(e^{i\chi}q,A+d\chi)$ therefore makes the exterior phase exactly $n\theta$. This constructs the asserted degree-zero exterior phase cleanup without attempting to extend a degree-$n$ angular map across the disk. For the planar minimizer in [F2], write $P=|P|e^{i\vartheta}$ on the exterior; $\vartheta-n\theta$ is single-valued, smooth and tends to zero because $P(z)=z^n(1+O(|z|^{-1}))$ for $n\ge0$ (use the conjugate construction for $n<0$). Applying the same cutoff extension to $-(\vartheta-n\theta)$ changes its exterior fields to $q^*=\rho_*e^{in\theta}$ and $A^*=n\,d\theta-\tfrac12*dh$; hence $A^*-n\,d\theta$ decays exponentially.

In canonical exterior gauge write $q=\rho e^{in\theta}$ and $\alpha=A-n\,d\theta$. Directly, $D_Aq=e^{in\theta}(d\rho-i\rho\alpha)$, so the real and imaginary terms are orthogonal and $|D_Aq|^2=|d\rho|^2+\rho^2|\alpha|^2$. Uniform convergence gives $\rho\ge\sqrt\xi/2$ outside a disk; thus finite kinetic energy implies $\alpha\in L^2$ there. Also $|\rho-\sqrt\xi|\le |\rho^2-\xi|/\sqrt\xi$, so finite potential energy gives $\rho-\sqrt\xi\in L^2$ there. On compact disks all fields are smooth and bounded. Consequently, for any two cleaned end traces and the cleaned minimizer, differences of connections and Higgs fields are globally in $L^2$; each Higgs field is bounded.

Apply step 3.1 first to $p_0$ and $p_*$, defining its finite energy to be $C_0$, and then to $p_*$ and $p_1$, defining its finite energy to be $C_1$. For $L\ge2\ell$, place the first collar on $[0,\ell]$, the constant planar minimizer on $[\ell,L-\ell]$, and the second collar on $[L-\ell,L]$. The profiles match smoothly because the collar cutoff is constant near its ends. The middle has no longitudinal energy and contributes exactly $T_n(L-2\ell)$ by [F2]–[F3]. At $L=2\ell$ this middle interval has zero length; the two collars meet at the constant value $p_*$, so the same upper bound holds. This admissible concatenation proves $\inf\mathcal E_L\le C_0+T_n(L-2\ell)+C_1$.

Combining steps 1.1 and 4.1 gives $0\le\inf\mathcal E_L-T_nL\le C_0+C_1-2\ell T_n$ for every $L\ge2\ell$; the right side is a finite constant independent of $L$, proving the bounded-remainder conclusion. If $p_0=p_1=p_*$, the constant extension $(A_1,A_2,q)=(A^*,q^*)$, $A_3=0$, has energy $T_nL$ and satisfies the angular and no-leakage conditions. The lower bound from step 1.1 then proves it is an exact translation-invariant minimum.

proof_steps.claim: For each fixed divisor, [F2] supplies a smooth pair satisfying the relevant first-order equations. Its square terms in step 1.1 vanish identically; the sequence estimates of steps 1.2–2.1 apply because [F2] gives finite energy and the same boundary sector. Hence its energy is exactly $2\pi\xi|n|$. The lower bound of step 3.1 applies to every admissible same-winding configuration, so this pair is an absolute transverse energy minimum, without radial or unit-winding assumptions.

Let $(a,\eta)$ be a smooth compactly supported variation of a minimizing pair, and set $A_t=A+ta$, $q_t=q+t\eta$; for any field expression $F$, define $\delta F:=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}F(A_t,q_t)$. For sufficiently small $t$, the fields remain in the same boundary sector; outside the compact support they equal the original fields. Thus the boundary-current limit in the disk identity is unchanged and the flux is unchanged by Stokes applied to $d a$. The energy along this variation is the constant $2\pi\xi|n|$ plus the squared $L^2$ norms of the two first-order residuals in step 1.1. Both residuals vanish at $t=0$; differentiating the squared norms gives $E'(0)=0$ and
$$E''(0)=2\int_{\mathbb R^2}\left(|\delta(D_{A,1}\pm iD_{A,2})q|^2+\frac{|\delta(B\mp e^2(\xi-|q|^2))|^2}{2e^2}\right)dx_1dx_2\ge0,$$
with the upper signs for $n\ge0$ and lower signs for $n\le0$ (either choice when $n=0$). Therefore the first variation vanishes and no smooth compactly supported same-sector perturbation lowers the energy. Distinct divisors give distinct possible minimizing fields, so no cross-divisor uniqueness follows.

proof_steps.claim: Conversely, let $\mathcal E$ be a framed torsion-free sheaf with the stated Hilbert polynomial. Choosing a basis of $V_1$ and using the fixed framed basis of $W$ identifies $M=V\oplus V\oplus W$ and the line maps with the two Euler blocks in the Statement. Any other such choice differs by one simultaneous element of $GL(V)$.

The remaining coefficients of the two linear maps are their $z_0$ coefficients, so write $\alpha=(z_0B_1-z_1,z_0B_2-z_2,z_0J)^T$ and $\beta=(-z_0C_1+z_2,z_0C_2-z_1,z_0I)$. The surjectivity of $\beta$ implies stability: if $U=\operatorname{span}\{B_{i_1}\cdots B_{i_m}I(W)\}$ were proper, it is invariant and the induced $B_1,B_2$ on $V/U$ commute because $[B_1,B_2]=-IJ$ has image in $U$. The Beilinson construction is natural under framed sheaf isomorphisms, so an isomorphism of framed sheaves induces maps on the cohomology vector spaces used in steps 1.2–6.2 and hence a single change of basis $g\in GL(V)$; the normalized Euler blocks force the recovered tuples to differ by $g\cdot(B_1,B_2,I,J)$. Conversely such a $g$ is an isomorphism of monads acting trivially on $W$, and therefore induces a framed sheaf isomorphism. This proves the pointwise inverse equivalence modulo $GL(V)$. For a finite-type data family, step 2.1 makes $\beta$ surjective on the total space, so $K=\ker\beta$ is locally free. The sequence $0\to V\mathcal O(-1)\to K\to\mathcal E\to0$ is exact and its terms before $\mathcal E$ are flat over the base. After tensoring with any residue field of the base, the first map remains sheaf-injective by step 1.1; hence $\operatorname{Tor}_1(k(s),\mathcal E)=0$. Since $\mathcal E$ is finite over each local ring of $\mathbb P^2\times S$ and its residue fiber is a vector space over the residue field, [F8] gives flatness over $S$. Under the stated relative cohomology and base-change hypotheses, the same constructions use vector bundles and are inverse for families.

Apply the family equivalence to $S=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$. proof_steps.claim: Fix $q>0$ and a nonzero $s_0$.
