The fibre groups, global edge and operator coefficient have been obtained without any algebraic GAGA, monad or inverse-normal-form premise. All conclusions therefore retain the stated arbitrary finite-rank unitary ASD scope, with the analytic inputs and full AC hypothesis explicit.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] [[thm-qftx-taubes-arbitrary-divisor-plane-vortex]]: for every effective finite divisor of degree $|n|$ there is a smooth finite-energy planar critical pair with flux $2\pi n$ (using conjugation for $n<0$); for the empty divisor it is the vacuum. The local unwound exterior gauge has $q=\sqrt\xi e^{h/2}$ and $A=-\tfrac12*dh$; that degree-changing exterior gauge is not asserted to extend globally. Separately, removing only the smooth degree-zero polynomial phase correction relative to $n\theta$ by a global cutoff gauge yields the canonical winding representative $q=\sqrt\xi e^{h/2}e^{in\theta}$, $A=n\,d\theta-\tfrac12*dh$.

proof_steps.claim: For an end trace with exterior phase $n\theta+\phi$, choose a smooth radial cutoff $\eta$ which is zero on a disk containing the noncanonical region and one outside a larger disk. The real function $\chi=-\eta\phi$ extends smoothly by zero to the whole plane; the allowed gauge transformation $(q,A)\mapsto(e^{i\chi}q,A+d\chi)$ therefore makes the exterior phase exactly $n\theta$. This constructs the asserted degree-zero exterior phase cleanup without attempting to extend a degree-$n$ angular map across the disk. For the planar minimizer in [F2], write $P=|P|e^{i\vartheta}$ on the exterior; $\vartheta-n\theta$ is single-valued, smooth and tends to zero because $P(z)=z^n(1+O(|z|^{-1}))$ for $n\ge0$ (use the conjugate construction for $n<0$). Applying the same cutoff extension to $-(\vartheta-n\theta)$ changes its exterior fields to $q^*=\rho_*e^{in\theta}$ and $A^*=n\,d\theta-\tfrac12*dh$; hence $A^*-n\,d\theta$ decays exponentially.

In canonical exterior gauge write $q=\rho e^{in\theta}$ and $\alpha=A-n\,d\theta$. Directly, $D_Aq=e^{in\theta}(d\rho-i\rho\alpha)$, so the real and imaginary terms are orthogonal and $|D_Aq|^2=|d\rho|^2+\rho^2|\alpha|^2$. Uniform convergence gives $\rho\ge\sqrt\xi/2$ outside a disk; thus finite kinetic energy implies $\alpha\in L^2$ there. Also $|\rho-\sqrt\xi|\le |\rho^2-\xi|/\sqrt\xi$, so finite potential energy gives $\rho-\sqrt\xi\in L^2$ there. On compact disks all fields are smooth and bounded. Consequently, for any two cleaned end traces and the cleaned minimizer, differences of connections and Higgs fields are globally in $L^2$; each Higgs field is bounded.

Apply step 3.1 first to $p_0$ and $p_*$, defining its finite energy to be $C_0$, and then to $p_*$ and $p_1$, defining its finite energy to be $C_1$. For $L\ge2\ell$, place the first collar on $[0,\ell]$, the constant planar minimizer on $[\ell,L-\ell]$, and the second collar on $[L-\ell,L]$. The profiles match smoothly because the collar cutoff is constant near its ends. The middle has no longitudinal energy and contributes exactly $T_n(L-2\ell)$ by [F2]–[F3]. At $L=2\ell$ this middle interval has zero length; the two collars meet at the constant value $p_*$, so the same upper bound holds. This admissible concatenation proves $\inf\mathcal E_L\le C_0+T_n(L-2\ell)+C_1$.

Combining steps 1.1 and 4.1 gives $0\le\inf\mathcal E_L-T_nL\le C_0+C_1-2\ell T_n$ for every $L\ge2\ell$; the right side is a finite constant independent of $L$, proving the bounded-remainder conclusion. If $p_0=p_1=p_*$, the constant extension $(A_1,A_2,q)=(A^*,q^*)$, $A_3=0$, has energy $T_nL$ and satisfies the angular and no-leakage conditions. The lower bound from step 1.1 then proves it is an exact translation-invariant minimum.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] [[thm-qftx-taubes-arbitrary-divisor-plane-vortex]]: for each effective finite divisor of degree $|n|$, the reconstructed smooth critical fields satisfy the corresponding first-order equations, have finite energy, and have flux $2\pi n$ with sign set by the orientation.

proof_steps.claim: For each fixed divisor, [F2] supplies a smooth pair satisfying the relevant first-order equations. Its square terms in step 1.1 vanish identically; the sequence estimates of steps 1.2–2.1 apply because [F2] gives finite energy and the same boundary sector. Hence its energy is exactly $2\pi\xi|n|$. The lower bound of step 3.1 applies to every admissible same-winding configuration, so this pair is an absolute transverse energy minimum, without radial or unit-winding assumptions.

Let $(a,\eta)$ be a smooth compactly supported variation of a minimizing pair, and set $A_t=A+ta$, $q_t=q+t\eta$; for any field expression $F$, define $\delta F:=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}F(A_t,q_t)$. For sufficiently small $t$, the fields remain in the same boundary sector; outside the compact support they equal the original fields. Thus the boundary-current limit in the disk identity is unchanged and the flux is unchanged by Stokes applied to $d a$. The energy along this variation is the constant $2\pi\xi|n|$ plus the squared $L^2$ norms of the two first-order residuals in step 1.1. Both residuals vanish at $t=0$; differentiating the squared norms gives $E'(0)=0$ and
$$E''(0)=2\int_{\mathbb R^2}\left(|\delta(D_{A,1}\pm iD_{A,2})q|^2+\frac{|\delta(B\mp e^2(\xi-|q|^2))|^2}{2e^2}\right)dx_1dx_2\ge0,$$
with the upper signs for $n\ge0$ and lower signs for $n\le0$ (either choice when $n=0$). Therefore the first variation vanishes and no smooth compactly supported same-sector perturbation lowers the energy. Distinct divisors give distinct possible minimizing fields, so no cross-divisor uniqueness follows.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] A square-zero smooth Dolbeault operator on a finite-rank bundle has local holomorphic frames, and intertwining maps are holomorphic. [[lem-qftx-local-integrable-dolbeault-frames]]

proof_steps.claim: In the chart w=λ₂/λ₁ on a real incidence fiber, the projected horizontal (0,1) directions are H₁=∂bar_z₁−w∂z₂ and H₂=∂bar_z₂+w∂z₁. Indeed these and the vertical ∂bar_w annihilate the holomorphic coordinates w, μ₁=z₁−bar_z₂w, μ₂=z₂+bar_z₁w. They are independent and commute; their coefficients are holomorphic in w. For a unitary connection A define the pulled-back (0,1) operator by the vertical ordinary derivative and ∇_A along H₁,H₂. Its mixed squares vanish by the displayed commuting generators and holomorphic w coefficients. Its horizontal square is F_A(H₁,H₂)=F_bar1bar2−w(F_1bar1+F_2bar2)+w²F_12, which vanishes for an ASD two-form in the positive orientation: the three coefficients are precisely its self-dual component. Thus the operator squares to zero on this chart, and on the other projective chart by the same tensorial calculation. Apply [F2] to obtain a genuine holomorphic bundle. Its restriction to every real line is the constant bundle E_x, with positive reality pairing induced by the unitary metric and framing at infinity. This pairing is holomorphic: its vertical derivative vanishes on the constant fibres, and differentiating horizontally gives zero by the original identity ∇_A h=0, with the conjugate pullback at σ interchanging the conjugate horizontal directions.

Restrict H and ∇ to the totally real graph locus M=HP¹. Its smooth real incidence is diffeomorphic to Z by (P,[v])↦[v], with inverse [v]↦(span(v,jv),[v]); the explicit charts in [F3] verify smoothness. Under this identification dp(D) is exactly the span of H₁,H₂ in step 1.1: write X_z=((z₁,-bar_z₂),(z₂,bar_z₁)) and solve v(1,w)^T=0. Therefore the restricted smooth connection has F(H₁,H₂)=0 for every w, so all three self-dual coefficients in step 1.1 vanish. Hence it is ASD. Evaluation intertwines the original holomorphic operator on E with the reconstructed vertical/horizontal Dolbeault operator: it is holomorphic vertically, and on D its derivative is exactly the canonical relative derivative δ by step 3.1. These directions generate the (0,1) tangent in step 1.1, proving equality of the full operators, not just of underlying bundles.

Starting from A in step 1.1, its constant real-line sections identify the reconstructed smooth H with E. Along every alpha-plane the recovered connection has the same derivative as A; the cotangent uniqueness in step 3.1 makes the full connections equal. The unitary reality pairing and framing also agree. Starting from a Ward bundle, step 4.1 proves evaluation is a holomorphic isomorphism from the reconstructed pullback to the original bundle, and step 5.2 preserves its reality pairing and metric. These constructions and identities apply to morphisms as well, so descend to inverse maps on based unitary gauge and framed holomorphic isomorphism classes. No irreducibility or absence of parallel sections was used.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] For every continuous map from a finite polyhedron into $\mathcal A_\infty$, with irreducible values on a subpolyhedron, the relative avoidance lemma supplies a homotopy fixed on that subpolyhedron and an open neighborhood of it whose endpoint is entirely irreducible. Its complete argument and exact batch-56 inputs were inspected; the configuration and stabilizer suppliers now have current ready Step 1 records ([[lem-qftx-relative-finite-parameter-irreducible-avoidance]]).

proof_steps.claim: The affine space $\mathcal A_\infty$ contains $A_0$. Apply [F2] to the constant map from a one-point polyhedron with empty subpolyhedron and value $A_0$. Its endpoint is an element of $\mathcal A_\infty^*$, proving nonemptiness.

Let $A,B\in\mathcal A_\infty^*$. The affine path $\gamma(t)=(1-t)A+tB$ is continuous in the Fréchet topology and has irreducible endpoints. Apply [F2] with $K=I$ and $L=\{0,1\}$. The resulting endpoint path remains in $\mathcal A_\infty^*$ and fixes both endpoints, so the locus is path-connected.

Apply [F2] to $F$ with $K=D^{j+1}$ and $L=\partial D^{j+1}=S^j$. Its boundary is already irreducible, so the endpoint is a map $G:D^{j+1}\to\mathcal A_\infty^*$ agreeing with $u$ on the boundary. Choose the based point $x_0\in S^j$ with $u(x_0)=A$. Since the disk is convex, $C_t(x)=(1-t)x+tx_0$ remains in the disk and fixes $x_0$. Then $G(C_t(x))$ is a homotopy from $G$ to the constant map at $A$ that fixes $x_0$ and remains in $\mathcal A_\infty^*$. Restricting it to $S^j$ gives a based nullhomotopy of $u$; by [F3], its class in $\pi_j(\mathcal A_\infty^*,A)$ is zero. Since $j$ and $u$ were arbitrary, every stated homotopy group vanishes.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F3] For the stated Sobolev index, the smooth irreducible projection $\mathcal A_\infty^*\to\mathcal A_\infty^*/\overline{\mathcal G}_\infty$ is a locally trivial topological principal $\overline{\mathcal G}_\infty$-bundle with its actual $C^\infty$ quotient topology; the Sobolev irreducible locus $\mathcal A_k^*$ is open. [[thm-qftx-sobolev-smooth-irreducible-gauge-bundle]]

proof_steps.claim: Choose the fixed integer $k>r/2+1$. The smooth clause of [F3], applied with the configuration data [F2], makes $q_*$ a locally trivial principal $\overline{\mathcal G}^\infty(P)$-bundle. By [F4], its total space is nonempty, path connected, and has $\pi_j=0$ for every $j\ge1$, so it is weakly contractible in the sense used in [F6]. For a constant central gauge section $u=\zeta I_N$, the local action formula gives $A^u=A$ because $u^{-1}Au=A$ and $du=0$; hence reduced and full gauge groups have the same orbits on $\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P)$.

The locus $\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P)$ is gauge invariant: in the chosen frame, the based holonomy subgroup of $A^u$ is $u(p_m)^{-1}\operatorname{Hol}_{p_m}(A)u(p_m)$, so it has the same invariant subspaces up to conjugation. It is open: by [F2], the inclusion $\mathcal A^\infty(P)\hookrightarrow\mathcal A_k(P)$ is continuous, as each fixed $H^k$ norm is bounded by finitely many smooth derivative seminorms on the finite compact atlas. The smooth irreducible locus is the inverse image of the Sobolev irreducible locus, which is open by [F3]. The full orbit projection $q$ is open because, for any open $U\subseteq\mathcal A^\infty(P)$, its saturation $q^{-1}(q(U))=\bigcup_{u\in\mathcal G^\infty(P)}U\cdot u$ is open. For fixed smooth $u$, the map $A\mapsto u^{-1}Au+u^{-1}du$ is continuous in every finite-atlas derivative seminorm by the Leibniz rule; its inverse is the same formula for $u^{-1}$, so each gauge translate is a homeomorphism. Therefore $q(\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P))$ is open and $q|_{\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P)}$ is an open quotient map onto this subset. The reduced and full actions have the same orbits there, so their quotient topologies identify the reduced orbit space homeomorphically with $q(\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P))$; this proves the claim about $\iota$ in the Statement. If $q$ had a continuous section, its restriction to this open subset would take each irreducible orbit to a point in that same orbit, hence into $\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P)$. Via the stated homeomorphism, this would give a continuous section of $q_*$, contradicting step 3.1. Thus $q$ has no continuous section.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F6] For a smooth-coefficient elliptic operator on a compact manifold, distributional solutions gain two Sobolev derivatives when the right-hand side gains the corresponding Sobolev order, with the stated elliptic estimate. [[thm-elliptic-differential-operators-on-compact-vector-bundles-have-parametrices-and-regularity]]

proof_steps.claim: For the smooth-space clause, fix now a smooth irreducible center $A\in\mathcal A_\infty^*$ and use the Banach slice and trivialization established in step 4.1. Put $U_A=\Phi_A(S_{A,\varepsilon}\times\bar{\mathcal G}_{k+1})$ and $V_A=\pi_k(S_{A,\varepsilon})$. Since $U_A$ is open in $\mathcal A_k^*$, $U_A\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*$ is open in the stated $C^\infty$ topology; set $S_A^\infty=S_{A,\varepsilon}\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*$ and $V_A^\infty=\pi_\infty(S_A^\infty)$. For a smooth $B\in U_A$, its unique reduced gauge class from step 4.1 has a representative $u\in\mathcal G_{k+1}$. It satisfies $d_A^*(B^{u^{-1}}-A)=0$. Locally in a bundle frame, write $C_j=uB_j u^{-1}-(\partial_j u)u^{-1}-A_j$. Substitution in $d_A^*C=0$, use of $\partial_i(u^{-1})=-u^{-1}(\partial_i u)u^{-1}$, and multiplication on the right by $u$ isolate the equation $g^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j u=R(A,B,g;u,u^{-1},du)$ on each chart. Every term in $R$ is a finite product of smooth coefficients (including first derivatives of $A,B$) and factors among $u,u^{-1},du$; hence the principal operator is the scalar smooth Laplacian on each matrix entry. If $u\in H^{r+1}$ for $r\ge k$, then this right-hand side lies in $H^r$ by [F7] and the smooth coefficient bounds. Elliptic regularity [F6] gives $u\in H^{r+2}$. Iteration proves $u$ smooth; changing its representative by an element of the finite center preserves smoothness. Thus every smooth point of the Banach saturation has a smooth trivialization representative, and $U_A\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*=\pi_\infty^{-1}(V_A^\infty)$.

Suppose smooth $B_j\to B$ in $C^\infty$ within $U_A\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*$. The Banach trivialization from step 4.1 gives convergence of their slice representatives in $H^k$ and of their reduced gauge classes in $H^{k+1}$. In a quotient chart around the limiting class from step 1.1, choose lifts $u_j,u$ that converge in $H^{k+1}$; this is possible because the finite center acts by disjoint translates. The equation in step 5.2 and elliptic estimates [F6] bootstrap convergence: if $u_j\to u$ in $H^{r+1}$, then the assumed $C^\infty$ convergence gives $B_j\to B$ in $H^{r+1}$, and [F7] makes the right-hand sides converge in $H^r$. Apply the elliptic estimate to $u_j-u$, using also their already known $H^{k+1}$ convergence for the $L^2$ term, to get $u_j\to u$ in $H^{r+2}$. Induction gives convergence in every Sobolev order, which on compact $M$ is the $C^\infty$ section topology. The slice representatives converge in $C^\infty$ by their action formula. Conversely the forward action is continuous in the $C^\infty$ topology by multiplication and differentiation of smooth sections. The saturation $U_A\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*$ is open, and $V_A^\infty$ is open in the quotient because the quotient map is open: the saturation of any open set is a union of its open gauge translates. The restricted map $S_A^\infty\times\bar{\mathcal G}_\infty\to\pi_\infty^{-1}(V_A^\infty)$ is therefore a homeomorphism for the actual quotient topology, and it is equivariant. This proves the smooth-space topological principal bundle claim.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F3] [[thm-interior-w-two-p-estimate-for-uniformly-elliptic-equations]]: for $p>2$ on a two-dimensional ball, the interior $W^{2,p}$ norm is bounded by the local $L^p$ norms of the solution and its Laplacian.

proof_steps.claim: To obtain derivative decay, fix $\alpha<\alpha'<\sqrt\kappa$ and use step 3.3 at rate $\alpha'$. On each unit ball centered at large $z$, both $w$ and $\Delta w=\kappa(1-e^{-w})$ are $O(e^{-\alpha'|z|})$. By [F3] and [F5], $w$ has a $C^{1,\beta}$ norm of that order on the concentric half-ball for some $\beta>0$. Thus the right-hand side has a $C^{0,\beta}$ norm of the same order, and [F4] gives $C^{2,\beta}$ decay on a smaller ball. Inductively, for each multi-index $\gamma$, differentiating $\Delta w=\kappa(1-e^{-w})$ gives $\Delta D^\gamma w=\kappa e^{-w}D^\gamma w+G_\gamma$, where $G_\gamma$ is a finite sum of products of lower derivatives of $w$ and is exponentially small by the induction hypothesis. Applying [F3] and [F4] on nested unit balls gives the same $e^{-\alpha'|z|}$ bound for two more derivatives. Since $e^{-\alpha'|z|}\le e^{-\alpha|z|}$ outside a fixed disk, every finite derivative has the stated rate.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [A4] The current framed Ward theorem proves the local integrable-Dolbeault frames, universal-line degree-zero base change/evaluation, unique incidence connection and compatibility of the pairing-induced positive metric. Its comparison input is absolute projective GAGA, not independently chosen parallel metrics or assumed base-change surjectivity. [[thm-qftx-framed-penrose-ward-correspondence-on-s4]]

proof_steps.claim: Starting with a framed ASD connection, [A4] constructs its holomorphic Ward bundle; the exact coupled cohomology-vanishing and diagonal argument [[lem-qftx-asd-twistor-vanishing-and-monad-reconstruction]] reconstructs the normalized three-term monad. Starting with regular ADHM data, [A5] identifies its normalized real monad and projection connection with this Ward bundle and connection. The equality of the two constructions is the first-order and inverse-extraction clause in [A5], so it is conditional on that exact real block proof, not on the P² citation alone.

By [A5], both composites on framed isomorphism classes are identities: ADHM data produce the Ward bundle whose monad extraction returns the same $U(k)$ orbit, and an ASD connection produces a Ward bundle whose matrix extraction returns an orbit reconstructing that framed connection. The charge of each resulting connection is $q_N=-k$ by [F2]–[F3]. Thus the claimed bijection and charge statement follow conditionally on [A4]–[A5].

The finite-dimensional quotient and $\mathbb P^2$ sheaf maps are $T$-equivariant by [A1]–[A2]. The Ward construction is natural under rotations and framing transformations by [A4]; the exact raw monad torus factors are directly calculated in the new block lemma cited by [A5], while the equivariance of inverse normalization remains part of [A5]. These exact interfaces make the composite $T$-equivariant. The same composition on first-order families is valid only under the base-change hypotheses of [A2]–[A4] and the deformation compatibility of [A5]. This proves the stated conditional torus and tangent clauses and leaves the positive-FI boundary separate.

fact_uses.text: [L2] A complex $L^1$ density defines a complex measure whose total variation is the integral of its modulus. ([[thm-complex-l-one-densities-define-complex-measures-with-prescribed-total-variation]])

proof_steps.claim: In the finite complex case, [L3] gives an integrable complex representative $h$ of $d\nu/d\mu$, and [L2] applied to that density yields the same formula $$|\nu|(E)=\int_E|h|\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F3] [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]: $N_1(0,C)$ has mean zero and covariance $C$, including $C=0$.

proof_steps.claim: For $Z_C\sim N_1(0,C)$, [F3] gives $\mathbb E Z_C=0$ and $\mathbb E Z_C^2=C$. Hence [F4] gives $T_Cf(x)=\mathbb E[(x+Z_C)^2]=x^2+C$. Therefore $T_3(T_1f)(0)=T_3(x^2+1)(0)=4=T_4f(0)$, in agreement with [F2]. The shell measures are normalized, so no determinant factor is introduced.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F1] [[def-qftx-finite-gaussian-shell-transform]]: for a positive-semidefinite covariance $C$, $T_Cf(x)=\int f(x+z)\,d\gamma_C(z)$, and $e^{-V_C(x)}=T_C(e^{-V})(x)$ for finite nonnegative Borel $V$.

proof_steps.claim: Put $f_V=e^{-V}$. Since $V$ is finite, nonnegative, and Borel, $f_V$ is a nonnegative Borel function. By [F1], $e^{-V_{C_1}(x)}=T_{C_1}f_V(x)$ and $e^{-V_{C_1+C_2}(x)}=T_{C_1+C_2}f_V(x)$.

Apply [F2] to $f_V$ to obtain $T_{C_2}(T_{C_1}f_V)(x)=T_{C_1+C_2}f_V(x)$, with the value $+\infty$ allowed for the first equality. Substituting the two identities from step 1.1 proves both displayed conclusions. Normalization is part of [F1], and no limit or differentiation is used.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F5] [[lem-qftx-finite-heavy-gaussian-square]]: for finite $d$, symmetric positive-definite $K$, and $j\in\mathbb R^d$, the normalized finite Gaussian source integral is $\exp(\tfrac12j^TK^{-1}j)$.

proof_steps.claim: By [F5], $Z_H(J)=\exp(\tfrac12J^TK^{-1}J)$; the normalized reference measure makes $Z_H(0)=1$, so no determinant factor remains in this ratio. By the definition of the Wilsonian action in [F2], taking $-\log$ gives $\Delta S_W(J)=-\tfrac12J^TK^{-1}J$.

fact_uses.text: [F5] Fubini interchanges absolutely integrable complex double integrals, and locally integrable functions with equal distribution pairings agree almost everywhere. ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]])

proof_steps.claim: Off-support representation: let $f\in L^2$ be compactly supported, let $\varphi\in C_c^\infty$ be supported off $\operatorname{supp}f$, and put $d:=\operatorname{dist}(\operatorname{supp}f,\operatorname{supp}\varphi)>0$. Using the adjoint identity of [F3], skew-adjointness from step 1.2 and the Schwartz principal-value formula [F2], and writing $K_j$ for the real-valued kernel, $$\langle R_jf,\varphi\rangle=\langle f,R_j^*\varphi\rangle=-\int f(y)\overline{R_j\varphi(y)}\,dy=-\iint K_j(y-x)f(y)\overline{\varphi(x)}\,dx\,dy=\iint K_j(x-y)f(y)\overline{\varphi(x)}\,dx\,dy,$$ where $\overline{R_j\varphi(y)}=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\int_{|y-x|>\varepsilon}K_j(y-x)\overline{\varphi(x)}\,dx$ is an absolutely convergent integral on the two supports (there $|x-y|\ge d>0$, so the limit may be taken inside the $y$-integration), Fubini applies over the bounded supports, and the last step uses the oddness $K_j(-z)=-K_j(z)$. Since this holds for every test function supported off $\operatorname{supp}f$, the $L^2$ class $R_jf$ agrees almost everywhere off $\operatorname{supp}f$ with the locally integrable function $x\mapsto\int K_j(x-y)f(y)\,dy$; this is the off-support representation (3) required of a Calderón–Zygmund operator.

fact_uses.text: [F10] For a function on a product of $\sigma$-finite measure spaces that is integrable with respect to the product measure, the iterated integrals exist and agree (Fubini). ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]])

proof_steps.claim: Distributional form for bounded compact data. Let $f\in L^\infty_c(\mathbb R^n)$ and $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$. The double integral $\iint\Phi(x-y)f(y)\partial_i\partial_j\varphi(x)\,dy\,dx$ is absolutely convergent: the integrand is supported in a bounded subset of $\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n$ and is dominated there by a constant times $|\Phi(x-y)|$, and $\Phi$ is locally integrable. Fubini [F10] and the substitution $z=x-y$ therefore give $\langle D_{ij}Nf,\varphi\rangle=\int f(y)\langle\Phi,D_{ij}\varphi(\cdot+y)\rangle\,dy=\int f(y)\langle D_{ij}\Phi,\varphi(\cdot+y)\rangle\,dy$, the last equality being the definition of the distributional derivative. Inserting the kernel identity proved in step 4.1, $\langle D_{ij}Nf,\varphi\rangle=\int f(y)\bigl[W_{ij}(\varphi(\cdot+y))-\frac{\delta_{ij}}{n}\varphi(y)\bigr]dy$. For $y$ in the compact support of $f$, subtract $\varphi(y)$ on $\varepsilon\le|z|<1$ using step 2.2. The resulting near integrand is bounded by $C_n\|\nabla\varphi\|_\infty|z|^{1-n}$; the far integral is bounded by $C_n\|\varphi\|_\infty\int_{1\le|z|\le R_0}|z|^{-n}dz$, where one $R_0>1$ contains all differences of the two supports. These bounds are uniform in $y$ and $\varepsilon$; multiplying by $|f(y)|$ gives an integrable majorant on its compact support. Dominated convergence now passes the truncation limit through the $y$ integral; another application of Fubini [F10] (the truncated double integral is absolutely convergent on the bounded region) gives $\int f(y)W_{ij}(\varphi(\cdot+y))\,dy=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\iint_{|x-y|\ge\varepsilon}k_{ij}(x-y)f(y)\varphi(x)\,dy\,dx$. Hence $\langle\partial_i\partial_jNf,\varphi\rangle=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\iint_{|x-y|\ge\varepsilon}k_{ij}(x-y)f(y)\varphi(x)\,dy\,dx-\frac{\delta_{ij}}{n}\int f\varphi$ for every test function, which is clause (iii).

fact_uses.text: [F6] Fubini interchanges absolutely integrable complex double integrals; under the assumed Countable Choice, locally integrable functions have equal regular distributions exactly when they agree almost everywhere. Distributional derivatives on Schwartz tests satisfy $\langle\partial^\beta u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\beta|}\langle u,\partial^\beta\varphi\rangle$. ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]], [[thm-differentiation-and-polynomial-multiplication-preserve-tempered-distributions]])

proof_steps.claim: For every $j$ the function $m_j=m\,\zeta(2^{-j}\cdot)$ is supported in the annulus $2^{j-1}\le|\xi|\le2^{j+1}$, where it agrees almost everywhere with $m_0(\xi)\zeta(2^{-j}\xi)$; we use this representative in the derivative estimates. Since $m_0$ is $C^{n_0}$ on that annulus and $\zeta$ is compactly supported and smooth, $m_j$ is represented by a compactly supported $C^{n_0}$ function, so $m_j\in L^1\cap L^2$ and $u_{m_j}$ is a well-defined regular tempered distribution. By [F3] the object $K_j=\mathcal F^{-1}(u_{m_j})$ is the regular distribution of the $L^2$ function $\mathcal F_2^{-1}m_j$; we use $K_j$ to denote that $L^2$ class, so that $\mathcal FK_j=u_{m_j}$ and $\|K_j\|_2\le\|m_j\|_2$. It has the smooth integral representative $G_j(x)=\int m_j(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi$: for every Schwartz test $\varphi$, Fubini applies with absolute bound $\|m_j\|_1\|\varphi\|_1$, giving $\int G_j\varphi=\int m_j\mathcal F^{-1}\varphi=\langle\mathcal F^{-1}u_{m_j},\varphi\rangle$. Thus [F6] identifies $G_j$ with the $L^2$ class. Every $\xi^\beta m_j$ is integrable on the fixed compact frequency support. Put $G_{j,\beta}(x)=\int(2\pi i\xi)^\beta m_j(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi$. The bounds $|e^{it}-1|\le|t|$ and $|e^{it}-1-it|\le t^2/2$ give continuity of $G_{j,\beta}$ and a coordinate difference-quotient remainder bounded uniformly in $x$ by $C_{j,\beta}|h|\|m_j\|_1$ as $h\to0$. Hence $\partial_rG_{j,\beta}=G_{j,\beta+e_r}$, proving $G_j\in C^\infty$. These derivatives are bounded; repeated integration by parts against rapidly decaying Schwartz tests therefore has no boundary term and identifies each classical derivative with its regular distributional derivative as defined in [F6]. We henceforth use this smooth representative for $K_j$ and its gradients.

Claim: for every multi-index $\gamma$ with $|\gamma|\le n_0$, the product $x^\gamma K_j$ is (the regular distribution of) an $L^2$ function and $$\bigl\|x^\gamma K_j\bigr\|_2=(2\pi)^{-|\gamma|}\bigl\|\partial^\gamma m_j\bigr\|_2.$$ Indeed, applying the first identity of [F4] to $u=K_j$ and using $\mathcal FK_j=u_{m_j}$ gives $\mathcal F(x^\gamma K_j)=(-1/(2\pi i))^{|\gamma|}\partial^\gamma u_{m_j}=c_\gamma u_{\partial^\gamma m_j}$ for the scalar $c_\gamma=(-1/(2\pi i))^{|\gamma|}$, the last equality because $\partial^\gamma m_j$ is continuous and compactly supported, hence a regular distribution, and differentiation of a regular distribution of a $C^{|\gamma|}$ function is the regular distribution of its classical derivative. Since $\partial^\gamma m_j\in C_c\subset L^2$, [F3] applied to $h=c_\gamma\partial^\gamma m_j$ identifies $x^\gamma K_j$ with the regular distribution of $\mathcal F_2^{-1}(c_\gamma\partial^\gamma m_j)$, and Plancherel gives $\|x^\gamma K_j\|_2=\|c_\gamma\partial^\gamma m_j\|_2=(2\pi)^{-|\gamma|}\|\partial^\gamma m_j\|_2$.

fact_uses.text: [F3] Absolutely integrable kernels permit Fubini and dominated convergence. [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[thm-dominated-convergence]]

proof_steps.claim: Let $\kappa_i$ be finitely many charts with smooth unitary frames, and let $\phi_i$ be a partition subordinate to compact subsets of those charts. Choose smooth cutoffs $\chi_i(y,z)$ supported where both points lie in chart $i$, equal to one near $y=z$ whenever $z\in\operatorname{supp}\phi_i$. Write volume as $w_i(z)\,d\kappa_i(z)$. Define $Z_t(y,z)$ in these frames by the finite sum of $\phi_i(z)\chi_i(y,z)w_i(z)^{-1}t^{-n/2}k_{i,z}((\kappa_i(y)-\kappa_i(z))/\sqrt t)$, interpreting each summand as a bundle map. In each summand the principal coefficients are frozen at the source $z$. Step 1.1, local equivalence of chart distance and $d$, and cutoff support give $\|Z_t(y,z)\|\le C_LH_{t,L}(y,z)$, where $H_{t,L}=t^{-n/2}(1+d(y,z)/\sqrt t)^{-L}$. Moreover $Z_tf\to f$ in $L^2$ for smooth $f$: put $\kappa_i(y)-\kappa_i(z)=\sqrt t\,v$, use the uniform integrable Schwartz bound, and use $\sum_i\phi_i=1$ and $\int k_{i,y}=I$. For $R_t=(\partial_t+P_y)Z_t$, the frozen principal part cancels $\partial_t$. The remaining principal term contains $A(y)-A(z)=O(d(y,z))$ and two derivatives of the frozen kernel; lower terms contain at most one derivative. The bound $d(y,z)t^{-1}H_{t,L+1}\le t^{-1/2}H_{t,L}$ therefore gives $\|R_t(y,z)\|\le C_Lt^{-1/2}H_{t,L}(y,z)$. Derivatives of cutoffs are supported away from the diagonal and obey the same bound by choosing additional Schwartz decay.

Define Volterra convolution by $(A*B)_t(y,z)=\int_0^t\int_M A_{t-s}(y,u)B_s(u,z)\,du\,ds$. The residual bound and step 3.1 show $\|R*R\|\le C H_{t,L}$, since $\int_0^t((t-s)s)^{-1/2}\,ds=\pi$ (substitute $s=t\sin^2\theta$). Iterating this bounded time kernel gives $\|R^{*(2m)}_t\|\le C^{2m}t^{m-1}H_{t,L}/(m-1)!$ after enlarging $C$. Convolving once more with $R$ gives $\|R^{*(2m+1)}_t\|\le 2C^{2m+1}t^{m-1/2}H_{t,L}/(m-1)!$ for $m\ge1$, by bounding $s^{m-1}\le t^{m-1}$ in the time integral; $R$ itself has its original bound. Consequently $Q=\sum_{m\ge1}(-1)^mR^{*m}$ converges absolutely on every positive-time compact set, has $\|Q_t\|\le C t^{-1/2}H_{t,L}$ for $t\le1$, and satisfies $Q+R+R*Q=0$. Fubini and associativity hold because every displayed absolute convolution bound is finite. Hence $S=Z+Z*Q$ satisfies $\|S_t-Z_t\|\le C\sqrt t H_{t,L}$ and $S_tf\to f$ in $L^2$ for smooth $f$.

Extend kernels causally by zero for negative time. The initial limit of $Z$ gives $(\partial_t+P_y)Z=\delta_0I+R$ in distributions. Applying this identity to the absolutely convergent convolutions of step 4.1 yields $(\partial_t+P_y)S=\delta_0I+R+Q+R*Q=\delta_0I$. These distribution identities can equivalently be verified first on $\varepsilon<s<t-\varepsilon$, tested against a compactly supported smooth function of time and space, and then passed to the endpoints using the integrable bounds from step 4.1. Thus no differentiation of a singular convolution is assumed pointwise. For smooth initial $f$, let $\psi$ be a smooth eigensection of $P$ with eigenvalue $\lambda$. Formal symmetry and the distribution equation give $a'(t)+\lambda a(t)=0$ for $a(t)=\langle S_tf,\psi\rangle$, with $a(0)=\langle f,\psi\rangle$. Therefore $a(t)=e^{-t\lambda}\langle f,\psi\rangle$. The two-sided integral bounds in step 3.1 make $S_t$ bounded on $L^2$ (apply Cauchy–Schwarz with weight $\|S_t(y,z)\|$). Completeness of the given eigenbasis proves $S_t=e^{-tP}$ on $L^2$. The series and convolutions define continuous kernels for $t>0$: on time intervals away from the endpoints use uniform convergence, and bound the omitted endpoint intervals by the integrable convolution estimates. Equality as distributions with the smooth given $K_t$ therefore gives $S_t(y,z)=K_t(y,z)$ everywhere. In particular the bound for $S$ is the stated bound for $K$.

Fix $x$ and put $y=\exp_x(\sqrt t\,a)$, $z=\exp_x(\sqrt t\,b)$. In a chart, Taylor expansion gives $(\kappa_i(y)-\kappa_i(z))/\sqrt t\to d\kappa_i|_x(a-b)$, the frozen symbol tends to $p_i(x,\xi)$, and all frame maps, partition weights and density factors tend to their values at $x$. Linear change of cotangent variables in the absolutely convergent Fourier integral transforms each limiting chart expression into $\phi_i(x)k_x(a-b)$: the coordinate Jacobian cancels $w_i(x)$ because normal-coordinate volume density at $x$ is one. Summing gives $k_x(a-b)$. All convergences are uniform on bounded $a,b$ by step 1.1. By step 4.1, $t^{n/2}\|K_t-Z_t\|\le C\sqrt t$, so it has zero limit. This proves the rescaled limit and all assertions for $n>0$. If $M$ is empty the claims are vacuous; for $n=0$, compact $M$ is finite and differential operators act separately on its fibers, so ordinary matrix exponentiation gives exactly the asserted finite-dimensional limit.

fact_uses.text: [F6] Absolutely integrable product integrals may be exchanged ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

proof_steps.claim: For $c>0$ and integer $m\ge0$, F3 bounds $|x|^m e^{-cx^2/2}$ on the tails, and it is bounded on a compact middle interval by continuity. Thus $|x|^me^{-cx^2}\le C e^{-cx^2/2}$. F1, F2 on both half-lines (reflect the negative half), and F7 give integrability of these majorants and $\int e^{-\pi x^2}\,dx=1$. In several dimensions bound a polynomial by a finite sum of monomials and factor the Gaussian; successive nonnegative integration gives the product of the finite one-dimensional bounds.

The product rule gives $(e^{\pi\xi^2}G(\xi))'=0$. Applying the finite-interval complex FTC to its real and imaginary parts shows this product is constant, equal to $G(0)=1$. Thus $G(\xi)=e^{-\pi\xi^2}$. F6 tensors this formula in $n$ coordinates; absolute integrability is supplied by step 1.1. Finally substitute $y=\sqrt t\,x$ using F7; the Jacobian is $t^{n/2}$ and the frequency becomes $\xi/\sqrt t$. This gives exactly the claimed formula. Countable choice is inherited from F2 and F7, and the argument uses neither later Schwartz theory nor a Fourier inversion theorem.

fact_uses.text: [F4] Tonelli and complex Fubini apply on sigma-finite positive product spaces ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

proof_steps.claim: Consequently $h_t(x)=\int k_t(x-y)u(y)\,dv(y)$, absolutely at every x because k_t is bounded and u integrable. The joint function is Borel measurable. By F4, F5 and translation invariance, its double absolute integral is $\int|u(y)|[\int k_t(x-y)\,dx]dv(y)=v(\mathbb R^n)$. Fubini therefore supplies a measurable integrable h_t and its stated norm bound. With the additional modulus-one Fourier factor the same double bound applies. F4 and F7 give $\widehat h_t(\xi)=\widehat k_t(\xi)\int e^{-2\pi iy\cdot\xi}u(y)\,dv(y)=\widehat k_t(\xi)\widehat\mu(\xi)$ by step 1.1.

For a compactly supported continuous $\varphi$, the double absolute integral after multiplication by $\varphi(x)$ is at most $\|\varphi\|_\infty v(\mathbb R^n)$. F4 exchanges the integrals. Since k_t is even, the inner test integral is $(k_t*\varphi)(y)$, and F6 gives uniform convergence to $\varphi(y)$. Thus the difference from $\int\varphi u\,dv$ has modulus at most $\|k_t*\varphi-\varphi\|_\infty\|u\|_{L^1(v)}\to0$. Step 1.1 identifies the limit with $\int\varphi\,d\mu$.

fact_uses.text: [F1] Absolutely integrable functions on sigma-finite products have equal iterated and product integrals. ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

proof_steps.claim: All integrands are bounded on the compact localized support. Extend by zero across the cylinder sides, where F already vanishes, and multiply interior derivatives by the subgraph indicator. These are integrable functions on bounded boxes. F1–F3 and the zero lower trace give $\int_Q\int_a^{h(y)}\partial_zF_n(y,z)\,dz\,dy=\int_QF_n(y,h(y))\,dy$. The endpoint derivative is not needed: F2 uses only the interior derivative and its continuous trace.

A_i^epsilon vanishes near the sides of the base box. F1–F3 along its ith coordinate show $\int_Q\partial_iA_i^\varepsilon=0$. In step 1.2 the integral over the omitted strip is bounded by epsilon times the derivative bound, and the endpoint values converge uniformly by continuity of F on the compact closure; Dh is bounded on the base. Letting epsilon decrease to zero gives $\int_Q\int_a^{h(y)}\partial_iF_i\,dz\,dy=-\int_QF_i(y,h(y))\partial_i h\,dy$. Add this for i<n to step 1.1 to obtain the asserted identity.

For an interior compactly supported field extend it by zero to a containing box. This extension is C1, since its support has positive distance from the domain complement. Fubini and FTC integrate each coordinate derivative to the difference of its two zero endpoint values. Summing these zero integrals gives zero total divergence.

fact_uses.text: [F7] Fubini applies to integrable functions on sigma-finite product measure spaces, and Lebesgue measure is sigma-finite and finite on bounded sets ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]]).

proof_steps.claim: By Fubini and integration by parts in the compactly supported $q$ variable, for every multi-index $\beta$ with $|\beta|\le k$ the distributional identity $D^\beta Nq=N(D^\beta q)$ holds. The right side is $C^{2,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ by [F4]. Starting with $Nq\in C^2$, induction on $|\beta|$ identifies each already-classical derivative $D^\beta Nq$ with this continuous representative: distributional injectivity gives equality almost everywhere, and [F8] rules out a nonzero continuous difference on any ball. Each such derivative is then $C^2$. The local estimate in [F4], applied to each $D^\beta q$ with support in $\overline D_2$, yields $Nq\in C^{k+2,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ with its norm on $\overline D_R$ bounded by $C_{k,\alpha,R}\|q\|_{C^{k,\alpha}}$. Since $Tq=-4\partial_zNq$, this gives the asserted $C^{k+1,\alpha}(D_R)$ bound.

For every compactly supported smooth test function $\varphi$, Fubini and the distributional derivative identity in step 1.1 give $\langle\partial_zNq,\varphi\rangle=\langle a*q,\varphi\rangle$, with $$(a*q)(z)=\int_{\mathbb C}a(z-\zeta)q(\zeta)\,dA(\zeta).$$ This integral is absolutely finite for each $z$, since $q$ is bounded, supported in $\overline D_2$, and $a$ is locally integrable. It is continuous: on a compact set of $z$-values let $\delta=|z-z'|<1$; the two disks of radius $2\delta$ around $z,z'$ contribute at most $C\|q\|_\infty\delta$, while on their complement $|\nabla a(w)|\le C|w|^{-2}$ and the mean value theorem bounds the difference by $C\|q\|_\infty\delta\log(C_0/\delta)$ for a fixed $C_0$. Since $Nq\in C^2$, both sides are continuous; [F6] makes them equal almost everywhere, and [F8] then makes them equal everywhere. Therefore $Tq=-4\partial_zNq=(1/\pi)\int q(\zeta)/(z-\zeta)\,dA(\zeta)$.

fact_uses.text: [F5] Fubini for L^1 functions on a sigma-finite product. [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]

proof_steps.claim: $A_n=2\pi^{(n-1)/2}/\Gamma((n+1)/2)$: compute $C:=\int_{B_n}|x_1|\,dx$ twice. Polar coordinates [F3] give $C=\int_0^1r^ndr\cdot A_n=A_n/(n+1)$; for $n\ge2$, slicing at $x_1=t$ gives, by [F5], [F14] and [F4], $C=\int_{-1}^1|t|V_{n-1}(1)(1-t^2)^{(n-1)/2}dt=2V_{n-1}(1)/(n+1)=2\pi^{(n-1)/2}/((n+1)\Gamma((n+1)/2))$, hence $A_n=(n+1)C=2V_{n-1}(1)=2\pi^{(n-1)/2}/\Gamma((n+1)/2)$. For $n=1$ the sphere is $S^0=\{-1,1\}$: the defining identity of [F3], applied to functions supported in the annulus $1<|x|<2$, shows that the measure $\sigma$ is the counting measure $\delta_{-1}+\delta_1$, so $A_1=\int_{S^0}|\omega_1|\,d\sigma=1+1=2$, while $2\pi^{0}/\Gamma(1)=2$ by $\Gamma(1)=1$ of [F15]. Hence $A_n=2\pi^{(n-1)/2}/\Gamma((n+1)/2)$ for every $n\ge1$, and $c_nA_n\pi/2=1$ by cancellation of $\Gamma((n+1)/2)$ and $\pi^{(n+1)/2}$.

Define the tempered distribution $W_j$ by the symmetric principal-value pairing $\langle W_j,\varphi\rangle:=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\int_{\varepsilon<|y|<1/\varepsilon}K_j(y)\varphi(y)\,dy$ for $\varphi\in\mathcal S$; the two-piece bound of 1.1 shows the limit exists, is finite, and is Schwartz-continuous. By [F10], $\langle\mathcal FW_j,\varphi\rangle=\langle W_j,\widehat\varphi\rangle=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\int_{\varepsilon<|y|<1/\varepsilon}K_j(y)\widehat\varphi(y)\,dy$; the double integrand is absolutely integrable since $\int_{\varepsilon<|y|<1/\varepsilon}|K_j(y)|\,dy\int_{\mathbb R^n}|\varphi(\xi)|\,d\xi<\infty$, so [F5] applies, giving $\int_{\varepsilon<|y|<1/\varepsilon}K_j(y)\widehat\varphi(y)\,dy=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\varphi(\xi)\Lambda_{\varepsilon,1/\varepsilon}(\xi)\,d\xi$. By 2.1 the bracket converges to $-i\xi_j/|\xi|$ pointwise off the null set $\{\xi=0\}$, and by the uniform bound of 2.1 it is dominated by a constant times $|\varphi(\xi)|$; [F6] therefore yields $\langle\mathcal FW_j,\varphi\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\varphi(\xi)(-i\xi_j/|\xi|)\,d\xi$, i.e. $\mathcal FW_j=m_j$ as tempered distributions.

fact_uses.text: [F4] Fubini's theorem for L^1 functions on a sigma-finite product. [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]

proof_steps.claim: Fix $\varepsilon>0$ and put $\Phi(s,t):=e^{-\varepsilon t}\cos(st)$ on $[0,1]\times[0,\infty)$. By [F14] the integrand $\Phi$ is product measurable, and [F5] with 1.2 gives $\int_{[0,1]\times[0,\infty)}|\Phi|\,d(\lambda\otimes\lambda)\le\int_{[0,1]}\bigl(\int_{[0,\infty)}e^{-\varepsilon t}\,d\lambda(t)\bigr)ds=1/\varepsilon<\infty$, so $\Phi\in L^1$ of the product and [F4] may be applied. By 1.3, 3.1 and 4.1, the outer $s$-integration of [F4] turns the $t$-inner integral into $\varepsilon/(\varepsilon^2+s^2)$, while the outer $t$-integration turns the $s$-inner integral into $e^{-\varepsilon t}\sin(t)/t$; hence $J_\varepsilon:=\int_{[0,\infty)}e^{-\varepsilon t}f(t)\,d\lambda(t)$ satisfies $J_\varepsilon=\int_0^1\varepsilon/(\varepsilon^2+s^2)\,ds$, and [F15] with the substitution $s=\varepsilon v$ followed by [F16] gives $J_\varepsilon=\int_0^{1/\varepsilon}dv/(1+v^2)=\arctan(1/\varepsilon)$.

fact_uses.text: [F4] [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: integrable complex functions on a sigma-finite product may be integrated in either order.

proof_steps.claim:
On $(\mathbb R^d,\gamma_{C_1})\times(\mathbb R^d,\gamma_{C_2})$, the sum map $(y,z)\mapsto y+z$ has characteristic function
$$\int e^{iu\cdot(y+z)}\,d(\gamma_{C_1}\times\gamma_{C_2}) =\exp(-u^TC_1u/2)\exp(-u^TC_2u/2) =\exp[-u^T(C_1+C_2)u/2].$$
The product measure exists by [F3], the integrand is bounded and therefore integrable, and [F4] justifies the iterated integral/product factorization. Since $C_1+C_2$ is positive semidefinite, [F2] and [F5] identify the pushforward under addition as $\gamma_{C_1+C_2}$. This includes singular and zero covariances.

fact_uses.text: [F9] Integrable product-space densities can be sliced and integrated in either order. [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]

proof_steps.claim: For either charged field $f=q,p$, expand $|(D_1+iD_2)f|^2=|Df|^2-B|f|^2+i\{\partial_1(\bar fD_2f)-\partial_2(\bar fD_1f)\}$. Expanding $[B-g^2(\xi-s)]^2/(2g^2)$ gives $B^2/(2g^2)+g^2(\xi-s)^2/2+Bs-\xi B$. Step 1.1 shows all the required nonnegative densities are integrable. If $G(R)=\int_{|x|=R}(|Dq|^2+|Dp|^2)ds$, then [F9] and finite energy give $\int G(R)dR<\infty$. Hence there are increasing radii $R_j\to\infty$ with $R_jG(R_j)\to0$, since an eventual positive lower bound on $RG(R)$ would force logarithmic divergence. Uniform vacuum amplitudes and [F8] bound the boundary-current integral by $C\sqrt{R_jG(R_j)}\to0$. Integrating the two algebraic identities on those disks, using [F11], limiting flux $2\pi n$ and [F10] gives the stated whole-plane identity. For negative n, conjugation reverses flux and changes $D_1+iD_2$ to $D_1-iD_2$ without changing energy.

First, if both end profiles have a=p=0, apply [F5] at $e=g$ and embed its whole single-field collar by $M=q/\sqrt2$, $\widetilde M=e^{i\beta}\bar q/\sqrt2$. Step 1.1 makes the embedded three-dimensional energy exactly its mathematical critical energy. For arbitrary fixed full-model ends in the class [F7], specialize [F6] to linear u and constant $b=g^{-2}$; the nonzero c and closed valid disk meet its hypotheses. It constructs actual finite collars from both ends to the selected profile of step 3.1, with the same flux, neutral disk and canonical vacuum frame, constant near each join. By [F9], the full energy is the slice energy plus nonnegative longitudinal terms, so step 2.1 bounds every competitor below by $T_nL$. Concatenating the two actual collars and the constant middle segment of length $L-2\ell$ gives energy $C_0+T_n(L-2\ell)+C_1$. The collars are constant near their inner faces, so the join is smooth also when the middle length is zero. Taking the infimum gives the claimed uniform $O(1)$ bound. Matching minimizing traces give the exact constant extension minimum. These magnetostatic constant-theta trial fields satisfy the Gauss scope of [F7]; no microscopic boundary dictionary follows.

fact_uses.text: [F4] An integrable function on a sigma-finite product space has almost-everywhere integrable sections and its integral is the iterated integral. This applies to the finite static energy on $\mathbb R^2\times[0,L]$. [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]

proof_steps.claim: The three-dimensional energy is the transverse planar energy on each slice plus nonnegative longitudinal Maxwell and scalar terms. By [F4] and the definition of $\tau_n$, every competitor has $E_{b,3}\ge\tau_nL$. For each fixed $\varepsilon>0$, the definition of the finite infimum provides one planar profile with energy below $\tau_n+\varepsilon$; gauge-clean it by step 5.1. Step 7.1 constructs collars from each fixed end trace to this profile, with one chosen width ell and finite total energy $C_\varepsilon$, independent of L. Concatenate the collars with its translation-invariant extension over length L-2ell. This is a smooth admissible competitor because each collar is constant near the inner face, and it has energy at most $(\tau_n+\varepsilon)(L-2\ell)+C_\varepsilon$. Taking the infimum proves the two-sided bounds. Dividing by L, taking limsup as L tends to infinity and then allowing each $\varepsilon>0$ to tend to zero gives limsup<=tau_n, while the lower bound gives liminf>=tau_n. Hence the limit is tau_n>0. No minimizer or uniform bound on $C_\varepsilon$ as epsilon tends to zero is used, so no generic $O(1)$ remainder follows.

fact_uses.text: [F3] Chebyshev: $|\{|u|>t\}|\le t^{-2}\int|u|^2$ for measurable $u$; layer cake: $\|g\|_q^q=q\int_0^\infty t^{q-1}|\{|g|>t\}|dt$; Fubini applies to absolutely integrable complex kernels ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]); Tonelli applies to nonnegative product-measurable integrands on $\sigma$-finite products ([[thm-chebyshev-markov-inequality-for-the-integral]], [[thm-layer-cake-formula-for-l-p-powers]], [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]); the $L^p$ and $L^{p'}$ norms are the quotient norms of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], Hölder's inequality is [[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]], and $C_c^\infty$ is dense in $L^p$ for finite $p$ ([[thm-complex-finite-simple-and-smooth-compact-support-density-for-finite-p]]).

proof_steps.claim: Sharp two-level interpolation. Let $S$ be any linear operator defined on $L^1+L^2$, weak $(1,1)$ with constant $A$ and $L^2$-bounded with constant $B$, and let $1<q<2$. For $f\in L^q$ and any $\delta>0$ put $f_0:=f\mathbf 1_{\{|f|>\delta t\}}$ and $f_1:=f\mathbf 1_{\{|f|\le\delta t\}}$ at height $t>0$; then $f_0\in L^1$ and $f_1\in L^2$, since $\|f_0\|_1\le(\delta t)^{1-q}\|f\|_q^q$ and $\|f_1\|_2^2\le(\delta t)^{2-q}\|f\|_q^q$. Hence $\{|Sf|>t\}\subseteq\{|Sf_0|>t/2\}\cup\{|Sf_1|>t/2\}$ and the weak $(1,1)$ bound for $Sf_0$ together with Chebyshev and the $L^2$ bound for $Sf_1$ give $|\{|Sf|>t\}|\le\frac{2A}{t}\int_{\{|f|>\delta t\}}|f|+\frac{4B^2}{t^2}\int_{\{|f|\le\delta t\}}|f|^2$. Integrating $t^{q-1}|\{|Sf|>t\}|$ over $(0,\infty)$ and exchanging the integrals by Tonelli gives $\|Sf\|_q^q\le q\bigl[\frac{2A\delta^{1-q}}{q-1}+\frac{4B^2\delta^{2-q}}{2-q}\bigr]\|f\|_q^q$, because $\int_0^{|f|/\delta}t^{q-2}dt=\frac{(|f|/\delta)^{q-1}}{q-1}$ and $\int_{|f|/\delta}^\infty t^{q-3}dt=\frac{(|f|/\delta)^{q-2}}{2-q}$; choosing $\delta:=A/(2B^2)$ when $A,B>0$ balances the two terms at a constant multiple of $A^{2-q}B^{2q-2}$, so that $$\bigl\|Sf\bigr\|_q\le C_q\,A^{\frac2q-1}B^{2-\frac2q}\|f\|_q\le C_q(A+B)\|f\|_q,$$ the last inequality because the exponents $\frac2q-1$ and $2-\frac2q$ are nonnegative and sum to one, so the weighted geometric mean is at most the sum; if $A=0$, let $\delta\downarrow0$, and if $B=0$, let $\delta\to\infty$ in the preceding inequality, obtaining $Sf=0$ in either case.

The case $2<p<\infty$: apply step 1.2 with $q=p'$ to the adjoint $T^*$, which by step 1.1 has weak $(1,1)$ constant $A$ and $L^2$ norm $B$: for every $g\in L^{p'}$, $\|T^*g\|_{p'}\le C_{p'}(A_2+B)\|g\|_{p'}$. Then for $f\in L^p\cap L^2$ and $g\in L^{p'}\cap L^2$ with $\|g\|_{p'}\le1$, the adjoint identity and Hölder's inequality give $|\int(Tf)g|=|\langle f,T^*\overline g\rangle|\le\|f\|_p\|T^*\overline g\|_{p'}\le C_{p'}(A_2+B)\|f\|_p$, To establish $Tf\in L^p$ before using norm recovery, put $u=Tf\in L^2$, $E_N=B(0,N)\cap\{|u|\le N\}$ and $a_N=(\int_{E_N}|u|^p)^{1/p}$. If $a_N>0$, take $g_N=\mathbf1_{E_N}|u|^{p-1}\theta_u/a_N^{p-1}$, with $\theta_u=\overline u/|u|$ on $u\ne0$ and zero otherwise. This test is bounded on a finite-measure set, hence lies in $L^{p'}\cap L^2$, and satisfies $\|g_N\|_{p'}=1$, $\int ug_N=a_N$. The preceding pairing bound gives $a_N\le C_{p'}(A_2+B)\|f\|_p$; if $a_N=0$ the same inequality is immediate. Since $E_N$ increases to a full-measure set, monotone convergence gives $\|Tf\|_p\le C_{p'}(A_2+B)\|f\|_p$; since $C_c^\infty\subseteq L^p\cap L^2$ is dense in $L^p$, this bound extends uniquely to all of $L^p$, and $C_{p'}(A_2+B)\le C_{n,p}(A_2+B)\max(p,(p-1)^{-1})$.

The exponent dependence can be made dimension-only. Put $D=A_2+B$. If $D=0$, then $B=0$ and $T=0$. Otherwise normalize $S=T/D$. Step 1.1 and the weak endpoint give weak $(1,1)$ constants at most $a_n=C_n$ for both $S$ and $S^*$, and their $L^2$ norms are at most one. The interpolation-and-duality lemma [F4] at $q=3/2$ and its conjugate $3$ gives $\|S\|_{3\to3},\|S^*\|_{3\to3}\le d_n$ with $d_n$ depending only on $n$. For $1<p\le2$, split $f=f\mathbf1_{\{|f|>t\}}+f\mathbf1_{\{|f|\le t\}}$. Weak $(1,1)$ on the first part and Chebyshev with the strong $(3,3)$ bound on the second yield $|\{|Sf|>t\}|\le2a_nt^{-1}\int_{|f|>t}|f|+8d_n^3t^{-3}\int_{|f|\le t}|f|^3$. Layer cake and Tonelli, as in step 1.2, give $\|Sf\|_p^p\le p[2a_n/(p-1)+8d_n^3/(3-p)]\|f\|_p^p\le K_n(p-1)^{-1}\|f\|_p^p$, with $K_n\ge1$ independent of $p$. The compatible $L^1$ and $L^3$ actions agree on their intersection by approximation with bounded compact-support functions in both norms. Thus $\|S\|_{p\to p}\le K_n/(p-1)$ for $1<p\le2$. Apply this estimate to $S^*$ at $p'=p/(p-1)$ and use the finite-support tests and density argument of step 2.2 to get $\|S\|_{p\to p}\le K_n(p-1)\le K_np$ for $p>2$. Consequently $\|T\|_{p\to p}\le K_nD\max(p,(p-1)^{-1})$ throughout the strict range.

Steps 2.1 and 2.2 prove boundedness and uniqueness in the two open ranges; the given $L^2$ bound handles $p=2$. Step 3.1 also proves the stronger bound with a dimensional constant independent of $p$, and hence the stated estimate.

fact_uses.text: [F6] Fubini for nonnegative integrands and translation invariance of Lebesgue measure: for measurable $G\ge0$ one has $\int_{\Omega'}\int_0^1G(x,t)\,dt\,dx=\int_0^1\int_{\Omega'}G(x,t)\,dx\,dt$, and for $|s|<\operatorname{dist}(\Omega',\partial\Omega)$ one has $\Omega'+se_i\subseteq\Omega$ and $\int_{\Omega'}F(x+se_i)\,dx=\int_{\Omega'+se_i}F(y)\,dy$. ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]], [[cor-c-one-change-of-variables-for-l-one-functions]])

proof_steps.claim: Integrating the estimate of step 1.1 over $\Omega'$ and applying Fubini and the translation invariance of [F6] (every point $x+te_i$ with $x\in\Omega'$, $t$ between $0$ and $h$, satisfies $\operatorname{dist}(x+te_i,\partial\Omega)>0$ because $|h|<\operatorname{dist}(\Omega',\partial\Omega)$) gives, for either sign of $h$, $$\int_{\Omega'}|\delta_h^iv|^p\,dx\le\frac1h\int_0^h\int_{\Omega'}|\partial_iv(x+te_i)|^p\,dx\,dt\le\int_\Omega|\partial_iv|^p\,dx,$$ so $\|\delta_h^iv\|_{L^p(\Omega')}\le\|D_iv\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$.

The coordinate argument in steps 1.1--3.1 works on any open $U$ with the segment condition: each translated set $U+the_i$ lies in $\Omega$, so Tonelli and change of variables bound its integral by the gradient norm on $\Omega$. For $p=\infty$, fix a compact $K\subset U$. The union of its segments is compact in $\Omega$, so choose a bounded open tube $T\Subset\Omega$ containing that union. For each finite $q\ge1$, the same coordinate argument applied to $u|_T$ gives $\|\delta_h^iu\|_{L^q(K)}\le\|D_iu\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}|T|^{1/q}$. If the quotient exceeded this essential bound by $\varepsilon$ on a positive-measure subset of $K$, its $L^q$ norm would exceed $(\|D_iu\|_\infty+\varepsilon)|E|^{1/q}$, a contradiction as $q\to\infty$. Exhausting $U$ by compact sets proves the $L^\infty$ coordinate bound.

Tangential strong convergence. For a tangential direction on $H$, smooth approximation [F3] and the fixed-$h$ translation bounds pass the segment formula to $u$: $\delta_h^iu(x)=\int_0^1D_iu(x+the_i)\,dt$ as $L^p(H)$ classes. Indeed Jensen and tangential change of variables bound the $L^p$ error between the averages of two gradient approximations by their $L^p(H)$ distance. Extend $D_iu$ by zero as an $L^p$ class on $\mathbb R^n$; tangential shifts preserve $H$, so [F9] gives $\|D_iu(\cdot+te_i)-D_iu\|_{L^p(H)}\to0$ uniformly for $|t|\le|h|$ as $h\to0$. Jensen and Tonelli applied to the segment formula therefore give $\|\delta_h^iu-D_iu\|_{L^p(H)}^p\le\int_0^1\|D_iu(\cdot+the_i)-D_iu\|_{L^p(H)}^pdt\to0$.

fact_uses.text: [F6] An integrable indicator on a bounded cylinder can be integrated along its vertical sections. ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

proof_steps.claim: In a specified finite gluing, apply this formula to every piece. Shared faces have the same surface measure and opposite normals by F1, so their two integrands sum pointwise to zero off the null edge sets. Each regular face has n-dimensional volume zero: in graph coordinates Fubini gives zero from its singleton vertical sections, and a rigid coordinate change preserves volume. Thus adding the piece volumes counts the final domain integral exactly, and only exposed face fluxes remain. This proves the cancellation statement.

fact_uses.text: [L5] Fubini evaluates absolutely integrable product-measurable integrands on a sigma-finite product space. ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]])

proof_steps.claim: Let $\mu_i$ be the law of $Y_i=g_i(X_i)$ and $\mu=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mu_i$ as in step 2.2. Step 3.1 shows that the product map $m$ is $\mu$-integrable. By [L2], [L3], and repeated use of [L5], $\mathbb E[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)]=\int_{\mathbb R^n}m\,d\mu=\prod_{i<n}\int_{\mathbb R}y\,d\mu_i=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$.

fact_uses.text: [F4] Complex Fubini holds for absolutely integrable product integrands ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

proof_steps.claim: By F1 and Gaussian integrability, the defining integral for $S_tf(x)$ is absolutely convergent. Inserting the definition of $\widehat f$, the product integrand has modulus $|f(y)|e^{-\pi t|\xi|^2}$, whose double integral is $\|f\|_1t^{-n/2}<\infty$. Use a Borel representative of f as supplied in F5's convolution construction; the resulting integrand is product measurable. F4 therefore gives $S_tf(x)=\int f(y)[\int e^{-\pi t|\xi|^2}e^{2\pi i(x-y)\cdot\xi}\,d\xi]\,dy=\int f(y)k_t(x-y)\,dy$ by F2. This last integral exists at every x since k_t is bounded; substitution $y\mapsto x-y$ gives the stated convolution convention.

fact_uses.text: [F3] Absolute Fubini applies on the sigma-finite Euclidean product ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

proof_steps.claim:
Let $f\in L^1$ and $\varphi\in\mathcal S$.  Schwartz decay makes $\varphi\in L^1$, so $\int\!\int|f(x)\varphi(\xi)|\,dx\,d\xi<\infty$.  Absolute Fubini is therefore applicable. [F2, F3]

$$\langle\mathcal Fu_f,\varphi\rangle =\int f(x)\!\left(\int\varphi(\xi)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi\right)dx =\int\widehat f(\xi)\varphi(\xi)\,d\xi.$$

Since $\widehat f$ is bounded, [F1] makes the last functional tempered.  This proves the $L^1$ assertion.

fact_uses.text: [F4] Fubini equates complex iterated integrals when the product integral of the modulus is finite ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

proof_steps.claim: Fubini now permits exchanging the integrals in the transform of the convolution representative. The inner $x$ integral is the translation transform from F5, giving $\widehat{f*g}(\xi)=\int g(y)e^{-2\pi iy\cdot\xi}\widehat f(\xi)\,dy=\widehat f(\xi)\widehat g(\xi)$. The convolution is defined arbitrarily on its null exceptional set; F6 makes that choice irrelevant at every frequency. This proves the asserted equality, including when either input is zero.

fact_uses.text: [F5] Absolute integrability permits Fubini ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

proof_steps.claim: Fix the other coordinates and integrate in coordinate $j$. For $u=f$ restricted to this line and $v=e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}$, both $u'v$ and $uv'$ are integrable on the line: multiply $u,u'$ by $1+x_j^2$ and use their bounded Schwartz seminorms. Also $uv\to0$ at both ends, since $x_ju$ is bounded. [F6] therefore gives the derivative identity in that coordinate. Integrating over the other coordinates is legitimate by [F2] and [F5], since the full integrals of $|\partial_jf|$ and $|f|$ are finite. Iteration using [F1] proves the first formula, including zero components of $\xi$ without division by them.

fact_uses.text: [F3] Fubini permits exchanging absolutely integrable complex product integrals ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

proof_steps.claim: Insert the inverse integral for $f_c$ into $\int f_c(x)g(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,dx$. The product integrand has modulus $|\widehat f(\eta)||g(x)|$ with double integral $\|\widehat f\|_1\|g\|_1$; measurability follows from coordinate pullbacks and the continuous exponential. F3 exchanges the integrals, giving $\int\widehat f(\eta)[\int g(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot(\xi-\eta)}\,dx]\,d\eta$, the required expression. Exchanging the roles of f and g proves the symmetric variant under its stated hypothesis. Countable choice is inherited from F1. No assertion that arbitrary products of two integrable functions are integrable is used.

fact_uses.text: [L2] Tonelli and Fubini apply on sigma-finite product spaces ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

proof_steps.claim: Use the stated countable choice and [L0] to choose Borel representatives $\tilde f,\tilde g$ of $f,g$ and define [L0, L1, L2, L4, given, choose, algebra] $$ H(x,y) := |\tilde f(x-y)|\,|\tilde g(y)|. $$ By [L1], $H$ is measurable on $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$. For each $y$, $$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} H(x,y)\,dx = |\tilde g(y)| \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} |\tilde f(x-y)|\,dx = \|\tilde f\|_1\,|\tilde g(y)| $$ by [L4].

Integrating the identity from step 1.1 in $y$ and applying [L2] gives [L2, step 1.1, algebra] $$ \iint_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}} H(x,y)\,dx\,dy = \|\tilde f\|_1\|\tilde g\|_1 < \infty. $$ Hence for almost every $x$, the section $y \mapsto \tilde f(x-y)\tilde g(y)$ is absolutely integrable, so $(f*g)(x)$ is defined there.

For those $x$, [L1, L2, L3, step 2.1, algebra] $$ |(f*g)(x)| \le \int |\tilde f(x-y)\tilde g(y)|\,dy $$ by [L3]. Another application of [L2] then yields $$ \|f*g\|_1 \le \iint |\tilde f(x-y)|\,|\tilde g(y)|\,dy\,dx = \|f\|_1\|g\|_1. $$ By [L1], the resulting $L^1$ class is independent of the chosen Borel representatives.

fact_uses.text:
[F5] Tonelli gives measurable section integrals for nonnegative product-measurable
functions; Fubini exchanges the iterated integrals of an $L^1$ product function.
([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]])

proof_steps.claim: Apply Tonelli [F5] to the nonnegative Borel function $|H(x,y)|\mathbf1_{B(0,m)}(x)\mathbf1_K(y)$. Using step 3.1 gives $\int_{B(0,m)}\int_K|\Phi(x-y)\widetilde f(y)|\,dy\,dx\le C_{m,R}\int_K|\widetilde f(y)|\,dy=C_{m,R}\|f\|_{L^1}<\infty,$ where the last equality uses [F2, F9] because $\widetilde f=f$ almost everywhere and $\beta_n$ completes to $\lambda_n$. Thus the complex function $H$ is in $L^1(B(0,m)\times K)$ for every $m$.

Fubini [F5] on each such product shows that for almost every $x\in B(0,m)$ the section $y\mapsto H(x,y)\mathbf1_K(y)$ is absolutely integrable, and its integral is an $L^1(B(0,m))$ function with integral of its absolute value at most the finite bound in step 4.1, by the integral triangle inequality [F8]. These section integrals agree with $Nf(x)$ wherever absolutely finite by [F13]. The balls $B(0,m)$ exhaust $\mathbb R^n$, so, writing $E_m$ for the measurable exceptional set in $B(0,m)$, [F15] gives $\lambda_n(\bigcup_{m\ge1}E_m)\le\sum_{m\ge1}\lambda_n(E_m)=0$. Thus $Nf$ is finite almost everywhere on all of $\mathbb R^n$; assign it value zero on this null set. Each compact set lies in some $B(0,m)$ by [F4], proving $Nf\in L^1_{\rm loc}(\mathbb R^n)$.

Let $\varphi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^n)$ and choose $m$ with $\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subset B(0,m)$. The function $H(x,y)=\Phi(x-y)\widetilde f(y)$ is Borel by [F3]. The pullback of the Borel function $-\Delta\varphi$ by the first-coordinate projection is Borel: the preimage of a Borel set $E$ is $E\times\mathbb R^n$, which belongs to the product sigma-algebra and hence to the Euclidean Borel sigma-algebra by [F3]. The test function is smooth, so $\Delta\varphi$ is continuous; [F16] gives its Borel measurability. Thus $G(x,y)=H(x,y)(-\Delta\varphi(x))$ is Borel by [F16]. Since $\Delta\varphi$ is bounded and compactly supported, step 4.1 shows $G$ is integrable on the product. Fubini therefore gives $\int_{\mathbb R^n}Nf(x)(-\Delta\varphi(x))\,dx=\int_K\widetilde f(y)\left(\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Phi(x-y)(-\Delta\varphi(x))\,dx\right)dy.$ The inner integral is $\varphi(y)$ by the translated point-source identity [F12]. Hence the right side is $\int_K\widetilde f(y)\varphi(y)\,dy$.

fact_uses.text: [F3] Fubini applies to absolutely integrable complex product functions on sigma-finite spaces ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

proof_steps.claim: By [F1], $\overline{g(x)}=\int\overline{\widehat g(\xi)}e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi$. The integrand after multiplying by $f(x)$ is jointly measurable and has absolute double integral $\|f\|_1\|\widehat g\|_1<\infty$, by [F1], [F2] and product integration. Hence [F3] gives $\int f\overline g=\int\overline{\widehat g(\xi)}[\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,dx]\,d\xi=\int\widehat f\overline{\widehat g}$. This also proves absolute integrability of the final product; the original product is integrable since $g$ is bounded and $f$ integrable.

fact_uses.text: [F4] [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: an integrable nonnegative density on $\mathbb R^2\times[0,L]$ has measurable slice integrals whose integral equals the total integral.

proof_steps.claim: Decompose the integrand into the transverse density $e_\perp(x,z)$, containing $F_{12}$, $D_1q,D_2q$ and the potential, and the nonnegative longitudinal density $e_\parallel(x,z)$, containing $F_{31},F_{32},D_3q$. Since the total density is nonnegative and integrable, [F4] gives $\mathcal E_L=\int_0^L E(\mathbf A_\perp(\cdot,z),q_z)\,dz+\int_{\Omega_L}e_\parallel\,dx\,dz$, where $\mathbf A_\perp=A_1dx_1+A_2dx_2$ and $E(\mathbf A_\perp(\cdot,z),q_z)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}e_\perp(x,z)dx$ for almost every $z$. The slice hypotheses and [F3] give $E(\mathbf A_\perp(\cdot,z),q_z)\ge T_n$ for each slice, while the longitudinal integral is nonnegative; hence $\mathcal E_L\ge T_nL$.

fact_uses.text: [F4] [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: integrable nonnegative energy densities on the polar-coordinate product can be integrated by radial slices; the section integrals are measurable and their total integral equals the plane integral.

proof_steps.claim:
For almost every $r$ larger than the nonzero-field radius, let $Q(r)=\int_{\partial D_r}(|q|^2-\xi)^2ds$ and $K(r)=\int_{\partial D_r}|D_{A,\tau}q|^2ds$, where $D_{A,\tau}$ is the covariant derivative in the unit tangent direction. The potential and kinetic terms of the finite energy, with polar coordinates and [F4], imply $Q,K\in L^1([R_0,\infty))$. For each integer $m\ge1$, the set $S_m=\{r\ge R_0:Q(r)>1/m\}$ has finite measure. Its complement has divergent $\int dr/r$, since removing a finite-measure set from a half-line cannot make the logarithmic integral finite. If $rK(r)\ge1/m$ for every sufficiently large $r\notin S_m$, then $\int K(r)dr\ge m^{-1}\int_{[R,\infty)\setminus S_m}dr/r=\infty$, contradiction. Thus there is an unbounded set of radii with $Q(r)\le1/m$ and $rK(r)<1/m$. By [A1] select an increasing sequence $r_m\to\infty$ from these sets. Along it, [F6] gives $\int_{\partial D_{r_m}}|q|^2ds\le2\pi\xi r_m+\sqrt{2\pi r_mQ(r_m)}=O(r_m)$, and
$$\left|\int_{\partial D_{r_m}}j\right|\le\left(\int_{\partial D_{r_m}}|q|^2ds\right)^{1/2}K(r_m)^{1/2}\longrightarrow0.$$

fact_uses.text: [L2] Tonelli and Fubini hold on the uncompleted product sigma-algebra. ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]])

proof_steps.claim:
Apply Tonelli in [L2] to $\mathbf 1_Z$. Since $(\mu 	imes 
u)(Z)=0$, it gives $$\int_X 
u(Z_x)\,d\mu = 0,\qquad \int_Y \mu(Z^y)\,d
u = 0.$$ The functions $x\mapsto
u(Z_x)$ and $y\mapsto\mu(Z^y)$ are measurable, so $A:=\{x:
u(Z_x)>0\}$ and $B:=\{y:\mu(Z^y)>0\}$ are measurable null sets by the zero-integral criterion in [L6]. For $x
otin A$, $f_x=g_x$ outside the null section $Z_x$; [L4] makes $f_x$ measurable for the completed factor measure. The analogous statement holds for $y
otin B$.

In the nonnegative case replace $g$ by $g^+=\max(g,0)$. Since $f\ge0$ and $f=g$ outside $Z$, one has $f=g^+$ there, both on the product and on sections outside $A,B$. Apply uncompleted Tonelli [L2] to $g^+$, with its base-measurable section-integral functions $I_g,J_g$. For each $x
otin A$, step 1.1 first transfers the section integral of $g^+$ to the completed factor and then transfers it to the equal-almost-everywhere $f_x$; thus $I_f(x)=I_g(x)$, and likewise $J_f=J_g$ outside $B$. The definitions set $I_f=0$ on the base-measurable set $A$ and $J_f=0$ on $B$, so these are base-measurable functions obtained by measurable piecewise gluing, not by an unqualified almost-everywhere measurability assertion on an incomplete space. Step 1.1 gives equal outer nonnegative integrals despite possible infinity, and also $\int f\,d\overline{\mu	imes
u}=\int g^+\,d(\mu	imes
u)$. Tonelli gives the asserted three-way equality.

If $f\in L^1(\overline{\mu	imes
u})$, apply [L1] separately to its finite real and imaginary parts, obtaining base-measurable extended-real $u,v$ equal to them almost everywhere. Their nonfinite sets are base measurable and null, because the completed measure extends the base measure; set $u,v$ to zero there and put $g=u+iv$. By completion there is a base-measurable null cover $Z$ of $\{f
e g\}$. Applying the nonnegative rules of step 1.1 to $|f|,|g|$ gives $\int|g|\,d(\mu	imes
u)=\int|f|\,d\overline{\mu	imes
u}<\infty$, so $g$ is in base $L^1$ before invoking Fubini or [L3]. Fubini [L2] gives base-measurable null exceptional parameter sets for the integrability of its sections. Enlarge them by the null-section exceptional sets obtained from $Z$ as in step 2.1. Outside the enlarged $A,B$, [L4] makes the real and imaginary $f$ sections measurable on the completed factor; step 1.1 applied to absolute values shows their integrals finite, so both sections are integrable before [L3] equates their integrals. Step 1.1 also identifies the base and completed integrals of each integrable $g$ section. Hence $I_f,J_f$ equal the base Fubini section functions outside the base-measurable null sets $A,B$ and are zero on those sets. Piecewise gluing makes them base measurable, and step 1.1 applied to their absolute values proves integrability. Now [L3] equates the outer integrals; on the completed product, $f$ and $g$ are already integrable and equal almost everywhere, so [L3] followed by completion agreement in step 1.1 equates their product integrals as well. This proves the stated equality in the real and complex cases.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F1] For \(k=\mathbb R\), the selected Borel definition uses the same product Milnor model and gives \(A_T(\mathbb R)=\mathbb R[u_1,\ldots,u_r]\) with \(u_i\) the coordinate character class. [[def-torus-equivariant-cohomology-cartan-model]] [[lem-torus-classifying-space-cohomology]]

proof_steps.claim: The rational character formula is [F2]. For the real formula, restrict a smooth character to the coordinate circles; the rational supplier [F2] gives its integer vector \(\mathbf n\). The associated one-dimensional representation \(\mathbb C_{\chi_{\mathbf n}}\) is the tensor product of the coordinate representations \(\mathbb C_{\chi_i}^{\otimes n_i}\), interpreting negative powers as duals; taking associated bundles preserves this tensor-product isomorphism. Additivity and duality in [F3] give \(c_1(L_{\chi_{\mathbf n}})=\sum_i n_i u_i\) over \(\mathbb R\) as well, since the real generators in [F1] are the coefficient images of the same tautological Euler classes. The formula is unique because restriction to each coordinate circle recovers \(n_i\).

The empty product is \(1\), concatenation of two finite character lists multiplies their products, so \(1\in\mathscr S_T(k)\) and \(\mathscr S_T(k)\) is multiplicatively closed. For each nontrivial character \(\mathbf n\ne0\), step 1.1 gives the nonzero linear polynomial \(\sum_i n_i u_i\); a polynomial ring over a field is an integral domain, so every finite product of these classes remains nonzero. If \(r=0\), the generating list is empty and the set is \(\{1\}\). Hence \(0\notin\mathscr S_T(k)\) in all cases.

For a continuous left \(T\)-action on \(X\), the projection \(ET\times_T X\to BT\) makes singular cohomology a module over \(A_T(k)\) by pullback and cup product; pulling back first Chern classes defines the character actions used in the localization. The Borel space and module are defined for empty \(X\) as zero, and for \(r=0\) the localization changes no module because \(\mathscr S_T(k)=\{1\}\). proof_steps.claim:
By [A1], for any sequence $(A_n)$ of nonempty sets the family
$\mathcal F=\{A_n:n\in\mathbb N\}$ has a choice function $g$. The composite
$n\mapsto g(A_n)$ is an indexed selector, even if some sets $A_n$ repeat.
Thus [F1] holds and supplies the countable-choice premise in the quotient
circle definition [F2].

For one factor, [F2] makes each quotient interval $q(I)$ open because
$q$ is open, and $q|_I$ is injective because $I$ has length less than $1$.
Its inverse chart is continuous: $q|_I$ is a continuous open bijection onto
$q(I)$. These charts cover the circle. If two charts overlap, local lifts
differ by an integer; this integer is locally constant, so each transition
map is locally a translation and hence smooth. The charts therefore define a
smooth one-manifold without boundary compatible with the quotient topology.

Addition and inversion on one factor are smooth in these charts. Near any
pair of points, choose local real lifts $x,y$ and an output chart around their
sum; after shrinking the input intervals, the coordinate expression for
addition is $x+y$ plus one fixed integer. Near any point, choose local lifts
for it and its inverse; the coordinate expression for inversion is $-x$ plus
one fixed integer. Both expressions are smooth. With the group law already
given by [F2], this is a Lie group by [F6]. Its underlying circle is compact,
Hausdorff and connected by [F2] and [F3], and it is abelian by the quotient
addition law.

The circle has a finite CW structure with one vertex $[0]$ and one open
$1$-cell, the image of $(0,1)$; its characteristic interval has both
endpoints attached to that vertex. For $T$, index product cells by subsets
$J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,r\}$: coordinates in $J$ lie in the open $1$-cell and
all other coordinates equal $[0]$. Each cell is an open cube of dimension
$|J|$, its closure meets only cells indexed by subsets of $J$, and its
characteristic cube is the product of the factor characteristic intervals;
identify each closed cube with a closed disk of the same dimension. The map
$q^r:[0,1]^r\to T$ is a continuous surjection because every coordinate class
has a representative in $[0,1]$ by [F2]. If $K$ is closed in the cube,
then $K$ is compact, $q^r(K)$ is compact, and $q^r(K)$ is closed because $T$
is Hausdorff by [F2] and [F3]. Thus $q^r$ is a quotient map. It is the
characteristic map for the top cell. Every lower-cell characteristic cube is
obtained by precomposing $q^r$ with the continuous coordinate insertion that
fixes omitted coordinates at $0$, so the quotient topology of $q^r$ already
makes every characteristic map continuous; conversely $q^r$ is itself one of
those maps. Hence this quotient topology is exactly the weak topology
determined by the finitely many characteristic cubes. This gives a finite CW
structure with the identity as a $0$-cell. The singleton
identity is a subcomplex, so [F7] gives the homotopy extension property for
its inclusion.

The normal bundle is the tangent line of the first factor at its fixed point; in the coordinates $z_1/z_0$ and $z_0/z_1$ its weights are $+1$ on $F_0$ and $-1$ on $F_\infty$.
