proof_steps.claim: Taking these principal opens over the finitely many affine charts gives a finite invariant open cover $\{D_a\}$ of $X\setminus F$. Every nonempty finite intersection is a $T$-invariant open subset of at least one $D_a$; [F2] therefore makes its localized Borel–Moore groups zero in every degree.

For a finite invariant open cover of $X\setminus F$, the augmented Čech complex with terms $j_{I!}\mathbb Q_{D_I}$, where $D_I$ is an intersection and $j_I:D_I\hookrightarrow X\setminus F$ is open, resolves the constant equivariant sheaf. At a point the indices containing it form a nonempty simplex, whose augmented cochain complex is contracted by its least index. Applying derived Hom into the normalized dualizing object gives a finite Čech spectral sequence for Borel–Moore homology: open base change identifies each term with the Borel–Moore group of an intersection $D_I$. Those groups vanish after localization by [F2]. Since the Čech filtration is finite and localization is exact by [F4], the abutment $S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(X\setminus F;\mathbb Q)$ is zero for every $j$.

The closed/open localization sequence for $i:F\hookrightarrow X$ and $X\setminus F$ contains $S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_{j+1}(X\setminus F)\to S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(F)\xrightarrow{i_*}S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(X)\to S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(X\setminus F)$. Both outside groups vanish by step 3.1, so $i_*$ is an isomorphism. If $F=\varnothing$, the same argument gives zero localized Borel–Moore homology for $X$; if $F=X$, $i_*$ is the identity. The proof used only the finite invariant affine cover and not Sumihiro's theorem or compactness.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] A square-zero smooth Dolbeault operator on a finite-rank bundle has local holomorphic frames, and intertwining maps are holomorphic. [[lem-qftx-local-integrable-dolbeault-frames]]

proof_steps.claim: In the chart w=λ₂/λ₁ on a real incidence fiber, the projected horizontal (0,1) directions are H₁=∂bar_z₁−w∂z₂ and H₂=∂bar_z₂+w∂z₁. Indeed these and the vertical ∂bar_w annihilate the holomorphic coordinates w, μ₁=z₁−bar_z₂w, μ₂=z₂+bar_z₁w. They are independent and commute; their coefficients are holomorphic in w. For a unitary connection A define the pulled-back (0,1) operator by the vertical ordinary derivative and ∇_A along H₁,H₂. Its mixed squares vanish by the displayed commuting generators and holomorphic w coefficients. Its horizontal square is F_A(H₁,H₂)=F_bar1bar2−w(F_1bar1+F_2bar2)+w²F_12, which vanishes for an ASD two-form in the positive orientation: the three coefficients are precisely its self-dual component. Thus the operator squares to zero on this chart, and on the other projective chart by the same tensorial calculation. Apply [F2] to obtain a genuine holomorphic bundle. Its restriction to every real line is the constant bundle E_x, with positive reality pairing induced by the unitary metric and framing at infinity. This pairing is holomorphic: its vertical derivative vanishes on the constant fibres, and differentiating horizontally gives zero by the original identity ∇_A h=0, with the conjugate pullback at σ interchanging the conjugate horizontal directions.

Restrict H and ∇ to the totally real graph locus M=HP¹. Its smooth real incidence is diffeomorphic to Z by (P,[v])↦[v], with inverse [v]↦(span(v,jv),[v]); the explicit charts in [F3] verify smoothness. Under this identification dp(D) is exactly the span of H₁,H₂ in step 1.1: write X_z=((z₁,-bar_z₂),(z₂,bar_z₁)) and solve v(1,w)^T=0. Therefore the restricted smooth connection has F(H₁,H₂)=0 for every w, so all three self-dual coefficients in step 1.1 vanish. Hence it is ASD. Evaluation intertwines the original holomorphic operator on E with the reconstructed vertical/horizontal Dolbeault operator: it is holomorphic vertically, and on D its derivative is exactly the canonical relative derivative δ by step 3.1. These directions generate the (0,1) tangent in step 1.1, proving equality of the full operators, not just of underlying bundles.

Starting from A in step 1.1, its constant real-line sections identify the reconstructed smooth H with E. Along every alpha-plane the recovered connection has the same derivative as A; the cotangent uniqueness in step 3.1 makes the full connections equal. The unitary reality pairing and framing also agree. Starting from a Ward bundle, step 4.1 proves evaluation is a holomorphic isomorphism from the reconstructed pullback to the original bundle, and step 5.2 preserves its reality pairing and metric. These constructions and identities apply to morphisms as well, so descend to inverse maps on based unitary gauge and framed holomorphic isomorphism classes. No irreducibility or absence of parallel sections was used.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] For every continuous map from a finite polyhedron into $\mathcal A_\infty$, with irreducible values on a subpolyhedron, the relative avoidance lemma supplies a homotopy fixed on that subpolyhedron and an open neighborhood of it whose endpoint is entirely irreducible. Its complete argument and exact batch-56 inputs were inspected; the configuration and stabilizer suppliers now have current ready Step 1 records ([[lem-qftx-relative-finite-parameter-irreducible-avoidance]]).

proof_steps.claim: The affine space $\mathcal A_\infty$ contains $A_0$. Apply [F2] to the constant map from a one-point polyhedron with empty subpolyhedron and value $A_0$. Its endpoint is an element of $\mathcal A_\infty^*$, proving nonemptiness.

Let $A,B\in\mathcal A_\infty^*$. The affine path $\gamma(t)=(1-t)A+tB$ is continuous in the Fréchet topology and has irreducible endpoints. Apply [F2] with $K=I$ and $L=\{0,1\}$. The resulting endpoint path remains in $\mathcal A_\infty^*$ and fixes both endpoints, so the locus is path-connected.

Apply [F2] to $F$ with $K=D^{j+1}$ and $L=\partial D^{j+1}=S^j$. Its boundary is already irreducible, so the endpoint is a map $G:D^{j+1}\to\mathcal A_\infty^*$ agreeing with $u$ on the boundary. Choose the based point $x_0\in S^j$ with $u(x_0)=A$. Since the disk is convex, $C_t(x)=(1-t)x+tx_0$ remains in the disk and fixes $x_0$. Then $G(C_t(x))$ is a homotopy from $G$ to the constant map at $A$ that fixes $x_0$ and remains in $\mathcal A_\infty^*$. Restricting it to $S^j$ gives a based nullhomotopy of $u$; by [F3], its class in $\pi_j(\mathcal A_\infty^*,A)$ is zero. Since $j$ and $u$ were arbitrary, every stated homotopy group vanishes.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F4] Proper pushforward is functorial, closed inclusions are proper, and cap product with an equivariant cohomology class sends $[X]_T$ to Borel–Moore degree $2d-q$. [[def-qftx-localized-equivariant-borel-moore-data]]

proof_steps.claim: Let $f:X\to Y$ be a proper $T$-equivariant map between smooth separated finite-type varieties with finite invariant affine covers and proper fixed loci $F_X,F_Y$. Its restriction $f^T:F_X\to F_Y$ is proper, and the square formed by $i_X,i_Y,f^T,f$ commutes because $f$ sends fixed points to fixed points. Functoriality of proper Borel–Moore pushforward gives $f_*i_{X*}=i_{Y*}f^T_*$. After localization both $i_{X*}$ and $i_{Y*}$ are isomorphisms by [F2], so applying their inverses and then the proper traces proves $p_{Y*}^{\mathrm{loc}}f_*=p_{X*}^{\mathrm{loc}}$. If $X\to\mathrm{pt}$ itself is proper, then $p_{F*}=p_{X*}i_*$; composing with $i_*^{-1}$ proves $p_*^{\mathrm{loc}}=p_{X*}$.

Let $ eta=(i_*)^{-1}(\alpha\cap[X]_T)$. On each component, the complex orientation and refined Gysin map give $i_a^!(\alpha\cap[X]_T)=i_a^*\alpha\cap[F_a]_T$. Since $\alpha\cap[X]_T=i_* eta$, the self-intersection formula [F3] gives $e_T(
u_a)\cap eta_a=i_a^*\alpha\cap[F_a]_T$. Properness of $F_a$ makes $e_T(
u_a)$ invertible after localization by [F3], hence $ eta_a=(i_a^*\alpha/e_T(
u_a))\cap[F_a]_T$. Applying $p_{a*}$ and summing the finitely many components yields the displayed formula. The degree is $2d-q$: division by the degree-$2c_a$ Euler class lowers the localized cohomological degree of the insertion from $q$ to $q-2c_a$, and capping with the degree-$2d_a$ fundamental class gives $2d_a-(q-2c_a)=2d-q$.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F3] For the stated Sobolev index, the smooth irreducible projection $\mathcal A_\infty^*\to\mathcal A_\infty^*/\overline{\mathcal G}_\infty$ is a locally trivial topological principal $\overline{\mathcal G}_\infty$-bundle with its actual $C^\infty$ quotient topology; the Sobolev irreducible locus $\mathcal A_k^*$ is open. [[thm-qftx-sobolev-smooth-irreducible-gauge-bundle]]

proof_steps.claim: Choose the fixed integer $k>r/2+1$. The smooth clause of [F3], applied with the configuration data [F2], makes $q_*$ a locally trivial principal $\overline{\mathcal G}^\infty(P)$-bundle. By [F4], its total space is nonempty, path connected, and has $\pi_j=0$ for every $j\ge1$, so it is weakly contractible in the sense used in [F6]. For a constant central gauge section $u=\zeta I_N$, the local action formula gives $A^u=A$ because $u^{-1}Au=A$ and $du=0$; hence reduced and full gauge groups have the same orbits on $\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P)$.

The locus $\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P)$ is gauge invariant: in the chosen frame, the based holonomy subgroup of $A^u$ is $u(p_m)^{-1}\operatorname{Hol}_{p_m}(A)u(p_m)$, so it has the same invariant subspaces up to conjugation. It is open: by [F2], the inclusion $\mathcal A^\infty(P)\hookrightarrow\mathcal A_k(P)$ is continuous, as each fixed $H^k$ norm is bounded by finitely many smooth derivative seminorms on the finite compact atlas. The smooth irreducible locus is the inverse image of the Sobolev irreducible locus, which is open by [F3]. The full orbit projection $q$ is open because, for any open $U\subseteq\mathcal A^\infty(P)$, its saturation $q^{-1}(q(U))=\bigcup_{u\in\mathcal G^\infty(P)}U\cdot u$ is open. For fixed smooth $u$, the map $A\mapsto u^{-1}Au+u^{-1}du$ is continuous in every finite-atlas derivative seminorm by the Leibniz rule; its inverse is the same formula for $u^{-1}$, so each gauge translate is a homeomorphism. Therefore $q(\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P))$ is open and $q|_{\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P)}$ is an open quotient map onto this subset. The reduced and full actions have the same orbits there, so their quotient topologies identify the reduced orbit space homeomorphically with $q(\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P))$; this proves the claim about $\iota$ in the Statement. If $q$ had a continuous section, its restriction to this open subset would take each irreducible orbit to a point in that same orbit, hence into $\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P)$. Via the stated homeomorphism, this would give a continuous section of $q_*$, contradicting step 3.1. Thus $q$ has no continuous section.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F7] For every integer $r>d/2$, multiplication is bounded on $H^r$, and the embeddings $H^s\hookrightarrow C^m$ hold when $s>d/2+m$; the finite-atlas estimates used in the smoothness bootstrap follow by localization and Hölder. [[cor-sobolev-algebra-above-the-critical-index]], [[thm-higher-order-sobolev-embedding]]

proof_steps.claim: Apply the inverse-function theorem [F4] to $\Phi_A(s,u):=s^u$ on the local Banach product $S_{A,\varepsilon}\times\bar{\mathcal G}_{k+1}$ near $(A,e)$; its derivative is $L_A$ from step 1.2. Shrink $\varepsilon$ so the slice remains in the open irreducible locus. At $(s,e)$, for $s=A+a$, the derivative is $L_s(b,\xi)=b+d_s\xi$ on $b\in\ker d_A^*$; this differs from $L_A$ only by $(b,\xi)\mapsto[a,\xi]$. Its operator norm is at most $C\|a\|_{H^k}$ by [F7]. Choose $\varepsilon$ so $C\varepsilon\|L_A^{-1}\|<1$; then [F5] makes $L_s$ an isomorphism for every $s$ in the slice. At an arbitrary $(s,u_0)$, write $u=u_0v$ near $u_0$ and use $s^{u_0v}=(s^{u_0})^v$. Applying the inverse action by $u_0$ to the target tangent and changing the gauge tangent by the invertible adjoint action identifies this derivative with $L_s$. Hence the derivative is an isomorphism at every point of the slice product, and the inverse-function theorem makes $\Phi_A$ a local diffeomorphism throughout.

For the smooth-space clause, fix now a smooth irreducible center $A\in\mathcal A_\infty^*$ and use the Banach slice and trivialization established in step 4.1. Put $U_A=\Phi_A(S_{A,\varepsilon}\times\bar{\mathcal G}_{k+1})$ and $V_A=\pi_k(S_{A,\varepsilon})$. Since $U_A$ is open in $\mathcal A_k^*$, $U_A\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*$ is open in the stated $C^\infty$ topology; set $S_A^\infty=S_{A,\varepsilon}\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*$ and $V_A^\infty=\pi_\infty(S_A^\infty)$. For a smooth $B\in U_A$, its unique reduced gauge class from step 4.1 has a representative $u\in\mathcal G_{k+1}$. It satisfies $d_A^*(B^{u^{-1}}-A)=0$. Locally in a bundle frame, write $C_j=uB_j u^{-1}-(\partial_j u)u^{-1}-A_j$. Substitution in $d_A^*C=0$, use of $\partial_i(u^{-1})=-u^{-1}(\partial_i u)u^{-1}$, and multiplication on the right by $u$ isolate the equation $g^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j u=R(A,B,g;u,u^{-1},du)$ on each chart. Every term in $R$ is a finite product of smooth coefficients (including first derivatives of $A,B$) and factors among $u,u^{-1},du$; hence the principal operator is the scalar smooth Laplacian on each matrix entry. If $u\in H^{r+1}$ for $r\ge k$, then this right-hand side lies in $H^r$ by [F7] and the smooth coefficient bounds. Elliptic regularity [F6] gives $u\in H^{r+2}$. Iteration proves $u$ smooth; changing its representative by an element of the finite center preserves smoothness. Thus every smooth point of the Banach saturation has a smooth trivialization representative, and $U_A\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*=\pi_\infty^{-1}(V_A^\infty)$.

Suppose smooth $B_j\to B$ in $C^\infty$ within $U_A\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*$. The Banach trivialization from step 4.1 gives convergence of their slice representatives in $H^k$ and of their reduced gauge classes in $H^{k+1}$. In a quotient chart around the limiting class from step 1.1, choose lifts $u_j,u$ that converge in $H^{k+1}$; this is possible because the finite center acts by disjoint translates. The equation in step 5.2 and elliptic estimates [F6] bootstrap convergence: if $u_j\to u$ in $H^{r+1}$, then the assumed $C^\infty$ convergence gives $B_j\to B$ in $H^{r+1}$, and [F7] makes the right-hand sides converge in $H^r$. Apply the elliptic estimate to $u_j-u$, using also their already known $H^{k+1}$ convergence for the $L^2$ term, to get $u_j\to u$ in $H^{r+2}$. Induction gives convergence in every Sobolev order, which on compact $M$ is the $C^\infty$ section topology. The slice representatives converge in $C^\infty$ by their action formula. Conversely the forward action is continuous in the $C^\infty$ topology by multiplication and differentiation of smooth sections. The saturation $U_A\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*$ is open, and $V_A^\infty$ is open in the quotient because the quotient map is open: the saturation of any open set is a union of its open gauge translates. The restricted map $S_A^\infty\times\bar{\mathcal G}_\infty\to\pi_\infty^{-1}(V_A^\infty)$ is therefore a homeomorphism for the actual quotient topology, and it is equivariant. This proves the smooth-space topological principal bundle claim.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F5] [[thm-higher-order-sobolev-embedding]] and [[thm-extension-theorem-for-bounded-smooth-domains]]: on each bounded disk, $W^{2,p}$ for $p>2$ supplies $C^{1,\beta}$ representatives for $0<\beta<1-2/p$.

proof_steps.claim: To obtain derivative decay, fix $\alpha<\alpha'<\sqrt\kappa$ and use step 3.3 at rate $\alpha'$. On each unit ball centered at large $z$, both $w$ and $\Delta w=\kappa(1-e^{-w})$ are $O(e^{-\alpha'|z|})$. By [F3] and [F5], $w$ has a $C^{1,\beta}$ norm of that order on the concentric half-ball for some $\beta>0$. Thus the right-hand side has a $C^{0,\beta}$ norm of the same order, and [F4] gives $C^{2,\beta}$ decay on a smaller ball. Inductively, for each multi-index $\gamma$, differentiating $\Delta w=\kappa(1-e^{-w})$ gives $\Delta D^\gamma w=\kappa e^{-w}D^\gamma w+G_\gamma$, where $G_\gamma$ is a finite sum of products of lower derivatives of $w$ and is exponentially small by the induction hypothesis. Applying [F3] and [F4] on nested unit balls gives the same $e^{-\alpha'|z|}$ bound for two more derivatives. Since $e^{-\alpha'|z|}\le e^{-\alpha|z|}$ outside a fixed disk, every finite derivative has the stated rate.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [A4] The current framed Ward theorem proves the local integrable-Dolbeault frames, universal-line degree-zero base change/evaluation, unique incidence connection and compatibility of the pairing-induced positive metric. Its comparison input is absolute projective GAGA, not independently chosen parallel metrics or assumed base-change surjectivity. [[thm-qftx-framed-penrose-ward-correspondence-on-s4]]

proof_steps.claim: Starting with a framed ASD connection, [A4] constructs its holomorphic Ward bundle; the exact coupled cohomology-vanishing and diagonal argument [[lem-qftx-asd-twistor-vanishing-and-monad-reconstruction]] reconstructs the normalized three-term monad. Starting with regular ADHM data, [A5] identifies its normalized real monad and projection connection with this Ward bundle and connection. The equality of the two constructions is the first-order and inverse-extraction clause in [A5], so it is conditional on that exact real block proof, not on the P² citation alone.

By [A5], both composites on framed isomorphism classes are identities: ADHM data produce the Ward bundle whose monad extraction returns the same $U(k)$ orbit, and an ASD connection produces a Ward bundle whose matrix extraction returns an orbit reconstructing that framed connection. The charge of each resulting connection is $q_N=-k$ by [F2]–[F3]. Thus the claimed bijection and charge statement follow conditionally on [A4]–[A5].

The finite-dimensional quotient and $\mathbb P^2$ sheaf maps are $T$-equivariant by [A1]–[A2]. The Ward construction is natural under rotations and framing transformations by [A4]; the exact raw monad torus factors are directly calculated in the new block lemma cited by [A5], while the equivariance of inverse normalization remains part of [A5]. These exact interfaces make the composite $T$-equivariant. The same composition on first-order families is valid only under the base-change hypotheses of [A2]–[A4] and the deformation compatibility of [A5]. This proves the stated conditional torus and tangent clauses and leaves the positive-FI boundary separate.

fact_uses.text: [F2] A map of pairs $f:(X,A)\to(Y,B)$ induces a commuting morphism from the long exact sequence of $(X,A)$ to that of $(Y,B)$, including the connecting maps. ([[thm-naturality-of-the-long-exact-sequence-of-a-pair]])

proof_steps.claim: The homomorphism induced by $(S^n,S^n\setminus F)\to(S^n,S^n\setminus\{x\})$ is projection onto the $x$ summand: all other summands factor through a pair $(U_z,U_z)$ and vanish. Its composite with the global map restricts the global class to its local generator. Hence the global tuple is diagonal.

For nested allowed neighborhoods, the inclusion of punctured pairs is an excision isomorphism and carries one restricted generator to the other. Their maps to the target pair commute. Thus their integer multipliers agree. Two arbitrary allowed neighborhoods have an allowed open intersection, so shrinking proves full independence.

fact_uses.text: [F4] A map of pairs $f:(X,A)\to(Y,B)$ induces a commuting morphism from the long exact sequence of $(X,A)$ to that of $(Y,B)$, including the connecting maps. ([[thm-naturality-of-the-long-exact-sequence-of-a-pair]])

proof_steps.claim: The singular pair sequence is exact and its connecting maps commute with every map of pairs, by F3 and F4. These assertions hold for arbitrary subspaces and hence for CW pairs.

In $D$ set $O=U\cup (W\times[0,2/3))$ and $N=V\cup(W\times(1/3,1])$. They are open and cover $D$. The closure of $D\setminus O$ is contained in $N$. Excision therefore identifies $H_n(O,O\cap N;G)$ with $H_n(D,N;G)$. Retraction of $N$ to $V$ and the pair exact sequence identify the latter with $H_n(D,V;G)$. The collapse $O\to U$ restricts on $O\cap N=W\times(1/3,2/3)$ to projection onto $W$. Both absolute maps are homotopy equivalences, so their commuting pair exact sequences give an isomorphism $H_n(O,O\cap N;G)\to H_n(U,W;G)$ by the exact-sequence injectivity and surjectivity chase. No inverse map of these pairs is needed. All maps commute with collapse to $(U\cup V,V)$, so the resulting isomorphism is the homomorphism of the original inclusion.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F3] First Chern classes are additive under tensor products, change sign for dual lines, and are natural under coefficient change. [[prop-first-chern-class-of-tensor-dual-and-conjugate-lines]]

proof_steps.claim: The rational character formula is [F2]. For the real formula, restrict a smooth character to the coordinate circles; the rational supplier [F2] gives its integer vector \(\mathbf n\). The associated one-dimensional representation \(\mathbb C_{\chi_{\mathbf n}}\) is the tensor product of the coordinate representations \(\mathbb C_{\chi_i}^{\otimes n_i}\), interpreting negative powers as duals; taking associated bundles preserves this tensor-product isomorphism. Additivity and duality in [F3] give \(c_1(L_{\chi_{\mathbf n}})=\sum_i n_i u_i\) over \(\mathbb R\) as well, since the real generators in [F1] are the coefficient images of the same tautological Euler classes. The formula is unique because restriction to each coordinate circle recovers \(n_i\).

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F6] With full AC, the Chern form class is the real coefficient image of the integral topological Chern class. [[thm-chern-weil-forms-represent-the-at-characteristic-classes-over-the-reals]], [[def-chern-classes-from-the-projective-bundle-relation]]

proof_steps.claim: For any two supplied connections on the same $G$-reduction, [F4] makes their Chern–Weil classes equal, so integration over the fixed orientation class gives the same $q_B$. In the $SU(2)$ defining representation, the associated connection matrix is $A_i$ because $\rho_*$ is the identity inclusion, and its curvature matrix is $\Omega_i=F_i$ by [F2, F3]. Put $C=i\Omega_i/(2\pi)=-\Omega_i/(2\pi i)$. Its entries have even form degree and commute, so the degree-four coefficient of $\det(I+C)$ is $\det C=\tfrac12((\operatorname{tr}_2C)^2-\operatorname{tr}_2(C\wedge C))$. By [F5], $\operatorname{tr}_2C=0$, and $C\wedge C=-\Omega_i\wedge\Omega_i/(4\pi^2)$; hence $c_2(\nabla)=\operatorname{tr}_2(\Omega_i\wedge\Omega_i)/(8\pi^2)$ and $\beta_B=-c_2(\nabla)$ because $B=-\operatorname{tr}_2$. The associated connection is Hermitian by [F7], so [F6] sends this de Rham class to the negative realification of $c_2(E)\in H^4(X;\mathbb Z)$. Evaluating by [F8] on the orientation class gives $q_B=-\langle c_2(E),[X]\rangle\in\mathbb Z$. Full AC is used only through the stated characteristic-class comparison and integral-class construction.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F1] For a product $G$ of complex general linear groups, equivariant Borel–Moore homology is $\operatorname{Hom}(k_X,\omega_X^G[-j])$; its normalized dualizing object restricts to the ordinary one, and the groups agree in the stable range with dimension-shifted Borel approximations. The case $G=T=(\mathrm{GL}_1)^r$ applies. [[def-equivariant-borel-moore-homology-and-correspondence-convolution]]

proof_steps.claim: Since $T=(\mathrm{GL}_1)^r$, [F1] supplies the normalized equivariant Borel–Moore groups and the stable scalar-frame construction. For $U_m=(\mathbb C^{m+1}\setminus\{0\})^r$, the quotient is $B_m=(\mathbb{CP}^m)^r$ and $\dim_{\mathbb C}U_m-\dim_{\mathbb C}T=rm$, giving the stated degree shift. AC is inherited from [F1] and is the only choice assumption added here.

The polar decomposition $T\cong K\times(\mathbb R_{>0})^r$ makes $K\hookrightarrow T$ a homotopy equivalence. Choose one contractible free $T$-space $E$; it is also free for $K$, and $E/K\to E/T$ has contractible fiber $T/K$. The Borel fibrations $(E\times X)/K\to E/K$ and $(E\times X)/T\to E/T$ have common fiber $X$, with identity map on that fiber. Their homotopy exact sequences therefore make $(E\times X)/K\to(E\times X)/T$ a weak equivalence. Model independence of the universal free contractible space identifies this with the product right Milnor model and the algebraic-torus approximation in [F1].

The operations in the Definition are the proper pushforward, open restriction, and support maps of [F2]; the cap action is the action of Borel cohomology through $E_K\times_KX\to B_K$. For smooth pure complex dimension $d$, the normalized dualizing object restricts to $\mathbb Q_X[2d]$, so the complex orientation gives $[X]_T$ degree $2d$. proof_steps.claim: If \(r=0\), \(BT\) is a point and the CW and paracompact assertions reduce to the compact manifold \(F\). For \(r\geq1\), [F1] gives \(BT\) its ordinary product CW topology, and [F3] makes it paracompact Hausdorff. By [F2], choose a finite CW complex \(K\) and a homotopy equivalence \(h:F\to K\). Since \(K\) is finite, its CW product with the CW complex \(BT\) has the ordinary product topology; hence \(BT\times K\) is a CW complex. The maps \(\mathrm{id}_{BT}\times h\) and the product of a homotopy inverse with \(\mathrm{id}_{BT}\) are homotopy inverses, since their coordinate homotopies are continuous in the product topology. Thus \(BT\times F\) has CW type. If \(F=\varnothing\), take \(K=\varnothing\).

If \(F=\varnothing\), the product is empty and paracompact Hausdorff, so assume \(F\ne\varnothing\). To prove paracompactness of \(BT\times F\), let \(\mathcal U\) be an open cover. For each \(x\in BT\) and \(y\in F\), choose a product neighborhood \(O_{x,y}\times V_{x,y}\) of \((x,y)\) contained in some member \(U_{x,y}\in\mathcal U\). Compactness of \(F\) selects finitely many \(y_1,\ldots,y_m\) whose \(V_{x,y_j}\) cover \(F\). Then \(O_x=\bigcap_{j=1}^m O_{x,y_j}\) is an open neighborhood of \(x\), and \(O_x\times F\) is covered by \(U_{x,y_1},\ldots,U_{x,y_m}\). Paracompactness of \(BT\) gives a locally finite open refinement \(\{W_\alpha\}\) of \(\{O_x\}\). For each \(\alpha\), choose \(x_\alpha\) with \(W_\alpha\subseteq O_{x_\alpha}\); the finitely many sets \((W_\alpha\times F)\cap U_{x_\alpha,y_j}\) cover \(W_\alpha\times F\), are open, and refine \(\mathcal U\). They are locally finite because a neighborhood \(N\times F\) meets sets indexed by only those \(\alpha\) for which \(W_\alpha\) meets \(N\), a finite set. Hence \(BT\times F\) is paracompact. It is Hausdorff as a product of Hausdorff spaces. The point and rank-zero cases satisfy the same conclusions.

The map $\nabla:W\to S^2$ extends over the cone on $\beta$ by the definition $\beta=\nabla\alpha$; hence it extends to a map $q:S^2\times S^2=W\cup_\alpha D^4\to C_\beta$. On $W$, $q$ is the fold into the bottom $S^2$ of $C_\beta$, so $q^*x=a+b$. On the open $4$-cell, the extension is the characteristic disk of $C_\beta$ with degree $+1$ by [A1], so $q^*y=ab$.

Let $i:W\hookrightarrow S^2\times S^2$ be the $2$-skeleton inclusion. The characteristic disk extends $i\alpha$ over $D^4$, so $\Sigma i\circ\Sigma\alpha$ is null. Define
$$r=(\Sigma p_1\vee\Sigma p_2)\circ\operatorname{pinch}:\Sigma(S^2\times S^2)\longrightarrow\Sigma S^2\vee\Sigma S^2,$$
where $p_1,p_2$ are the projections and the pinch is [F3]. On the first suspended wedge summand, the first projection branch is the identity up to linear rescaling of the suspension coordinate and the second branch is constant; on the second summand the roles reverse. Thus $r\circ\Sigma i\simeq\operatorname{id}_{\Sigma W}$. Applying $r$ to the nullhomotopy in the first sentence gives $\Sigma\alpha\simeq *$. Composing with $\Sigma\nabla$ gives $\Sigma\beta\simeq *$. By the definition of the suspension homomorphism, this is $2[\Sigma h]=0$ because $[\beta]=2[h]$ from step 2.1 and [F1] identifies $[h]$ as the generator.

proof_steps.claim: The Hopf map is a locally trivial circle bundle: in the chart $z_0\ne0$ with $w=z_1/z_0$, the section is $(1,w)/\sqrt{1+|w|^2}$ and the fiber coordinate is $z_0/|z_0|$; use $(w,1)/\sqrt{1+|w|^2}$ and $z_1/|z_1|$ in the other chart. These formulas give continuous inverse bundle charts. Put $a_i([z])=|z_i|^2/(|z_0|^2+|z_1|^2)$, $b_i=\max(0,a_i-1/4)$ and $\rho_i=b_i/(b_0+b_1)$. At least one $a_i\ge1/2$, so the denominator is positive, and $\operatorname{supp}\rho_i\subseteq\{a_i\ge1/4\}\subseteq\{z_i\ne0\}$. This is a finite numeration with closed supports subordinate to the charts. By [F6] the Hopf bundle is Hurewicz and hence Serre. By [F1], $\pi_2(S^1)=\pi_3(S^1)=0$; the LES [F2] therefore makes $h_*:\pi_3(S^3)\to\pi_3(S^2)$ an isomorphism. By [F3] its source is generated by the identity, so $[h]$ generates $\pi_3(S^2)\cong\mathbb Z$.

The coefficient $H(f)$ is invariant under a based homotopy $H_t$ of attaching maps. A comparison $C_{f_0}\to C_{f_1}$ is the identity on $S^2$; on a cone point $[x,t]$ it equals $H_{2t}(x)$ for $0\le t\le1/2$ and the target cone point $[x,2t-1]$ for $1/2\le t\le1$. The formulas agree at the seam, respect the tip, and are continuous by quotient descent. Reversing the homotopy gives its homotopy inverse: the composites insert a path followed by its reverse, which contracts by shrinking its traversed homotopy parameter, and then a linear cone reparametrization removes the constant collar. Both maps restrict to the identity on the bottom sphere and have relative top-cell degree $+1$, so cup-product naturality preserves $H$. Since step 1.1 identifies every homotopy class with $[h\circ d_m]$ for a unique integer $m$, step 2.1 implies that any attachment with $H(f)=m$ has class $m[h]$.

Induct on $N\ge3$. The base sphere $S^{2N-1}$ has dimension at least five, so [F3] makes its homotopy groups in degrees $1,2,3,4$ zero. Exactness [F2] at degrees one and two therefore gives $\pi_1(SU(N-1))\cong\pi_1(SU(N))$ and $\pi_2(SU(N-1))\cong\pi_2(SU(N))$; at degree three it gives $\pi_3(SU(N-1))\cong\pi_3(SU(N))$. The component exact sequence and the connected fiber and base show $SU(N)$ is path connected: the map on components is onto, and its kernel is the image of the one-point component set of the fiber. Starting from [step 1.1], induction gives all three displayed low groups and connectedness for every $N$.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F1] [[lem-qftx-round-s4-spin-twist-index-one]] gives the explicit quaternionic Clifford model, parallel chirality, unitary spin-twist connections, chiral kernel dimension one and cokernel zero, and selfadjoint full Dirac domain $H^1$.

proof_steps.claim: For any given spin four-manifold the local quaternionic model glues by its specified Spin(4) lift. In that quaternionic spin model, right multiplication by a quaternionic unit $j$ is an antiunitary map $J_0$ on $S^+\oplus S^-$, with $J_0^2=-1$. It commutes with the four Clifford matrices and $\Gamma$ and is parallel: the transition and connection matrices act from the left and hence commute with right multiplication. The same operation $J_E$ on the $SU(2)$ twist is parallel, antiunitary and has square $-1$. Define $J_5=\Gamma J_0$ on the spin factor. Then $J_5^2=-1$, it anticommutes with each of the four tangent Clifford matrices, and it anticommutes with $c_5=i\Gamma$ because anti-linearity changes $i$ to $-i$. Thus it is the pseudoreal Spin(5) structure, since even products of Clifford matrices commute with it. On the complex tensor product set $J=J_5\otimes J_E$; it is well-defined and antiunitary, $J^2=1$, and $JD_5=-D_5J$. Hence $J$ preserves the kernel and $iD_5$ commutes with $J$.

Chirality anticommutes with $D_4$ and is parallel, so $D_5^2=D_4^2-\partial_t^2$. It has scalar positive principal symbol and smooth coefficients. Formal symmetry follows from unitary connection compatibility and periodic integration by parts. The same shifted-resolvent argument applies to $D_4$ and $D_5$ on a general compact background: each square has scalar positive principal symbol, and [F2] gives the inverse of its positive shift from $L^2$ to $H^2$; multiplying by $D_j\mp i$ gives surjectivity of $D_j\pm i$ and the $H^1$ selfadjoint domain exactly as in [F1]. An $L^2$ weak chiral cokernel vector also has square zero distributionally; testing against smooth sections and using their $H^2$ density puts it in the adjoint domain of the selfadjoint square, hence in $H^2$, and [F2] then makes it smooth. This justifies identifying the cokernel with the negative-chirality kernel. Weak kernels are smooth by the same argument. For a zero mode $\psi$, integration by parts gives $0=\|D_5\psi\|^2=\|D_4\psi\|^2+\|\partial_t\psi\|^2$. Thus $\psi$ is independent of $t$ and lies in $\ker D_4$; conversely every such spinor gives a periodic product zero mode. In general its complex dimension is $n_++n_-$, identifying the smooth negative-chirality kernel with the cokernel by the formal $L^2$ adjoint. For the concrete round twist this dimension is $1$ by [F1]. This avoids any unproved general spectral-flow identity.

The constant central automorphism acts by $-1$ on both chiral spinor kernels and cokernels, and fixes the background connection. Its scalar on the inverse determinant line is $(-1)^{-n_+}(-1)^{n_-}=(-1)^{n_+-n_-}$. For the actual round twist [F1] gives dimensions one and zero, hence scalar $-1$. Parallel transport along a constant path is the identity for any connection. Closing by the inverse endpoint identification gives $z_*^{-1}\circ\mathrm{PT}=-1$; tensor powers give $(-1)^N$. This is an actual finite-dimensional exterior-power action, not an assumption equating a periodic eta invariant with holonomy.

For any finite-dimensional complex vector space $V$ with anti-linear involution $J$, every $v$ has the unique decomposition $v=(v+Jv)/2+i(v-Jv)/(2i)$ with both displayed real components fixed by $J$. Thus $V=V^J\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C$ and $\dim_{\mathbb R}V^J=\dim_{\mathbb C}V$. Apply this to $V=\ker D_5$ using steps 1.1–1.2. The restriction of $iD_5$ is real and skew-adjoint, because $D_5$ is selfadjoint and $J(iD_5)=(iD_5)J$. Its real kernel has dimension $n_++n_-$. This has the same parity as $n_+-n_-$, since their difference is $2n_-$. For the concrete round twist the real dimension and parity are one by [F1].

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] For any smooth unitary ASD rank-two bundle on the specified sphere, the determinant connection is flat. This lemma is proved independently of inverse ADHM or projective GAGA. [[lem-qftx-u-n-determinant-flat-charge-normalization]]

proof_steps.claim: Stabilize a rank-one raw datum by $W'=\mathbb C\oplus\mathbb C$, $I'=(I,0)$ and $J'=(J,0)^t$, retaining $V,B_1,B_2$. Then $I'J'=IJ$, $I'I'^\dagger=II^\dagger$ and $J'^\dagger J'=J^\dagger J$. The word span is unchanged and $\ker J'=\ker J$, so both moments and regularity are unchanged. On the finite stereographic chart the raw kernel matrix annihilates the added framing line, and its orthogonal projection is $P_1\oplus1$. Thus [A1] produces a smooth rank-two ASD connection whose restriction to that chart is a line connection plus the flat added line and whose charge is $q_2=-k$. By [F2] its determinant curvature vanishes. On that chart this curvature is exactly the first line's curvature, so the whole rank-two curvature is zero there. Smoothness makes it zero also at infinity, hence $q_2=0$ and $k=0$. Thus no regular rank-one zero-FI datum exists for $k>0$, conditional on the exact retained rank-two input. By [F6], a regular complex rank-one orbit would have such a zero-real-moment representative, so the same emptiness conclusion applies to the complex regular quotient.

Independently, stabilize any framed unitary ASD line connection by the trivial framed flat line. The result is a smooth unitary ASD rank-two connection. final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F3] A closed subset and its open complement give the equivariant Borel–Moore long exact sequence through support localization. [[thm-constructible-six-functors-proper-base-change-and-verdier-duality]]

proof_steps.claim: The closed/open localization sequence for $i:F\hookrightarrow X$ and $X\setminus F$ contains $S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_{j+1}(X\setminus F)\to S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(F)\xrightarrow{i_*}S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(X)\to S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(X\setminus F)$. Both outside groups vanish by step 3.1, so $i_*$ is an isomorphism. If $F=\varnothing$, the same argument gives zero localized Borel–Moore homology for $X$; if $F=X$, $i_*$ is the identity. The proof used only the finite invariant affine cover and not Sumihiro's theorem or compactness.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F4] Framed unitary ASD determinant reduction and the exact trace Chern-Weil normalization give q_N=-c₂[S⁴]. [[lem-qftx-u-n-determinant-flat-charge-normalization]]

proof_steps.claim: The explicit incidence chart fixes vertical complex orientation followed by the positive base orientation to be the complex orientation of Z. The pullback of the positive point Thom class on S⁴ is the positive normal Thom class of its fiber CP¹; [F5] identifies its absolute class as the Poincaré dual of that fiber. A linear CP¹ has dual H²: H restricts with integral one to the line, and the integral projective cohomology ring gives H² as its positive degree-four generator. Hence π*u=H² for the positive generator u of H⁴(S⁴). Smooth evaluation gives E_twistor≅π*H, so c₂(E_twistor)=kH² is equivalent to c₂(H)[S⁴]=k. By [F4] this is q_N=-k; the same calculation verifies the forward map's charge clause. Framing is transported by evaluation at infinity. All constructions use incidence, evaluation and unique relative connections, so commute with the specified projective rotations and framing transformations. They therefore give the claimed T-equivariant bijection and all stated invariants, conditional on the exact absolute GAGA comparison [A1].

final_edge_fact_uses.text:
[F7] The finite algebraic resolution gives
$\operatorname{ch}(F)=N-kH^2$, $c_1(F)=0$, $c_2(F)=kH^2$,
$\chi(F)=N-2k$; its line cycle class is the topological hyperplane class, and
the positive incidence fiber calculation gives $\pi^*u=H^2$.
[[lem-qftx-positive-real-monad-charge-normalization]]

proof_steps.claim: The finite monad resolution and its locally free cohomology give the algebraic Chern character and Chern classes in [F7]. Its same finite line resolution yields the topological classes after the hyperplane cycle class is identified with the Euler class of the complex normal line. The positive incidence-fiber Thom calculation in [F7] gives $\pi^*u=H_{\rm top}^2$. If the topological bundle is $\pi^*E$, naturality gives $\pi^*c_2(E)=kH_{\rm top}^2=k\pi^*u$; since $\pi^*u$ is a generator, $c_2(E)=ku$. This is conditional on the pullback hypothesis and asserts no Ward correspondence.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [A1] AC is inherited through the equivariant Borel–Moore and Thom suppliers. [[def-qftx-proper-fixed-locus-localized-pushforward]] [[lem-qftx-fixed-embedding-bm-euler-self-intersection]]

proof_steps.claim: The map $i:F\hookrightarrow X$, its components $i_a$, and the localized groups are intrinsic; the finite affine cover is only a hypothesis used to prove [F2]. Since $i_*$ is the same canonical proper pushforward for every such cover, its inverse is unique. Therefore the definition $p_*^{\mathrm{loc}}=p_{F*}(i_*)^{-1}$ is independent of the cover.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F3] The fixed locus is smooth, its normal weights are nontrivial, the complex-oriented Gysin map satisfies $i_a^!i_{a*}\beta=e_T(\nu_a)\cap\beta$, and $e_T(\nu_a)$ is a unit after localization when $F_a$ is proper. [[lem-qftx-fixed-embedding-bm-euler-self-intersection]]

proof_steps.claim:
Let $ eta=(i_*)^{-1}(\alpha\cap[X]_T)$. On each component, the complex orientation and refined Gysin map give $i_a^!(\alpha\cap[X]_T)=i_a^*\alpha\cap[F_a]_T$. Since $\alpha\cap[X]_T=i_* eta$, the self-intersection formula [F3] gives $e_T(
u_a)\cap eta_a=i_a^*\alpha\cap[F_a]_T$. Properness of $F_a$ makes $e_T(
u_a)$ invertible after localization by [F3], hence $ eta_a=(i_a^*\alpha/e_T(
u_a))\cap[F_a]_T$. Applying $p_{a*}$ and summing the finitely many components yields the displayed formula. The degree is $2d-q$: division by the degree-$2c_a$ Euler class lowers the localized cohomological degree of the insertion from $q$ to $q-2c_a$, and capping with the degree-$2d_a$ fundamental class gives $2d_a-(q-2c_a)=2d-q$.

If $F=\varnothing$, [F2] makes the localized Borel–Moore groups of $X$ zero and the component sum is empty. If $F$ is finite, every $F_a$ is a point and $e_T(\nu_a)$ is the product of its nonzero tangent-character classes, so each summand is the stated reciprocal-Euler term. If $c_a=0$, the normal bundle is rank zero and its complex-oriented Euler class is $1$. These cases agree with the formula and the degree computation above.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F4] $SU(N)$ is path connected, $\pi_1(SU(N))=\pi_2(SU(N))=0$, and $\pi_3(SU(N))\cong\mathbb Z$. [[lem-qftx-low-unitary-homotopy-inputs]]

proof_steps.claim:
Suppose $r=3$. By [F3, F4], $\pi_0(\mathcal G_m(P))\cong\pi_3(SU(N))\cong\mathbb Z$. The evaluation LES [F2, F6] has the component segment
$$\pi_1(SU(N))\longrightarrow\pi_0(\mathcal G_m(P))\longrightarrow\pi_0(\mathcal G(P))\longrightarrow\pi_0(SU(N)).$$
The outer terms are one-point sets by [F4]. The induced map on components is surjective by exactness, and its fibers are the orbits of $\pi_1(SU(N))$ on $\pi_0(\mathcal G_m(P))$ in the action clause of [F6]. That acting group is trivial, so each fiber is a singleton and the middle map is a bijection. Thus $\mathcal G(P)$ has infinitely many components. Since $\mathcal G(P)\to\overline{\mathcal G}(P)$ is a covering with $N$ sheets, components downstairs correspond to orbits of the finite deck group on components upstairs: a path downstairs lifts by [F7] to a path whose endpoint differs from its starting lift by one deck transformation, and each deck orbit is therefore one quotient component. Each orbit has at most $N$ elements, so infinitely many components remain.

Suppose $r=4$. By [F3] and [F5], $\pi_1(\mathcal G_m(P))\cong\pi_5(SU(N))\ne0$. In the evaluation LES, the map $\pi_1(\mathcal G_m(P))\to\pi_1(\mathcal G(P))$ has preceding term $\pi_2(SU(N))=0$ by [F4]; exactness makes it injective. The finite covering in [F2] induces an injection $\pi_1(\mathcal G(P))\hookrightarrow\pi_1(\overline{\mathcal G}(P))$ by [F6]. Hence $\pi_1(\overline{\mathcal G}(P))$ contains a nonzero subgroup. The two cases establish the statement for every $r,N,P$.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F5] For every $N\ge2$ and every bundle on $S^3$, the reduced smooth gauge group has infinitely many path components; for every bundle on $S^4$, its fundamental group at the identity is nontrivial. [[thm-qftx-reduced-gauge-group-sphere-nontriviality]]

proof_steps.claim: Suppose $q_*$ had a continuous section. Apply [F6] to the nonempty principal bundle in step 2.1. Its structure group $\overline{\mathcal G}^\infty(P)$ would be path connected and have $\pi_j=0$ for every $j\ge1$. If $r=3$, this contradicts the infinitely many components in [F5]. If $r=4$, it contradicts the nonzero fundamental group in [F5]. Thus $q_*$ has no continuous section.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F1] The global charge form is $\beta_B=\frac{1}{8\pi^2}B(F\wedge F)$, and $q_B=\int_X\beta_B$; the Hodge star and the self-dual/ASD decomposition are those fixed by the orientation and metric. [[def-qftx-instanton-number-and-asd-sector]]

proof_steps.claim: Write $F_i=F_i^++F_i^-$ with $*_{g_X}F_i^+=F_i^+$ and $*_{g_X}F_i^-=-F_i^-$. Let $a=\int_X B(F_i^+\wedge *_{g_X}F_i^+)$ and $b=\int_X B(F_i^-\wedge *_{g_X}F_i^-)$. Orthogonality of the two Hodge eigenspaces [F3] makes the cross terms vanish; positivity of $B$ [F2] gives $a,b\geq0$. Consequently $\int_XB(F_i\wedge *_{g_X}F_i)=a+b$, while $\int_XB(F_i\wedge F_i)=a-b$. By [F1], $S_B=(a+b)/g^2$ and $q_B=(a-b)/(8\pi^2)$.

For nonnegative $a,b$, $a+b\geq|a-b|$, so the claimed bound follows after division by $g^2>0$. If $q_B>0$, then $a>b$ and equality is equivalent to $b=0$. Its integrand is the continuous nonnegative squared norm of $F_i^-$; if $F_i^-$ were nonzero at a point, it would be bounded away from zero on a neighborhood of positive Riemannian volume, contradicting $b=0$. Thus $F_i^-=0$. If $q_B<0$, equality in $a+b\geq b-a$ is equivalent to $a=0$; the same continuity and positivity argument gives $F_i^+=0$. If $q_B=0$, equality forces $a+b=0$, so nonnegativity gives $a=b=0$ and both components vanish, hence $F_i=0$. Conversely each of the three stated conditions makes its corresponding norm vanish and gives equality.
