proof_steps.claim: We record a partition construction. Let $Z$ be a reduced separated complex algebraic variety of finite type and let $\mathcal C$ be a finite list of closed subsets of $Z$. There is a finite partition of $Z$ into irreducible smooth locally closed strata such that every member of $\mathcal C$ is a union of strata and every stratum is open dense in its own irreducible closure. If $Z=\varnothing$ take the empty partition. Otherwise let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_m$ be the irreducible components of $Z$, finitely many by [F1]. Remove from $Z_i$ its nonsmooth locus, the other components $Z_j$, and every $C\cap Z_i$ with $C\in\mathcal C$ and $C\nsupseteq Z_i$. Each removed set is closed, and each is proper in the irreducible $Z_i$; by [F3] and [F2] the nonsmooth locus has smaller dimension, and by [F2] the other removed sets do too, so the result $U_i$ is a nonempty dense open subset of $Z_i$ and is contained in or disjoint from every $C\in\mathcal C$. The $U_i$ are pairwise disjoint and open in $Z$, because their complement is the finite union of the removed closed sets and the sets $Z_j$ with $j\ne i$. The remainder $Z':=Z\setminus\bigcup_iU_i$ is closed and meets each $Z_i$ in a proper closed subset, so $\dim Z'<\dim Z$ by [F2]. Partition $Z'$ by the same construction with $\mathcal C$ replaced by the restrictions of all members of $\mathcal C$ and of all $Z_i$ to $Z'$, and iterate. The dimension of the remainder strictly decreases at every round, so the recursion terminates; because each round respects the restricted lists, every member of $\mathcal C$ is a union of strata and every stratum is open dense in its irreducible closure. The closure of a stratum emitted in a recursion round is a component of that round's closed remainder; it meets no earlier stratum and no other stratum emitted in that round, and the added component restrictions make it a union of subsequent strata. Thus this partition also has the frontier property.

Now construct the target strata in rounds on a closed residual subvariety $R\subseteq Y$, starting with $R=Y$; at each stage keep finite lists of prescribed closed subsets of $R$ and of $f^{-1}(R)$, initially the given lists and later those lists enlarged by the restrictions of the closures of all previously emitted strata. Apply step 1.1 to $f^{-1}(R)$ with the maintained source list, obtaining a finite partition into irreducible smooth locally closed strata $Z_\alpha$. Fix an irreducible component $R_i$ of $R$ and remove from it its nonsmooth locus, the other components of $R$, and every maintained target prescribed closed subset not containing $R_i$; by [F1] this leaves a nonempty dense open subset $V_i^0\subseteq R_i$. For each $\alpha$ the image $f(Z_\alpha)$ is irreducible and lies in a component of $R$, so its closure in $R$ is an irreducible closed subset of some component. If that closure is not $R_i$, then its intersection with $R_i$ is a proper closed subset, and we remove it from $V_i^0$; if the closure equals $R_i$, then $f|_{Z_\alpha}$ is dominant, $Z_\alpha$ is smooth and irreducible, and [F4] supplies a dense open subset of $R_i$ over which $Z_\alpha\to R_i$ is smooth, with nonempty fibres over the closed points after shrinking to lie in the image. There are finitely many $\alpha$, so intersecting $V_i^0$ with all the supplied dense opens contained in the images produces a nonempty dense open $V_i\subseteq R_i$ such that every $Z_\alpha$ whose image closure is not $R_i$ has no point over $V_i$, while every $Z_\alpha$ whose image closure is $R_i$ maps smoothly and onto $V_i$.

Finally let $S\to T$ be one emitted restriction onto a target stratum. Zero-dimensional smooth strata are locally single points: they are zero-dimensional Noetherian varieties, hence finite sets of closed points, so their analytic charts and maps to a zero-dimensional target require no implicit-function or constant-rank theorem. A standard smooth presentation with no equations already gives open coordinate charts. In the remaining positive-dimensional cases, the stratum $S$ is a smooth complex variety by construction, so by [F3] it is locally standard smooth over $\mathbb C$; the defining equations of a standard smooth presentation near a point have an invertible Jacobian minor, and [F5] turns them into holomorphic charts of $S$ near that point, with holomorphic transition maps. Similarly $T$ carries holomorphic charts. The map $S\to T$ is a morphism of classical varieties, so in these charts its components are restrictions of regular functions on affine charts, hence locally polynomial quotients with nonvanishing denominators in the ambient coordinates and therefore holomorphic in the chart parameters. At every point the differential of $S\to T$ is surjective by the smoothness of the restriction and the criterion of [F5]; since surjectivity onto a target of dimension $n$ is the nonvanishing of some $n\times n$ minor, the rank stays full on a neighbourhood, and the holomorphic constant rank theorem exhibits the map near each point as a linear projection in suitable holomorphic coordinates. Hence the restriction is a submersion of complex manifolds, in particular a submersion of the underlying real smooth manifolds. No properness or topological triviality is used, and AC is inherited exactly through the cited suppliers.

fact_uses.text: [F5] For $X=\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb C[t_1,\ldots,t_m]/I)$ the tangent space at a $\mathbb C$-point is the kernel of the Jacobian of any finite generating list of $I$ ([[thm-zariski-tangent-space-jacobian-kernel]]); Grassmannian matrix charts and their transition maps are algebraic regular maps ([[lem-grassmannian-standard-affine-charts]]). A smooth complex algebraic variety is locally standard smooth, so it admits near each point a standard smooth presentation with $n\ge c\ge0$ whose defining equations have an invertible Jacobian minor and the holomorphic implicit function theorem exhibits the variety as a holomorphic graph over its tangent coordinates ([[def-ag-standard-smooth-algebra]], [[thm-holomorphic-implicit-function-theorem]], [[thm-regular-equals-smooth-over-perfect-field]]); consequently the algebraic tangent plane of that graph is also the analytic tangent space, and the derivative of any holomorphic arc lying in the variety lies in it.

proof_steps.claim: Put $d=\dim S$ and let $G$ be the graph of the map $(x,y)\mapsto(T_xS,[x-y])$ from $S\times Y$ to $\operatorname{Gr}(d,n)\times\mathbb P^{n-1}$; it is algebraic by [F5], because on chart domains the tangent plane is the kernel of the Jacobian matrix of local equations, whose basis entries are regular ratios on each fixed nonzero-minor chart and the secant coordinates are regular since $x\ne y$. Let $Z$ be the reduced closure of $G$ in $\overline S\times Y\times\operatorname{Gr}(d,n)\times\mathbb P^{n-1}$. The graph $G$ is isomorphic to $S\times Y$, hence irreducible by [F6], and $\overline S$, $Y$, $\operatorname{Gr}(d,n)$ and $\mathbb P^{n-1}$ are irreducible; the ambient product is therefore irreducible by [F6], and its closed subset $Z$, the closure of the irreducible $G$, is irreducible as well. Let $B=Z\setminus G$, a proper closed subset, and let $g:Z\to Y$ be the projection; it is dominant because it is onto on $G$.

Let $p_0$ be a complex covector annihilating the complex plane $T$. In a Grassmannian matrix chart around $T$ write $T(s)$ as the graph of a holomorphic matrix $A(s)$ with $A(0)=A_0$, possible for small $s$ because $T(s)\to T$; every annihilator of the graph of $A(s)$ has the form $q(s)=(-A(s)^tb,b)$ for $b\in(\mathbb C^{n-d})^*$, and $b$ can be chosen with $(-A_0^tb,b)=p_0$ because $p_0$ annihilates $T$. The resulting $q(s)$ is holomorphic and annihilates each $T(s)$. Since $x(s)\in S$ for $s\ne0$, its derivative lies in $T_{x(s)}S=T(s)$ by [F5], so $q(s)(x'(s))=0$ for $s\ne0$. Differentiating $x(s)-y=s^mv(s)$ gives $x'(s)=s^{m-1}(mv(s)+sv'(s))$, and dividing by $s^{m-1}$ and letting $s\to0$ yields $p_0(mv(0))=0$, hence $p_0(v(0))=0$. Every annihilator of $T$ therefore kills $v(0)$, so $v(0)\in T$ and the limiting complex secant line $[u]$ lies in $T$.

fact_uses.text: [F2] Over a perfect field, reduced finite-type varieties have regular points, regularity equals smoothness, and the smooth locus is open. Geometric regularity descends from field extension, and nonempty finite-type schemes over an algebraically closed field have rational closed points. ([[thm-nonempty-regular-locus-reduced-variety-perfect-field]], [[thm-regular-equals-smooth-over-perfect-field]], [[thm-smooth-locus-open]], [[lem-ag-geometric-regularity-field-tests]], [[cor-weak-nullstellensatz-algebraically-closed-coordinate-form]])

proof_steps.claim: If a finite-type group is geometrically reduced, over $\bar k$ its reduced group has a smooth point by [F2]. Translate that point to the identity and then to every rational closed point. All closed points are smooth. The nonsmooth locus is closed and, if nonempty, has a closed point by [F2], so it is empty. By geometric-regularity descent in [F2], the group is smooth over $k$. This proof does not assume affineness. For the reduction of an arbitrary group over $\bar k$, multiplication and inverse restrict to it: the pullback of a nilpotent ideal vanishes on a reduced source, and products of reduced finite-type schemes over the perfect field are reduced. Thus its reduction is again a group to which the same argument applies.

If $G$ is smooth and connected, its geometric base extension is smooth, reduced, and connected by step 1.1. At a smooth point the local ring is a regular domain, so two different irreducible components cannot meet. The finitely many components are open and closed, and connectedness leaves one; hence the geometric scheme is integral. This proves geometric integrality. AC is inherited from [F1]–[F2].

fact_uses.text: [F9] A nonempty reduced finite-type scheme over a perfect field has a nonempty open regular locus, and regularity is equivalent to smoothness over a perfect field; the smooth locus of a locally finitely presented morphism is open ([[thm-nonempty-regular-locus-reduced-variety-perfect-field]], [[thm-regular-equals-smooth-over-perfect-field]], [[thm-smooth-locus-open]]). The classical and scheme smoothness conventions agree by [[cor-smooth-variety-classical-scheme-conventions-agree]].

proof_steps.claim: The subscheme $O_K$ is smooth over $K$: it is reduced by step 3.1 and finite type over the perfect field $K$; by [F9] its regular locus is a nonempty open subset, regularity equals smoothness over $K$, and the smooth locus $\mathrm{Sm}$ is a nonempty open subset stable under the $K$-automorphisms $g\in G(K)$. Since every $K$-point of $O_K$ is of the form $g\cdot x_K$ (the fibre over a $K$-point of $O_K$ is a nonempty finite-type $K$-scheme, hence has a $K$-point by [F6]), and since a nonempty open subset of a finite-type $K$-scheme contains a $K$-point by [F6], $\mathrm{Sm}$ meets $G(K)\cdot x_K$; then $x_K\in\mathrm{Sm}$ and all $K$-points of $O_K$ lie in $\mathrm{Sm}$. The closed complement $O_K\setminus\mathrm{Sm}$, if nonempty, would contain a closed $K$-point by [F6], contradicting the preceding conclusion. Thus $\mathrm{Sm}=O_K$.

fact_uses.text: [F2] Finite smooth frontier partitions respecting finite families of closed subsets exist by the dimension-decreasing construction of [[lem-complex-algebraic-morphisms-admit-compatible-finite-smooth-stratifications]], whose source-partition proof uses the finite component decomposition, the strict dimension drop of proper closed subvarieties and the density of the regular locus ([[lem-classical-variety-noetherian-components]], [[lem-dimension-nonempty-open-subset]], [[thm-nonempty-regular-locus-reduced-variety-perfect-field]], [[thm-regular-equals-smooth-over-perfect-field]]).

proof_steps.claim: Replace every prescribed locally closed subset $A$ by the two prescribed closed subsets $\overline A$ and $\overline A\setminus A$; their difference recovers $A$, and it suffices to respect the resulting finite list of closed subsets. Refine the smooth-partition construction of [F2] to construct, for a closed residual variety $R$ together with a finite list of prescribed closed subsets and finitely many previously fixed smooth strata outside $R$ whose closures must be respected, a Whitney partition of $R$ compatible with all of them: take the irreducible components $R_i$ of $R$, remove their nonsmooth loci and their intersections with the other components, and remove every prescribed closed subset not containing $R_i$, obtaining dense smooth opens $L_i$; then for every previously fixed upper stratum $S$, remove $R_i\cap\overline S$ when $R_i\not\subseteq\overline S$, and when $R_i\subseteq\overline S$ use [F3] to remove the closure in $R_i$ of the exceptional subset of [F3], which is proper because it has dimension smaller than $\dim R_i$. Finitely many upper strata leave nonempty dense smooth opens $U_i\subseteq R_i$, and [F3] makes each $U_i$ Whitney-regular with every incident previously fixed upper stratum.

Emit the $U_i$ as strata, add their closures $R_i$ to the list of closed subsets to be respected, and recurse on the closed complement $R\setminus\bigcup_iU_i$, whose dimension drops because every component lost a dense open subset. The recursion terminates by induction on dimension, producing a finite partition of $R$ into smooth irreducible locally closed strata. Strata of the same round have no frontier relation, since each $U_i$ misses all other components $R_j$. Every pair of incident strata has its upper stratum emitted earlier, and when the lower stratum was emitted step 1.1 imposed Whitney (a) and (b) with that upper stratum; boundaries have strictly smaller dimension by [F2]. The respected closures make every stratum closure a union of strata. In a quasi-projective ambient space, cover it by finitely many affine coordinate charts and apply the affine-chart version of [F3]; a sequence in $R$ converging to a point meets only finitely many components of the chart intersections, so passing to a subsequence in one component reduces the conditions to the chart version. Thus Whitney partitions compatible with a finite list of closed sets and with fixed external upper strata exist.

Construct the map-compatible partitions by decreasing target residual dimension. Start with target residual $R=Y$ and source residual $f^{-1}(R)=X$, and at each later round maintain the original closed-set lists together with the closures of all previously emitted source and target strata. Partition the source residual $f^{-1}(R)$ by step 2.1, so that it is Whitney-compatible with all previously emitted source strata. For each irreducible component $R_i$ of $R$, choose a dense smooth open $L_i\subseteq R_i$ as in step 1.1, respecting the target prescriptions and Whitney-regular with all previously emitted target strata. For every new source stratum $Z_\alpha$ compute the closure of its image in $R$; if that closure is not $R_i$, remove its intersection with $R_i$, a proper closed subset; if the closure is $R_i$, then $Z_\alpha\to R_i$ is dominant and [F4] supplies a dense open subset of $R_i$ on which the restriction is smooth and onto. Intersecting the finitely many resulting dense opens with $L_i$ gives a nonempty dense open $V_i\subseteq R_i$.

Emit the $V_i$ as target strata and the nonempty pieces $Z_\alpha\cap f^{-1}(V_i)$ as source strata. Each such piece is open in the smooth irreducible stratum $Z_\alpha$, hence smooth irreducible and locally closed, and it is Whitney-regular with every incident previously fixed upper source stratum, because Whitney conditions are local and were imposed on all of $Z_\alpha$ in step 2.1; with the pieces of the same round it has no frontier relation except through closures, which the later rounds make unions of strata because every closure is added to the respected list. Each piece maps smoothly and onto $V_i$ by its selection in step 3.1, and target strata are Whitney-regular with earlier target strata since $V_i\subseteq L_i$. Source frontier relations inside $f^{-1}(\bigcup_iV_i)$ are inherited from the source partition, and a stratum closure over $R_i$ misses every $V_j$ with $j\ne i$.

Remove $\bigcup_iV_i$ from $R$, restrict both residuals and both lists, add all newly emitted stratum closures to the respective lists, and repeat. The target dimension strictly decreases each round, so after finitely many rounds every target point and every source point has been placed: a source point lies over one emitted target stratum and is contained in one emitted piece. Future source partitions are chosen Whitney-compatible with every earlier source stratum by step 2.1, and future target opens are chosen Whitney-compatible with earlier target strata in step 3.1, so every incident pair is covered; the closure-bookkeeping makes all stratum closures unions of strata. Each emitted piece is irreducible and nonempty, so [F7] makes it analytically connected and identifies its analytic closure with the algebraic closure tracked by the construction. This yields finite smooth Whitney frontier stratifications of $X$ and $Y$, respecting all prescribed subsets (including the strata of any prescribed finite algebraic stratification, which were treated as prescribed sets in step 1.1), with each source stratum mapping smoothly and surjectively onto one target stratum.

fact_uses.text:
[F14] [[thm-regular-equals-smooth-over-perfect-field]]: under AC, for a perfect
field $k$ and a finite-type $k$-scheme $X$, $X$ is regular (every local ring
$\mathcal O_{X,x}$ is regular local) if and only if $X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$
is smooth in the local-standard-smooth sense.

proof_steps.claim: Setup and conventions. By [F2] the classical varieties $X$ and $Y$ are quasi-compact locally ringed spaces over $k$ covered by affine models, every point of either is a closed point with residue field $k$, polynomial principal opens form a basis of the topology, and their structure sheaves are sheaves of $k$-valued functions; by [F27] the irreducible classical varieties $X$ and $Y$ correspond to integral, hence reduced, finite-type $k$-schemes and $f$ to a $k$-morphism of those schemes; they are Noetherian by [F6]. Write $m=\dim X$ and $n=\dim Y$ [F7]. The field $k$ is perfect by [F13], and by hypothesis the structure morphism $X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is smooth [F3], so [F14] makes $X$ regular. Every $k$-morphism of finite-type $k$-schemes is of finite type: on affine charts $\operatorname{Spec}A\subseteq Y$ and $\operatorname{Spec}B\subseteq X$ with $f(\operatorname{Spec}B)\subseteq\operatorname{Spec}A$, the algebra $B$ is generated as an $A$-algebra by finitely many $k$-algebra generators [F4], so $f$ is locally of finite type [F5], and it is quasi-compact because $X$ is Noetherian, so that every open subset of $X$ is quasi-compact [F5, F6]; the same argument applies to the restriction of $f$ to any open subvariety of $X$.

The dominant case: reduction to the regular locus of the target. Suppose now that $f$ is dominant. The regular locus $Y_{\mathrm{reg}}$ [F12] of $Y$, a reduced finite-type $k$-scheme over the perfect field $k$ [F27], is a nonempty open subset of $Y$ whose intersection with every irreducible component of $Y$ is dense open in that component [F11]; since $Y$ is irreducible, $Y_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is nonempty, open and dense, hence irreducible [F9], and $\dim Y_{\mathrm{reg}}=\dim Y=n$ [F8]. At every $y\in Y_{\mathrm{reg}}$ the local ring $\mathcal O_{Y_{\mathrm{reg}},y}\cong\mathcal O_{Y,y}$ is regular [F12, F15, F16], and $Y_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is of finite type over the perfect field $k$ [F2, F13], so $Y_{\mathrm{reg}}\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is smooth by [F14]. The open subvariety $Y_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is itself a classical variety over $k$: it is quasi-compact because $Y$ is Noetherian [F6], and its intersections with the affine models of $Y$ are covered by principal opens, which are affine models by [F17]. Similarly $X_0:=f^{-1}(Y_{\mathrm{reg}})$ is an open subvariety of $X$, hence a classical variety over $k$, it is nonempty because the dense subset $f(X)$ meets the nonempty open set $Y_{\mathrm{reg}}$ [F9, F10], it is irreducible with $\dim X_0=\dim X=m$ [F8, F9], and its structure morphism $X_0\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is smooth by locality on the source [F3]. The restriction $f_0:=f|_{X_0}\colon X_0\to Y_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is a finite-type morphism of classical varieties: on affine charts $\operatorname{Spec}A\subseteq Y_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and $\operatorname{Spec}B\subseteq X_0$ with $f_0(\operatorname{Spec}B)\subseteq\operatorname{Spec}A$ the algebra $B$ is generated as an $A$-algebra by finitely many $k$-algebra generators [F4, F5], and $f_0$ is quasi-compact because $X_0$ is Noetherian, so that every open subset of $X_0$ is quasi-compact [F5, F6].

Boundary and scope dispositions. Empty: in the non-dominant case $f^{-1}(U)=\varnothing$ and the empty morphism $\varnothing\to U$ is smooth vacuously (step 1.2); in the dominant case $X$ and $Y$ are nonempty because irreducible [F9], the open sets $Y_{\mathrm{reg}}$, $U$ and $V$ are nonempty by steps 1.3, 2.1 and 5.1, and the fibres over $V$ are nonempty by step 5.1, so no empty-fibre convention is invoked in claim 2. Zero: the target dimension $n=0$ is admitted; then $C=Z=\varnothing$, $U=Y_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and the rank computation of step 3.1 reads $0\le\operatorname{rank}d_xf_0\le 0$, while the fibre clause gives a single fibre of pure dimension $r=m$; the relative dimension $r=0$ is likewise admitted in step 5.1, where smooth fibres of pure dimension zero are finite reduced $k$-schemes, and nothing in the argument divides by $r$. One: no step divides by a natural number, selects a basis, or requires a positive dimension, codimension, or number of equations; the cases $n=1$ with $r=0$ or $r=1$ are covered by the same steps 2.1 through 5.1. Degenerate: the smoothness of $X$ is essential for claim 1 and is used through the critical-locus bound [F18] in step 2.1 and the submersion criterion [F20] in step 4.1; the constant cusp family $X=\operatorname{Spec}k[x,y,z]/(y^2-x^3)\to\mathbb A^1_k$, $(x,y,z)\mapsto z$, is a dominant morphism of irreducible classical varieties over $k$ to a smooth target whose every fibre is the singular cusp, so that no nonempty open $U$ has $f^{-1}(U)\to U$ smooth, as recorded on the counterexample page of this pair. The target $Y$ need not be smooth outside $Y_{\mathrm{reg}}$: for the fold $f\colon\mathbb A^1_k\to\mathbb A^1_k$, $t\mapsto t^2$, the differential vanishes at $0$, the fibre over $0$ is the non-reduced $\operatorname{Spec}k[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$, and $U=\mathbb A^1_k\setminus\{0\}$ is the best possible dense open, while the constant morphism $\mathbb A^1_k\to\mathbb A^1_k$ with value $0$ has $f^{-1}(U)=\varnothing$ for $U=\mathbb A^1_k\setminus\{0\}$; the fibres of step 5.1 are not asserted to be irreducible or connected. Endpoints: the statement has no interval parameter; the boundary $n=0$ versus $n\ge1$ is handled in step 2.1 through the convention $\dim\varnothing=-\infty\le-1$ of [F19] and the trivial lower bound in step 3.1, and the open sets $U,V$ are dense but need not be all of $Y$, as the fold example shows; the generic fibre dimension is constant over $V$ by construction and not merely bounded. Nonempty-choice: AC is declared as [F1] and enters exactly through the AC-assuming suppliers [F11] (density of the regular locus), [F12] (the classical regular-point tangent test), [F14] (regularity versus smoothness), [F18] (the critical-locus dimension bound), [F20] (the submersion criterion) [F26] (generic fibre dimension), and [F28] (closed-point density), cited at steps 1.3, 2.1, 3.1, 4.1 and 5.1; the finite-type verification of step 1.1, the fibre-product pasting and base-change smoothing of step 5.1, and the remaining linear algebra are choice-free, and no family of nonempty sets is selected anywhere. Biconditional directions: the statement asserts no equivalence, so the forward and reverse directions of a biconditional are not applicable; the two equivalences used in the proof — the submersion criterion [F20], applied in the direction "surjective differential at a classical point implies smoothness there" in step 4.1, and regularity-versus-smoothness [F14], applied in the direction "regular implies smooth" in step 1.3 for $Y_{\mathrm{reg}}$ — are used only in those directions, and no converse of the theorem is claimed.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] [[def-aqft-local-operator-and-dimension]]: finite-jet local operators have assigned engineering mass weight; in four dimensions a term $C\mathcal O_D/\Lambda^{D-4}$ has dimension four with dimensionless $C$.

proof_steps.claim: Each factor $\partial_\mu\phi$ has engineering dimension two, so $\mathcal O_8$ has dimension eight. It has four field factors, each differentiated once, and the contractions with $\eta$ make it a Lorentz scalar; the stipulated internal group is trivial. Thus it is an invariant member of the declared $r=1$, $q=4$, $D=8$ finite-jet data. The coefficient $C_8/\Lambda^4$ gives a dimension-four Lagrangian term, as required by [F2].

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F1] [[def-qftx-localized-equivariant-borel-moore-data]]: normalized equivariant Borel–Moore groups use the ordinary dualizing object without a quotient-stack shift, the smooth complex-oriented fundamental class has degree $2d$, and equivariant cohomology acts by cap product.

proof_steps.claim: The complex-oriented fundamental class has normalized Borel–Moore degree $4kN$. Capping it with $\mathcal E_{\widetilde m}$ of degree $4kN$ gives a degree-zero Borel–Moore class, so the stipulated localized proper trace has scalar coefficients in $S_{T_m}^{-1}R_{T_m}$.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] Proper equivariant pushforwards, restrictions to invariant opens, the support localization triangle, and coherent base change are available in the bounded constructible category. [[thm-constructible-six-functors-proper-base-change-and-verdier-duality]]

proof_steps.claim: The operations in the Definition are the proper pushforward, open restriction, and support maps of [F2]; the cap action is the action of Borel cohomology through $E_K\times_KX\to B_K$. For smooth pure complex dimension $d$, the normalized dualizing object restricts to $\mathbb Q_X[2d]$, so the complex orientation gives $[X]_T$ degree $2d$. These constructions respect the stable comparison of [F1].

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [A1] AC is inherited through the normalized equivariant Borel–Moore construction and its concentration supplier. [[def-qftx-localized-equivariant-borel-moore-data]] [[thm-qftx-finite-affine-atlas-bm-concentration]]

proof_steps.claim: By [F2], $i_*$ is an isomorphism in each degree after localization, so its inverse is a unique $S_T^{-1}R_T$-linear map. The proper inclusion $i$ and the proper map $p_F$ give the stated Borel–Moore pushforwards by [F1].

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F1] The normalized Borel–Moore groups, proper equivariant pushforwards, cap products, and fundamental classes use the preceding localized Borel–Moore definition. [[def-qftx-localized-equivariant-borel-moore-data]]

proof_steps.claim: By [F2], $i_*$ is an isomorphism in each degree after localization, so its inverse is a unique $S_T^{-1}R_T$-linear map. The proper inclusion $i$ and the proper map $p_F$ give the stated Borel–Moore pushforwards by [F1].

Composition of the inverse with $p_{F*}$ is therefore a well-defined degree-preserving map on the localized Borel–Moore groups. The insertion convention is well-defined because [F1] supplies the cap action and the smooth complex orientation gives $[X]_T$ degree $2d$. If $X\to\mathrm{pt}$ is proper, functoriality gives $p_{X*}=p_{F*}i_*$, so $p_*^{\mathrm{loc}}=p_{F*}i_*(i_*)^{-1}=p_{X*}$. If $F=\varnothing$, then $F\to\mathrm{pt}$ is proper and [F2] forces the localized groups of $X$ to be zero, so the defined trace is the zero map. For $r=0$, $T$ is trivial, $F=X$, $i$ is the identity, and the properness hypothesis makes this the usual proper pushforward.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] [[thm-adhm-fixed-point-instanton-count]]: the fixed points for $N=1,k=1$ are indexed by the one one-box partition, and their tangent character is computed from the ADHM deformation complex.

proof_steps.claim: There is exactly one partition of $k=1$ for $N=1$, namely $Y_1=\{(0,0)\}$, so [F2] gives the unique fixed point. Here $\mathbf V_{\vec Y}=e_1$ and $\mathbf W=e_1^{-1}$, whence $\mathbf V^\vee\mathbf V=1$, $\mathbf V^\vee\mathbf W^\vee=1$, and $t_1t_2\mathbf W\mathbf V=t_1t_2$. Substitution in the tangent character gives $t_1+t_2$; the two additive weights are $\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2$, so the Euler class is $\epsilon_1\epsilon_2$.

The degree-one coefficient is the sum over the single fixed point, so it equals $(\epsilon_1\epsilon_2)^{-1}$. This is a formal equivariant fixed-point contribution, not an asserted continuum path-integral value.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] [[thm-adhm-fixed-point-instanton-count]]: fixed points are indexed by two-tuples of partitions of total size one, and the tangent character is $\mathbf V^\vee\mathbf V(t_1+t_2-1-t_1t_2)+\mathbf V^\vee\mathbf W^\vee+t_1t_2\mathbf W\mathbf V$.

proof_steps.claim: A two-tuple of partitions with total size one places its single box in exactly one of the two colors, so the only possibilities are $(\{(0,0)\},\varnothing)$ and $(\varnothing,\{(0,0)\})$. Their quotient representatives have $V$-characters $e_1$ and $e_2$, respectively.

For the first point, the ADHM convention [F1] gives $\mathbf W=e_1^{-1}+e_2^{-1}$ and $\mathbf W^\vee=e_1+e_2$, while $\mathbf V=e_1$. Substitution in [F2] gives $$t_1+t_2+\frac{e_2}{e_1}+t_1t_2\frac{e_1}{e_2}.$$ The corresponding additive weights are $\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2,a_2-a_1,\epsilon_1+\epsilon_2+a_1-a_2$, so their product is $E_1$. Interchanging the two colors gives the second displayed character and $E_2$.

Each fixed-point contribution is the reciprocal of its Euler product, so the degree-one coefficient is $E_1^{-1}+E_2^{-1}$. The TikZ drawing only records the two one-box colorings and is not used in this calculation.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F1] [[def-aqft-scheme-and-wilson-coefficients]]: the coefficient space is $\mathbb C^N$, its realification $\rho_N$ is an isometry to $\mathbb R^{2N}$, and $t=\log(\mu/\mu_0)$ is dimensionless.

proof_steps.claim: For $\Delta=C-D\in\mathbb C^2$, the triangle inequality and $(a-b)^2\ge0$ for $a,b\ge0$ give $|{-}\Delta_1+\Delta_2|^2\le(|\Delta_1|+|\Delta_2|)^2\le2(|\Delta_1|^2+|\Delta_2|^2)$. Also $|{-}2\Delta_2|^2=4|\Delta_2|^2$. Adding these bounds gives $\|A\Delta\|_2^2\le2|\Delta_1|^2+6|\Delta_2|^2\le6\|\Delta\|_2^2$. The row $q=2$ gives the complex $H^2(\mathcal E(-3))\otimes\mathcal O(-1)\to H^2(\mathcal E\otimes\Omega_Z^2)\otimes\mathcal O\to H^2(\mathcal E\otimes\Omega_Z^1(-1))\otimes\mathcal O(1)$. All higher differentials vanish because all other rows are zero. Its only cohomology is the degree-zero hypercohomology of the diagonal resolution, namely $\mathcal E$; the first and last terms are exact because the other total degrees vanish. The maps are linear in the homogeneous output coordinates, since each Koszul differential is contraction with the universal linear section. Thus this is the stated monad; its cohomology vector spaces are canonical, and changing bases acts by $GL(U)\times GL(K)\times GL(U')$.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] For the standard projective cover and $k=0,-1,-r-1$, the actual analytic twisting sheaves have acyclic intersections; their analytic sheaf cohomology is the normally convergent Laurent–Čech complex. Uniqueness of Laurent coefficients forces every coefficient to vanish. Thus both degree-zero groups vanish.

A one-cochain on the two-chart overlap has a normally convergent Laurent expansion $g(t)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}a_nt^n$. Coboundaries subtract the entire $t$-series with $n\ge0$ and the series $t^{-k}f_\infty(1/t)$ with $n\le-k$. These two tails converge on their respective entire charts by [F2]; the cover is acyclic for both twists because $r=1$ and $k=1,2$. For $k=1$ they exhaust every integer exponent, so the analytic first cohomology is zero. For $k=2$ the sole remaining exponent is $n=-1$; its coefficient cannot be a coboundary, and it identifies the analytic first cohomology with $\mathbb C$.

proof_steps.claim: By [A1], a sheaf class has a global smooth closed representative $\alpha$. Its vertical restriction has harmonic part $s(x)\sigma_x$, where $s(x)=\int_{L_x}\iota_x(\alpha_V)$ componentwise in $E_x$. This is smooth by integration over compact fibres. Solve $\gamma_x=B(\alpha_V-s\sigma_x)$; then $\bar\partial_V\gamma_x=\alpha_V-s\sigma_x$. Step 2.1 makes $\gamma$ smooth. A change of unit quaternionic frame acts by an $SU(2)$ fibre isometry and a change of unitary $E$ frame acts by a matrix constant on each fibre; both preserve the equation. Uniqueness from $H^{0,0}(\mathcal O(-2))=0$ makes these local solutions agree. Hence $\gamma$ is global and $\alpha_H:=\alpha-s\sigma-\bar\partial_F\gamma$ annihilates vertical tangent, proving the asserted decomposition. The fixed-fibre $B=\bar\partial^*G$ construction and smooth-parameter difference-quotient argument in [F2], with the estimates [F5], make that primitive smooth over the base. The same fibrewise uniqueness makes it agree across frame and chart changes. Denote the horizontal correction by $\phi(s)$; then $\psi(s)=s\sigma+\phi(s)$ has zero mixed differential. If $s$ is the image of a closed representative $\alpha$, [F2]'s decomposition and closedness say that its horizontal remainder solves this same mixed equation. The difference is fibrewise holomorphic in $\mathcal O(-1)^{\oplus2}\otimes E_x$, hence zero by [F4]. Thus $\psi(s)=\alpha-\bar\partial_F\gamma$ is closed for a class image. The differential can still have a horizontal degree-two component for arbitrary $s$; the curvature component of the metric splitting is retained.

These local forms are regular on the complete projective fibre. For $w=1/t$, the horizontal vectors are $\widetilde H_i=wH_i$, $\widetilde\theta^i=w^{-1}\theta^i$, and $\widetilde e=w^2e$. By [F4] that difference is zero. This proves that the coordinate calculation computes the actual global correction, despite using a different horizontal splitting for its displayed coefficients.

The local expression equals the intrinsically constructed differential by step 3.1. The same construction and calculation apply in any stereographic chart with the unit round metric. Thus it patches smoothly across the base overlap and infinity; a chartwise solution satisfies the invariant operator equation globally. For the class image $s$, the residual vanishes by step 1.1, and the nonzero frame in step 5.1 gives $(\nabla_A^*\nabla_A+2)s=0$. More generally a connection-preserving smooth bundle map commutes with the componentwise vertical projection and inverse, and transports the unique mixed correction; thus the edge and residual construction are natural for such maps, including direct sums. S\otimes\mathcal O \arrow[r,"\beta"] \arrow[d,"H"] &

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F3] A closed subset and its open complement give the equivariant Borel–Moore long exact sequence through support localization. [[thm-constructible-six-functors-proper-base-change-and-verdier-duality]]

proof_steps.claim: The closed/open localization sequence for $i:F\hookrightarrow X$ and $X\setminus F$ contains $S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_{j+1}(X\setminus F)\to S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(F)\xrightarrow{i_*}S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(X)\to S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(X\setminus F)$. Both outside groups vanish by step 3.1, so $i_*$ is an isomorphism. If $F=\varnothing$, the same argument gives zero localized Borel–Moore homology for $X$; if $F=X$, $i_*$ is the identity. The proof used only the finite invariant affine cover and not Sumihiro's theorem or compactness.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F3] The preceding lemma supplies the exact P² diagonal monad and its framed vanishings under the stated cohomology/base-change assumptions; its algebraic/analytic family comparison uses the exact projective GAGA interface and the stated base-change hypotheses. [[lem-qftx-p2-beilinson-diagonal-and-framed-vanishing]]

proof_steps.claim: Conversely, let $\mathcal E$ be a framed torsion-free sheaf with the stated Hilbert polynomial. The preceding Beilinson lemma constructs its monad, with terms $V_1\mathcal O(-1)$, $M\mathcal O$, and $V_2\mathcal O(1)$ of ranks $k,2k+N,k$. Its restriction to $L_\infty$ remains exact at the ends because $\mathcal E$ is locally free there. Put $K=\ker\beta|_{L_\infty}$. The sequence $0\to V_1\mathcal O(-1)\to K\to W\mathcal O\to0$ splits since $\operatorname{Ext}^1(W\mathcal O,V_1\mathcal O(-1))=V_1\otimes W^*\otimes H^1(\mathcal O(-1))=0$.

The remaining line extension $0\to V_1\mathcal O(-1)\oplus W\mathcal O\to M\mathcal O\to V_2\mathcal O(1)\to0$ has class in $\operatorname{Hom}(V_2,V_1)\otimes H^1(\mathcal O(-2))$, since $H^1(\mathcal O(-1))=0$. Twist by $\mathcal O(-1)$ and take cohomology. The connecting map $V_2\to V_1\otimes H^1(\mathcal O(-2))$ is an isomorphism: the adjacent groups $H^0(\mathcal O(-1))$ and $H^1(\mathcal O(-1))$ vanish, while $H^1(\mathcal O(-2))\cong\mathbb C$. Thus $V_2$ is identified with $V_1$ by this canonical extension class. Choosing a basis of $V_1$ and using the fixed framed basis of $W$ identifies $M=V\oplus V\oplus W$ and the line maps with the two Euler blocks in the Statement. Any other such choice differs by one simultaneous element of $GL(V)$.

The remaining coefficients of the two linear maps are their $z_0$ coefficients, so write $\alpha=(z_0B_1-z_1,z_0B_2-z_2,z_0J)^T$ and $\beta=(-z_0C_1+z_2,z_0C_2-z_1,z_0I)$. The coefficients of $z_0z_1$ and $z_0z_2$ in $\beta\alpha=0$ force $C_1=B_2$ and $C_2=B_1$; the $z_0^2$ coefficient is then $[B_1,B_2]+IJ=0$. This recovers the stated ADHM form. The surjectivity of $\beta$ implies stability: if $U=\operatorname{span}\{B_{i_1}\cdots B_{i_m}I(W)\}$ were proper, it is invariant and the induced $B_1,B_2$ on $V/U$ commute because $[B_1,B_2]=-IJ$ has image in $U$. Their dual actions on the nonzero annihilator $U^\perp\subset V^*$ commute, so [F6] gives a common eigen-covector $\lambda\ne0$ with $\lambda I=0$. At the corresponding affine point, $\lambda\beta=0$, contradicting surjectivity.

The Beilinson construction is natural under framed sheaf isomorphisms, so an isomorphism of framed sheaves induces maps on the cohomology vector spaces used in steps 1.2–6.2 and hence a single change of basis $g\in GL(V)$; the normalized Euler blocks force the recovered tuples to differ by $g\cdot(B_1,B_2,I,J)$. Conversely such a $g$ is an isomorphism of monads acting trivially on $W$, and therefore induces a framed sheaf isomorphism. This proves the pointwise inverse equivalence modulo $GL(V)$. For a finite-type data family, step 2.1 makes $\beta$ surjective on the total space, so $K=\ker\beta$ is locally free. The sequence $0\to V\mathcal O(-1)\to K\to\mathcal E\to0$ is exact and its terms before $\mathcal E$ are flat over the base. After tensoring with any residue field of the base, the first map remains sheaf-injective by step 1.1; hence $\operatorname{Tor}_1(k(s),\mathcal E)=0$. Since $\mathcal E$ is finite over each local ring of $\mathbb P^2\times S$ and its residue fiber is a vector space over the residue field, [F8] gives flatness over $S$. Under the stated relative cohomology and base-change hypotheses, the same constructions use vector bundles and are inverse for families.

Apply the family equivalence to $S=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$. A first-order deformation of the ADHM data is $(\dot B_1,\dot B_2,\dot I,\dot J)$ satisfying $d\mu_{\mathbb C}=0$; infinitesimal changes of basis are $d_0(\xi)=([\xi,B_1],[\xi,B_2],\xi I,-J\xi)$. Differentiating the monad gives the chain perturbation $(\dot\alpha,\dot\beta)$ with $\beta\dot\alpha+\dot\beta\alpha=0$, and a change by $d_0(\xi)$ is the corresponding chain homotopy. Since the family construction and its inverse commute with this dual-number base change, they induce inverse linear maps on first-order framed deformations and on the quotient tangent spaces $\ker d_1/\operatorname{im}d_0$.

If $k=0$, $V=0$, all four maps and both equations are the unique zero-dimensional maps, stability and costability are vacuous, and the monad is $0\to W\mathcal O\to0$. Its middle cohomology is the framed bundle $W\mathcal O$ with Hilbert polynomial $N\binom{m+2}{2}$. Conversely, [F3] constructs this same zero-term monad from every framed sheaf with that polynomial, so the framing identifies each such sheaf with $W\mathcal O$. Thus both moduli spaces are points, and all empty-matrix and Euler-block conventions are satisfied.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [A1] Absolute projective GAGA supplies the exact coherent tensor equivalence and cohomology comparison. The relative-family comparison map is constructed in its current proof and is not a separate assumed theorem. [[thm-qftx-projective-gaga-for-monad-data]]

proof_steps.claim: For any Ward bundle use [F3] to form the analytic vector bundle H over a complex-open neighborhood U of every real line in G=Gr(2,4), with holomorphic evaluation p*H≅e*E on the universal family. On a graph chart X:A→B, incidence is (X,[λ])↦[λ,Xλ]. The distribution D=ker(de) consists of matrix variations v with vλ=0 and no λ variation. It is a holomorphic involutive rank-two subbundle, since it is tangent to the fibers of the submersion e. The restriction of p*Ω¹_U to D has kernel B*⊗O(-1) on each projective-line fiber and target D*≅O(1)². The O(-1) vanishings in [F3] give Ω¹_U≅p_*D*. Equivalently, on the graph chart a linear covector on Hom(A,B) restricts to a section on all kernels vλ=0; the map is injective because those kernels span Hom(A,B), and both coefficient spaces have dimension four. This gives the holomorphic sheaf isomorphism without any extra analytic base-change assumption.

The explicit incidence chart fixes vertical complex orientation followed by the positive base orientation to be the complex orientation of Z. The pullback of the positive point Thom class on S⁴ is the positive normal Thom class of its fiber CP¹; [F5] identifies its absolute class as the Poincaré dual of that fiber. A linear CP¹ has dual H²: H restricts with integral one to the line, and the integral projective cohomology ring gives H² as its positive degree-four generator. Hence π*u=H² for the positive generator u of H⁴(S⁴). Smooth evaluation gives E_twistor≅π*H, so c₂(E_twistor)=kH² is equivalent to c₂(H)[S⁴]=k. By [F4] this is q_N=-k; the same calculation verifies the forward map's charge clause. Framing is transported by evaluation at infinity. All constructions use incidence, evaluation and unique relative connections, so commute with the specified projective rotations and framing transformations. They therefore give the claimed T-equivariant bijection and all stated invariants, conditional on the exact absolute GAGA comparison [A1].

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [A2] Local coherent polydisc acyclicity: “Assume AC. Let $F$ be coherent analytic on a neighborhood of a point $x$ in $\mathbb C^N$. There is a coordinate polydisc $W$ about $x$ such that for every nonempty coordinate polydisc $D\subset W$ and every $q>0$, $H^q(D,F|_D)=0$. Scalar sheaf cohomology on such $D$ is computed by its smooth Dolbeault resolution. One can choose $W$ subordinate to a partial finite-rank free resolution of $F$ of length exceeding $2N$. The assertion is local in the supplied resolution neighborhood; no untwisted projective Cartan A/B or global Stein generation theorem is asserted.” ([[thm-qftx-gaga-analytic-local-coherent-polydisc-acyclicity]]). Only its positive-degree polydisc vanishing clause is used below.

proof_steps.claim: Suppose $1\le r\le3$ and fix $x\in P^r$. Apply [A1] to $\mathcal F$ at $x$ with length $2r$ to obtain a chart neighborhood $W_0$ with a partial free resolution. Its first relation kernel $K_0$ is coherent by [A1]. Apply [A1] again to $K_0$ at $x$ with length $2r$, and choose a neighborhood $W_1\subseteq W_0$ on which that kernel resolution is defined. Apply [A2] to $\mathcal F$ at $x$ to obtain a polydisc neighborhood $W_2$. Choose concentric coordinate polydiscs $D'_x\Subset D_x$ with $\overline{D_x}\subseteq W_1\cap W_2$. Then $D'_x$ is a neighborhood of $x$.

The sets $D'_x$ cover $P^r$. Compactness [F1] gives finitely many centers $x_1,\ldots,x_s$ whose smaller polydiscs still cover; set $U_i=D_{x_i}$ and $U'_i=D'_{x_i}$. Each singleton $U_i$ and $U'_i$ is $\mathcal F$-acyclic by [A2]. For every nonempty finite intersection of at least two of the $U_i$, the intersection lemma [F4] applies using the length-$2r$ resolution of $\mathcal F$ on the closure of any participating $U_i$. It also applies to the corresponding intersections of the $U'_i$, since their closures lie inside those same resolution neighborhoods. Thus both finite covers are acyclic for $\mathcal F$.

To compare two finite admissible covers, retain the given presentation $\pi_I$ on every nonempty intersection $U_I$ of either parent cover, and write $K_I=\ker\pi_I$; there are only finitely many such coherent kernels by [A1]. First shrink each parent cover to open sets $B_i$ with $\overline{B_i}\subset U_i$, still covering $P^r$: at every point choose a coordinate polydisc with compact closure in some parent member, take a finite subcover by compactness [F1], and for each parent member take the union of its finitely many assigned polydiscs. Do this for both parent covers. At a point $x$, repeat step 1.2 for $\mathcal F$ and its new presentation kernel. In addition, for every parent intersection $U_I$ containing $x$, use [A1] to choose a length-$2r$ resolution neighborhood of its particular kernel $K_I$. Intersect these finitely many neighborhoods. Choose nested polydiscs $D'_x\Subset D_x$ whose closures lie in this intersection and in one selected $B_i$ from each parent cover. Also choose $\overline{D_x}$ disjoint from every $\overline{B_j}$ whose parent $U_j$ does not contain $x$; those are finitely many closed sets missing $x$. Compactness gives a finite cover $\mathcal W$ by some of the $D'_x$, with the selected parent assignments. As in steps 1.2, 2.1 and 3.1, its intersections are $\mathcal F$-acyclic and have surjective finite-presentation section maps. Now take a nonempty refined intersection $T=D'_{x_0}\cap\cdots\cap D'_{x_k}$ and one parent cover. Let $I$ be its distinct assigned parent indices. Since $D'_{x_0}$ meets each selected $B_i$, the avoidance condition implies $x_0\in U_i$ for every $i\in I$. Hence the closure of $D'_{x_0}$ lies inside a resolution neighborhood for this very $K_I$. Applying [F4] to $K_I$ on $T$ gives $H^1(T,K_I)=0$, so [F9] proves surjectivity of the section map of the SAME parent presentation $\pi_I|_T$. Its section map on $U_I$ is surjective by parent admissibility. Moreover $\overline T$ is compact in $U_I$, since each refined polydisc has compact closure in its assigned parent. Thus [F5] applies to $\Gamma(U_I,\mathcal F)\to\Gamma(T,\mathcal F)$ using that common presentation. By [F3], the resulting target quotient topology agrees with the chosen one on $T$. This works for both parent covers and all tuples; no newly chosen presentation is substituted for a parent presentation without proving its section surjectivity.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F5] [[thm-acyclic-resolution-theorem-for-right-derived-functors]]: a sheaf resolution by acyclic sheaves computes the right-derived functors of global sections by its global-section complex.

proof_steps.claim: Let $D\subseteq W$ be a nonempty coordinate polydisc. By [F3], the smooth Dolbeault sequence on $D$ is an exact resolution of $\mathcal O_D$. Its terms are modules over the sheaf of smooth functions, so [F4] makes them acyclic; [F5] therefore identifies $H^q(D,\mathcal O_D)$ with the cohomology of the displayed global Dolbeault complex. By [F6] that global complex has zero cohomology in degrees $1\le q\le N$, and it is zero in degrees $q>N$. Hence $H^q(D,\mathcal O_D)=0$ for every $q>0$.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F9] Under DC and supplied projective-resolution data, a right module is flat exactly when its first Tor with every left module vanishes ([[thm-a-right-module-is-flat-exactly-when-tor-one-with-every-left-module-vanishes]]).

proof_steps.claim: AC implies DC: for a nonempty set $Y$ and a serial relation $R\subseteq Y\times Y$, the family of successor sets $\{\{z\in Y:yRz\}:y\in Y\}$ consists of nonempty sets. [A1] gives a choice function on this family; composing it with the successor-set map gives a self-map $s:Y\to Y$ with $yRs(y)$. For any prescribed $y_0$, [F10] gives the sequence $y_{k+1}=s(y_k)$. For any $A$-module $N$, let $F_0$ be free on its underlying set and let $\epsilon_0:F_0\twoheadrightarrow N$ send each standard basis vector to the element it names, using [F11]. A free module on any set is projective: given a surjection $E\twoheadrightarrow Q$ and a map from the free module to $Q$, [A1] chooses a preimage in $E$ for the image of each basis vector, and [F11] extends that assignment to a lift. Put $K_0=\ker\epsilon_0$; recursively, for each $j\ge0$, take $F_{j+1}$ free on the set $K_j$, let $\epsilon_{j+1}:F_{j+1}\twoheadrightarrow K_j$ send each basis vector to the element it names, and set $K_{j+1}=\ker\epsilon_{j+1}$. The differential $F_{j+1}\to F_j$ is $\epsilon_{j+1}$ followed by the inclusion $K_j\hookrightarrow F_j$. The sequence is exact by the definitions of the kernels, each $F_j$ is projective by the lifting argument, and [F10] supplies the recursion. Thus every $A$-module has the projective-resolution data required by [F8] and [F9], and AC supplies their DC hypothesis.

Put $C=B/A$, which is defined because step 2.1 proves $A\hookrightarrow B$. For any left $A$-module $M$, apply [F8] under the DC and resolution construction in step 1.1 to the short exact sequence of right $A$-modules $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$. The long exact sequence gives $\operatorname{Tor}_1^A(A,M)\to\operatorname{Tor}_1^A(B,M)\to\operatorname{Tor}_1^A(C,M)\to A\otimes_A M\to B\otimes_A M$. The first two Tor groups vanish: $A$ is free over itself and $B$ is flat by step 2.2. The final map is injective by step 3.2, so exactness forces $\operatorname{Tor}_1^A(C,M)=0$ for every $M$. By [F9], $C=B/A$ is a flat $A$-module.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F7] An exact resolution by $\Gamma$-acyclic objects computes the right-derived functor when the initial object and every resolution cycle lie in the domain of the supplied injective-resolution data; DC is the choice hypothesis ([[thm-acyclic-resolution-theorem-for-right-derived-functors]]).

proof_steps.claim: Every cycle in the exact resolution of step 2.1 is an abelian sheaf on $X$, so it lies in the all-abelian-sheaves domain of the injective-resolution datum in [F8]. By [F9], full AC [A1] supplies the DC required by the acyclic-resolution theorem [F7]. Applying [F7] to that resolution and the global-sections functor gives, canonically, $H^q(X,\mathcal O(E))\cong H^q(\Gamma(X,\mathcal A^{0,\bullet}(E)))=H^q_{\bar\partial}(X,E)$ for every $q\ge0$.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F10] [[def-cohomological-delta-functor]], [[thm-right-derived-functors-form-a-cohomological-delta-functor]], and [[thm-derived-functors-are-universal-delta-functors]]: under DC, the right derived functors of the additive left exact global-sections functor form a universal cohomological delta functor; full AC supplies DC.

proof_steps.claim: By [F10], $H^\bullet(X,-)$ is universal, and by [F11] so is $\check H^\bullet(X,-)$. Their degree-zero identifications with $\Gamma(X,-)$ agree by [F9], so [F11] gives a unique natural isomorphism $\check H^q(X,\mathcal F)\cong H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ in every degree. The canonical fixed-cover Čech-to-derived maps are compatible with refinement by [F8]; their connecting-map compatibility is the same lift-and-differentiate construction $u(a)=db$ in step 2.1, computed in a resolution. They therefore induce a morphism of delta functors with this degree-zero identity, so universality identifies their limit with this unique isomorphism. This is the asserted canonical comparison. Full AC supplies DC for [F10] and the choices in step 1.1; no compact-support cohomology is used.

final_edge_fact_uses.text:
[A1] Under full AC, the batch-67 scalar cohomology theorem states
$H^0(\mathbb P^r,\mathcal O)=\mathbb C$ and
$H^q(\mathbb P^r,\mathcal O)=0$ for $q>0$ for $0\le r\le3$.
[[thm-qftx-gaga-analytic-projective-dolbeault-scalar-cohomology]]

proof_steps.claim: First the holomorphic monad maps have homogeneous linear entries. Indeed, in the $m=1$ sequence of [F10], $H^1(\mathbb P^r,\mathcal O)=0$ by [A1], so restriction $H^0(\mathbb P^r,\mathcal O(1))\to H^0(\mathbb P^{r-1},\mathcal O(1))$ is surjective and its kernel is the defining hyperplane coordinate times $H^0(\mathcal O)=\mathbb C$. Starting with $r=0$, where $\mathcal O(1)$ on a point has one-dimensional section space, induction shows that every section is a linear combination of the homogeneous coordinates: subtract the global coordinate lifts of its restriction, then the remaining section is a constant multiple of the defining coordinate. This applies to entries of both $\operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal O(-1),\mathcal O)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal O,\mathcal O(1))$. Thus no algebraic/analytic comparison is needed to introduce their four coefficient maps. By [A1] and [F9], the hyperplane sequences and analytic scalar theorem give exactly the negative-twist vanishings required by [F1]. Apply [F1] to the pairing isomorphism; it gives the unique constant Hermitian lift $H$ with the signed identities there. Thus no algebraic cohomology group is being substituted for the analytic lifting groups.

For the algebraic $\mathbb P^3_A=\operatorname{Proj}A[\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\mu_1,\mu_2]$ family category, [F11] directly supplies the needed $\mathcal O(-1)$ and $\mathcal O(-2)$ groups over $A$ and $H^0(\mathcal O_A)=A$. Separately, on the analytic first-order thickening each twist has the split underlying analytic sheaf $\mathcal O_A(d)=\mathcal O(d)\oplus\epsilon\mathcal O(d)$; finite direct sums commute with sheaf cohomology, so [F9] gives the same vanishings there. Thus a holomorphic family pairing can be lifted analytically, whereas algebraic family sheaves use [F11]; neither computation substitutes algebraic cohomology for an analytic group or invokes GAGA. Both yield constant $A$-valued chain maps. In both categories the two kernel/image sequences identify global sections with the same constant coefficient kernel of $\beta_A$, so the specified global-section base-change condition is respected by this identification. Repeating the obstruction and ambiguity calculation of [F1] over these coefficient modules lifts the family pairing uniquely to an $A$-linear constant chain isomorphism with Hermitian middle matrix $H_A$; its inverse exists because its reduction is invertible. Global section base change identifies $H^0(F_A)$ with the constant coefficient kernel $L_A$ in $S_A$. Its reduction is injective, so a full-rank minor is a unit and $L_A$ is a direct summand.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F5] Under AC, ringed-space module sheaves have enough injectives; their injective resolutions are flasque, flasque restrictions are cohomologically acyclic, and the acyclic-resolution theorem applies under DC, which follows from AC. Cohomology sheaves are sheafifications of presheaf cohomology. [[lem-ringed-space-module-sheaves-enough-injectives]], [[thm-flasque-sheaves-acyclic]], [[thm-acyclic-resolution-theorem-for-right-derived-functors]], [[lem-image-sheaf-is-sheafification-presheaf-image]], [[thm-sheafification-universal-property]], [[def-higher-direct-image-sheaf]], [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]

proof_steps.claim: At a complex point, coherent algebraic and analytic modules are finite-dimensional complex vector spaces, so the absolute assertions hold in dimension zero. Flatness in [A1] makes analytification exact stalkwise, including for nonreduced finite-type schemes. Tensor associativity gives tensor compatibility and compatibility with quotient restriction to a hyperplane. A finite algebraic presentation analytifies to a finite analytic presentation, so [A3] ensures its cokernel is coherent. For a closed analytic embedding, direct image is exact on stalks and preserves flabby sheaves: its sections over an open are the original sections over the intersection with the closed subspace. Pushing forward a flabby resolution therefore identifies cohomology on the closed subspace and its direct image. These facts apply to the hyperplane sequences below.

For finitely presented algebraic $\mathcal F$, a finite presentation computes the sheaf $\mathcal H om(\mathcal F,\mathcal G)$ as a kernel between finite powers of $\mathcal G$. Exact analytification and [A3] therefore identify its analytification with analytic $\mathcal H om(\mathcal F^{an},\mathcal G^{an})$. Step 4.1 in degree zero identifies morphisms. A finite locally free resolution of $\mathcal F$ computes global $\operatorname{Ext}^q$ by the hypercohomology of its Hom complex: locally free Hom is exact, and an injective resolution gives the resulting double-complex comparison. Termwise cohomology comparison and finiteness of the resolution identify algebraic and analytic Ext in every degree. Thus full faithfulness and cohomology/Ext comparison in dimension $r$ are proved before essential surjectivity.

To complete the family comparison after the absolute equivalence of step 9.1, first establish the local-section formula: for any morphism of ringed spaces $f:Y\to B$ and module sheaf $M$, take the module-injective resolution from [F5]. Each term is flasque, its restriction to $f^{-1}U$ is flasque for every open $U\subset B$, and hence its sections there compute $H^q(f^{-1}U,M)$ by the acyclic-resolution theorem. The cohomology sheaf of $f_*I^\bullet$ is the sheafification of its presheaf cohomology: kernels are computed on opens, image sheaves are the sheafifications of presheaf images, and the assertion follows on stalks by exactness of filtered colimits. Thus $R^qf_*M=(U\mapsto H^q(f^{-1}U,M))^\#$, compatibly with restrictions and scalar multiplication. This argument covers analytic ringed spaces as well as schemes.

Write $Y=X\times S$ and let $\eta_Y:Y^{an}\to Y$, $\eta_S:S^{an}\to S$ be analytification maps. For every algebraic open $U\subset S$, [F6] gives $H^q(p^{-1}U,\mathcal E)\to H^q((p^{an})^{-1}\eta_S^{-1}U,\mathcal E^{an})$. Composing with the presheaf-to-sheaf map of step 10.1, then sheafifying on $S$, gives the $\mathcal O_S$-linear map $R^qp_*\mathcal E\to\eta_{S*}R^qp^{an}_*\mathcal E^{an}$. Pull back and tensor with $\mathcal O_{S^{an}}$ to obtain $c_q:(R^qp_*\mathcal E)^{an}\to R^qp^{an}_*\mathcal E^{an}$; explicitly $a\otimes[\xi]$ maps to $a$ times the analytically pulled-back germ of $\xi$. Tensor balancing proves well-definedness. This constructs an actual comparison morphism without assuming its invertibility or a relative-GAGA theorem.

For an algebraic finite-type base map $S'\to S$, apply the same class-pullback construction to the pulled-back family. Tensor associativity identifies its analytification with the analytic pullback family. The square of the two comparison morphisms and the algebraic and analytic base-change maps commutes, since all maps pull back the same local cohomology classes and [F6] respects compositions. Whenever both families satisfy the Statement's locally-free and fiber-base-change hypotheses, step 12.1 makes their comparison morphisms invertible, so it identifies their base-change maps. This proves the complete stated family range, including the closed-fiber maps, without asserting arbitrary analytic-family algebraization. Full AC is inherited through [F1] and the resolution construction [F5]. The exact analytic suppliers [A1], [A3]–[A5] remain prerequisite proof obligations until their actual carriers are checked; the internal Serre argument above does not certify them.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F4] Proper pushforward is functorial, closed inclusions are proper, and cap product with an equivariant cohomology class sends $[X]_T$ to Borel–Moore degree $2d-q$. [[def-qftx-localized-equivariant-borel-moore-data]]

proof_steps.claim: Let $f:X\to Y$ be a proper $T$-equivariant map between smooth separated finite-type varieties with finite invariant affine covers and proper fixed loci $F_X,F_Y$. Its restriction $f^T:F_X\to F_Y$ is proper, and the square formed by $i_X,i_Y,f^T,f$ commutes because $f$ sends fixed points to fixed points. Functoriality of proper Borel–Moore pushforward gives $f_*i_{X*}=i_{Y*}f^T_*$. After localization both $i_{X*}$ and $i_{Y*}$ are isomorphisms by [F2], so applying their inverses and then the proper traces proves $p_{Y*}^{\mathrm{loc}}f_*=p_{X*}^{\mathrm{loc}}$. If $X\to\mathrm{pt}$ itself is proper, then $p_{F*}=p_{X*}i_*$; composing with $i_*^{-1}$ proves $p_*^{\mathrm{loc}}=p_{X*}$.

Let $ eta=(i_*)^{-1}(\alpha\cap[X]_T)$. On each component, the complex orientation and refined Gysin map give $i_a^!(\alpha\cap[X]_T)=i_a^*\alpha\cap[F_a]_T$. Since $\alpha\cap[X]_T=i_* eta$, the self-intersection formula [F3] gives $e_T(
u_a)\cap eta_a=i_a^*\alpha\cap[F_a]_T$. Properness of $F_a$ makes $e_T(
u_a)$ invertible after localization by [F3], hence $ eta_a=(i_a^*\alpha/e_T(
u_a))\cap[F_a]_T$. Applying $p_{a*}$ and summing the finitely many components yields the displayed formula. The degree is $2d-q$: division by the degree-$2c_a$ Euler class lowers the localized cohomological degree of the insertion from $q$ to $q-2c_a$, and capping with the degree-$2d_a$ fundamental class gives $2d_a-(q-2c_a)=2d-q$.

fact_uses.text: [L2] The meet $B\wedge C$ is represented by the pullback of $b$ and $c$ ([[thm-the-meet-of-subobjects-is-their-pullback]]).

proof_steps.claim: To prove the converse, assume $B\nleq C$. By [L2], let $p:P\rightarrowtail B$ be the pullback subobject of $b$ and $c$. If $p$ were epic, then [L3] would make it an isomorphism, forcing $b$ to factor through $c$. So $p$ is not epic.

The morphisms $q$ and $0_{B,Q}$ are therefore distinct, so [L1] gives some $u:G\to B$ with $q u\ne0$. If $b u$ factored through $c$, the pullback property in [L2] would force $u$ to factor through $p$, hence $q u=0$, impossible. Thus $b u:G\to A$ factors through $B$ but not through $C$.

fact_uses.text: [L4] The meet of two subobjects is represented by their pullback, and the image of a morphism is the least subobject through which that morphism factors ([[thm-the-meet-of-subobjects-is-their-pullback]], [[thm-the-image-is-the-least-subobject-through-which-a-morphism-factors]]).

proof_steps.claim: Conversely, assume every filtered colimit functor is exact. Let $I$ be a small directed poset indexing a family of monomorphisms $b_i:B_i\rightarrowtail A$, and let $c:C\rightarrowtail A$ represent a fixed subobject of $A$. For each $i\in I$, form the pullback square ```tikzcd P_i \arrow[r] \arrow[d] & C \arrow[d, "c"] \\ B_i \arrow[r, "b_i"'] & A. ``` By [L4], the top-left leg represents $B_i\wedge C$. These pullback squares assemble into a diagram in $\mathcal A^I$. Because the filtered colimit functor $\operatorname*{colim}_I$ is exact, [L2] and [L3] say that it preserves finite limits, so its colimit square ```tikzcd P \arrow[r] \arrow[d] & C \arrow[d, "c"] \\ B \arrow[r, "b"'] & A ``` is again a pullback.

The same argument inside $C$ shows that the image of $P\to C$ is $\bigvee_i(B_i\wedge C)$.

Because the square of step 1.2 is a pullback, [L4] identifies the image of $P\to C$ with the meet of the subobject represented by $\operatorname{im}(b)$ and the fixed subobject $C$. Using step 2.1, this gives $$\left(\bigvee_i B_i\right)\wedge C=\bigvee_i(B_i\wedge C),$$ which is exactly AB5 by [L1].

Those lines form a nonempty complex-open subset of the line family of $P$. Choose affine coordinates $(x,y)$ with the original line given by $y=0$. This open family contains the projective lines $y=b$ for all sufficiently small complex $b$, so their union contains a nonempty open subset of $P$. A section of $\mathcal E(-2)|_P$ vanishes on each such line because $H^0(\mathbb P^1,\mathcal O(-2)^{\oplus N})=0$. It therefore vanishes on that open subset. final_edge_fact_uses.text: [A3] Local coherent polydisc acyclicity: “Assume AC. Let $F$ be coherent analytic on a neighborhood of a point $x$ in $\mathbb C^N$. proof_steps.claim: Let two finite presentations be given near a point $x$, with coherent relation kernels $K,K'$ by [A2]. Apply [A3] to both kernels and intersect the resulting polydisc neighborhoods with the presentation neighborhoods. On a sufficiently small coordinate polydisc $D$ in this intersection, $H^1(D,K)=H^1(D,K')=0$. The long exact sequence [F5] for each presentation then proves that both section maps on $D$ are surjective. More generally, on any common open set $W$ where both presentations are defined and their section maps are surjective, lift the images of the finitely many basis sections of the first free module through the second section surjection. These lifts form a holomorphic matrix $A$ on $W$ with $\pi'A=\pi$. Multiplication by $A$ is continuous for compact-convergence because its entries are bounded on compact subsets; it induces the identity continuously between the quotient topologies. Reversing the presentations gives the reverse continuous identity. Thus the quotient topologies agree on each common presentation neighborhood. A holomorphic change of chart preserves compact-convergence because it and its inverse send compact subsets to compact subsets.

proof_steps.claim: For $g\in GL(V)$ put $x'=g\cdot x$ and $M(g)^2=\sum_i\|B_i'\|^2+\|I'\|^2+\|J'\|^2$. A fixed word frame $C(x)$ exists by [F2]. Each column of $gC(x)=C(x')$ is a product of at most $k-1$ matrices $B_i'$ followed by $I'$ on a unit framing vector. Submultiplicativity and operator norm bounded by Frobenius norm give $\|g\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le A_x(1+M(g))^k$ for $A_x=\sqrt{k}\|C(x)^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. If $x$ is costable, the rows consisting of coordinate rows of $JB_{i_1}\cdots B_{i_m}$ span $V^*$: their common annihilator is the largest common $B_i$-invariant subspace in $\ker J$, hence zero. The same finite dimension-growth argument as for columns gives a row basis $D(x)$ using words of length at most $k-1$. Since $D(x')=D(x)g^{-1}$, the identical norm estimate gives $\|g^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le A_x'(1+M(g))^k$. This also proves costability is open, since it is covered by the nonvanishing determinants of finitely many such row frames.

Diagonalize $H$ by [F4], with real eigenvalues $\lambda_i$. Along the preceding path the squared $B_i'$ entries have factors $e^{2t(\lambda_a-\lambda_b)}$, the squared $I'$ entries have $e^{2t\lambda_a}$ and the squared $J'$ entries have $e^{-2t\lambda_a}$. The log determinant is affine in $t$. Hence $F_\zeta''$ is a sum of $4w^2|z|^2e^{2tw}$ over those entries and their listed weights $w$, and is nonnegative. It can vanish only when $[H,B_i']=0$, $HI'=0$ and $J'H=0$. Stability of $x'$ then forces $H=0$, by applying $H$ to all spanning word vectors. Thus the path is strictly convex for every nonzero $H$. Given two critical matrices $g_1,g_2$, diagonalize the positive matrix $(g_2g_1^{-1})^\dagger(g_2g_1^{-1})$ and take the positive logarithms of its eigenvalues to write $g_2g_1^{-1}=u e^H$ with $u$ unitary and $H$ Hermitian. The endpoints of $e^{tH}g_1$ are both critical, after removing $u$ by invariance. Strict convexity forces $H=0$, so $g_2=ug_1$. This proves uniqueness of the unitary orbit at either level.

At a balanced datum $x$, let $L_x:\operatorname{Herm}(V)\to\operatorname{Herm}(V)$ be $H\mapsto\frac{d}{dt}\mu_{\mathbb R}(e^{tH}\cdot x)|_{t=0}$. Step 4.1 gives $2\operatorname{tr}(H L_xH)=F_\zeta''(e^{tH})|_{t=0}>0$ for nonzero $H$, so $L_x$ is injective and hence invertible in finite equal dimensions. The map $(H,y)\mapsto\mu_{\mathbb R}(e^H\cdot y)-\zeta I$ is smooth. To see smoothness of the exponential in the matrix entries directly, differentiate its absolutely convergent power series: on a bounded matrix set, an order-$r$ derivative of its degree-$m$ term is bounded by a constant times $m^r R^{m-r}/m!$, a summable majorant; this applies through real block matrices as in [F4]. By [F5] the balancing $H=H(y)$ is locally $C^r$ for every finite $r$, and uniqueness glues these branches to the same smooth map. The same invertible derivative along the Hermitian gauge directions in $T_xX^s$ proves that the real-level locus is a smooth submanifold. The unitary group is compact (closed bounded matrices), its action there is free by [F2] and proper (inverse images are closed subsets of $U(V)$ times a compact coordinate projection); therefore its quotient is smooth by [F6]. The map to the complex quotient is smooth using local submersion sections in [F6]. On any word-frame chart [F2], the local balancing map just constructed, followed by the unitary quotient map, is its smooth inverse; step 4.1 proves independence of all choices. Thus the bijections are diffeomorphisms. The compact torus commutes with gauge actions and preserves both the complex equation and $\mu_{\mathbb R}$, so the bijections are equivariant. For $k=0$ all matrices and equations are empty and all quotients are points, proving every boundary case stated. No sheaf or ASD identification was used.

proof_steps.claim: The closed/open localization sequence for $i:F\hookrightarrow X$ and $X\setminus F$ contains $S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_{j+1}(X\setminus F)\to S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(F)\xrightarrow{i_*}S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(X)\to S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(X\setminus F)$. proof_steps.claim: Conversely, let $\mathcal E$ be a framed torsion-free sheaf with the stated Hilbert polynomial. The preceding Beilinson lemma constructs its monad, with terms $V_1\mathcal O(-1)$, $M\mathcal O$, and $V_2\mathcal O(1)$ of ranks $k,2k+N,k$. Its restriction to $L_\infty$ remains exact at the ends because $\mathcal E$ is locally free there. Put $K=\ker\beta|_{L_\infty}$. The sequence $0\to V_1\mathcal O(-1)\to K\to W\mathcal O\to0$ splits since $\operatorname{Ext}^1(W\mathcal O,V_1\mathcal O(-1))=V_1\otimes W^*\otimes H^1(\mathcal O(-1))=0$.

The remaining line extension $0\to V_1\mathcal O(-1)\oplus W\mathcal O\to M\mathcal O\to V_2\mathcal O(1)\to0$ has class in $\operatorname{Hom}(V_2,V_1)\otimes H^1(\mathcal O(-2))$, since $H^1(\mathcal O(-1))=0$. Twist by $\mathcal O(-1)$ and take cohomology. The connecting map $V_2\to V_1\otimes H^1(\mathcal O(-2))$ is an isomorphism: the adjacent groups $H^0(\mathcal O(-1))$ and $H^1(\mathcal O(-1))$ vanish, while $H^1(\mathcal O(-2))\cong\mathbb C$. Thus $V_2$ is identified with $V_1$ by this canonical extension class. Choosing a basis of $V_1$ and using the fixed framed basis of $W$ identifies $M=V\oplus V\oplus W$ and the line maps with the two Euler blocks in the Statement. Any other such choice differs by one simultaneous element of $GL(V)$.

On $L_\infty$, the complex is $0\to V\mathcal O_{L_\infty}(-1)\xrightarrow{(-z_1,-z_2,0)^T}(V\oplus V\oplus W)\mathcal O_{L_\infty}\xrightarrow{(z_2,-z_1,0)}V\mathcal O_{L_\infty}(1)\to0$. The first two $V$ summands form the Euler resolution of the zero sheaf on the line, while the $W$ summand passes unchanged to middle cohomology. The framing is therefore the canonical identification $\mathcal E|_{L_\infty}=W\otimes\mathcal O_{L_\infty}$. In the Grothendieck group, the monad gives $[\mathcal E]=[(V\oplus V\oplus W)\mathcal O]-[V\mathcal O(-1)]-[V\mathcal O(1)]$. Taking Euler characteristics after twisting by $\mathcal O(m)$ and using $\chi(\mathcal O(d))=\binom{d+2}{2}$ yields $\chi(\mathcal E(m))=N\binom{m+2}{2}-k$.

If $k=0$, $V=0$, all four maps and both equations are the unique zero-dimensional maps, stability and costability are vacuous, and the monad is $0\to W\mathcal O\to0$. Its middle cohomology is the framed bundle $W\mathcal O$ with Hilbert polynomial $N\binom{m+2}{2}$. Conversely, [F3] constructs this same zero-term monad from every framed sheaf with that polynomial, so the framing identifies each such sheaf with $W\mathcal O$. Thus both moduli spaces are points, and all empty-matrix and Euler-block conventions are satisfied.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [A1] Absolute projective GAGA supplies the exact coherent tensor equivalence and cohomology comparison. The relative-family comparison map is constructed in its current proof and is not a separate assumed theorem. [[thm-qftx-projective-gaga-for-monad-data]]

proof_steps.claim: For any Ward bundle use [F3] to form the analytic vector bundle H over a complex-open neighborhood U of every real line in G=Gr(2,4), with holomorphic evaluation p*H≅e*E on the universal family. On a graph chart X:A→B, incidence is (X,[λ])↦[λ,Xλ]. The distribution D=ker(de) consists of matrix variations v with vλ=0 and no λ variation. It is a holomorphic involutive rank-two subbundle, since it is tangent to the fibers of the submersion e. The restriction of p*Ω¹_U to D has kernel B*⊗O(-1) on each projective-line fiber and target D*≅O(1)². The O(-1) vanishings in [F3] give Ω¹_U≅p_*D*. Equivalently, on the graph chart a linear covector on Hom(A,B) restricts to a section on all kernels vλ=0; the map is injective because those kernels span Hom(A,B), and both coefficient spaces have dimension four. This gives the holomorphic sheaf isomorphism without any extra analytic base-change assumption.

The explicit incidence chart fixes vertical complex orientation followed by the positive base orientation to be the complex orientation of Z. The pullback of the positive point Thom class on S⁴ is the positive normal Thom class of its fiber CP¹; [F5] identifies its absolute class as the Poincaré dual of that fiber. A linear CP¹ has dual H²: H restricts with integral one to the line, and the integral projective cohomology ring gives H² as its positive degree-four generator. Hence π*u=H² for the positive generator u of H⁴(S⁴). Smooth evaluation gives E_twistor≅π*H, so c₂(E_twistor)=kH² is equivalent to c₂(H)[S⁴]=k. By [F4] this is q_N=-k; the same calculation verifies the forward map's charge clause. Framing is transported by evaluation at infinity. All constructions use incidence, evaluation and unique relative connections, so commute with the specified projective rotations and framing transformations. They therefore give the claimed T-equivariant bijection and all stated invariants, conditional on the exact absolute GAGA comparison [A1].

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [A2] Local coherent polydisc acyclicity: “Assume AC. Let $F$ be coherent analytic on a neighborhood of a point $x$ in $\mathbb C^N$. There is a coordinate polydisc $W$ about $x$ such that for every nonempty coordinate polydisc $D\subset W$ and every $q>0$, $H^q(D,F|_D)=0$. Scalar sheaf cohomology on such $D$ is computed by its smooth Dolbeault resolution. One can choose $W$ subordinate to a partial finite-rank free resolution of $F$ of length exceeding $2N$. The assertion is local in the supplied resolution neighborhood; no untwisted projective Cartan A/B or global Stein generation theorem is asserted.” ([[thm-qftx-gaga-analytic-local-coherent-polydisc-acyclicity]]). Only its positive-degree polydisc vanishing clause is used below.

proof_steps.claim: Suppose $1\le r\le3$ and fix $x\in P^r$. Apply [A1] to $\mathcal F$ at $x$ with length $2r$ to obtain a chart neighborhood $W_0$ with a partial free resolution. Its first relation kernel $K_0$ is coherent by [A1]. Apply [A1] again to $K_0$ at $x$ with length $2r$, and choose a neighborhood $W_1\subseteq W_0$ on which that kernel resolution is defined. Apply [A2] to $\mathcal F$ at $x$ to obtain a polydisc neighborhood $W_2$. Choose concentric coordinate polydiscs $D'_x\Subset D_x$ with $\overline{D_x}\subseteq W_1\cap W_2$. Then $D'_x$ is a neighborhood of $x$.

The sets $D'_x$ cover $P^r$. Compactness [F1] gives finitely many centers $x_1,\ldots,x_s$ whose smaller polydiscs still cover; set $U_i=D_{x_i}$ and $U'_i=D'_{x_i}$. Each singleton $U_i$ and $U'_i$ is $\mathcal F$-acyclic by [A2]. For every nonempty finite intersection of at least two of the $U_i$, the intersection lemma [F4] applies using the length-$2r$ resolution of $\mathcal F$ on the closure of any participating $U_i$. It also applies to the corresponding intersections of the $U'_i$, since their closures lie inside those same resolution neighborhoods. Thus both finite covers are acyclic for $\mathcal F$.

To compare two finite admissible covers, retain the given presentation $\pi_I$ on every nonempty intersection $U_I$ of either parent cover, and write $K_I=\ker\pi_I$; there are only finitely many such coherent kernels by [A1]. First shrink each parent cover to open sets $B_i$ with $\overline{B_i}\subset U_i$, still covering $P^r$: at every point choose a coordinate polydisc with compact closure in some parent member, take a finite subcover by compactness [F1], and for each parent member take the union of its finitely many assigned polydiscs. Do this for both parent covers. At a point $x$, repeat step 1.2 for $\mathcal F$ and its new presentation kernel. In addition, for every parent intersection $U_I$ containing $x$, use [A1] to choose a length-$2r$ resolution neighborhood of its particular kernel $K_I$. Intersect these finitely many neighborhoods. Choose nested polydiscs $D'_x\Subset D_x$ whose closures lie in this intersection and in one selected $B_i$ from each parent cover. Also choose $\overline{D_x}$ disjoint from every $\overline{B_j}$ whose parent $U_j$ does not contain $x$; those are finitely many closed sets missing $x$. Compactness gives a finite cover $\mathcal W$ by some of the $D'_x$, with the selected parent assignments. As in steps 1.2, 2.1 and 3.1, its intersections are $\mathcal F$-acyclic and have surjective finite-presentation section maps. Now take a nonempty refined intersection $T=D'_{x_0}\cap\cdots\cap D'_{x_k}$ and one parent cover. Let $I$ be its distinct assigned parent indices. Since $D'_{x_0}$ meets each selected $B_i$, the avoidance condition implies $x_0\in U_i$ for every $i\in I$. Hence the closure of $D'_{x_0}$ lies inside a resolution neighborhood for this very $K_I$. Applying [F4] to $K_I$ on $T$ gives $H^1(T,K_I)=0$, so [F9] proves surjectivity of the section map of the SAME parent presentation $\pi_I|_T$. Its section map on $U_I$ is surjective by parent admissibility. Moreover $\overline T$ is compact in $U_I$, since each refined polydisc has compact closure in its assigned parent. Thus [F5] applies to $\Gamma(U_I,\mathcal F)\to\Gamma(T,\mathcal F)$ using that common presentation. By [F3], the resulting target quotient topology agrees with the chosen one on $T$. This works for both parent covers and all tuples; no newly chosen presentation is substituted for a parent presentation without proving its section surjectivity.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F4] [[thm-smooth-function-module-sheaves-are-acyclic]]: sheaves of modules over the smooth-function sheaf on a smooth manifold are acyclic for global sections.

proof_steps.claim: Let $D\subseteq W$ be a nonempty coordinate polydisc. By [F3], the smooth Dolbeault sequence on $D$ is an exact resolution of $\mathcal O_D$. Its terms are modules over the sheaf of smooth functions, so [F4] makes them acyclic; [F5] therefore identifies $H^q(D,\mathcal O_D)$ with the cohomology of the displayed global Dolbeault complex. By [F6] that global complex has zero cohomology in degrees $1\le q\le N$, and it is zero in degrees $q>N$. Hence $H^q(D,\mathcal O_D)=0$ for every $q>0$.
